_note: by_crop_type is the colour-AGNOSTIC mechanic and must never name the colour a cultivar ripens to (16 of 41 live tomato cultivars do not ripen red). by_cultivar carries the colour sequence. `gives` is a consequence, never a permission — see the module header. `detail` is guide-only and is NOT rendered on the planting card.

pepper.window_label: correct mature green → first colour break → the cultivar's own final ripe colour

window.look: full size for that cultivar, skin glossy and taut, and — the actual test — fully developed, firm and crisp when you squeeze it. A mature pod detaches easily from the plant; an immature one clings. For flat-podded chile types, mature also means filled out and thick-fleshed with a blunt rather than soft tip. If a pod is still lengthening, it is not there yet: wait until growth stops, then give it another week or so
window.gives: the firmest wall and best structural texture of the whole window — the stage for stuffing, pickling, roast-and-peel and anything that has to hold its shape. Flavour is at its most vegetal and least sweet here.

window.look: streaks, blotches or a blush of the ripe colour appearing on a still-mostly-green pod (in New Mexican chile this part-coloured state is called the pinto stage)
window.gives: cooks essentially as a green pod with the first ripening sugars behind it, so slightly rounder and less grassy. It is also the readable field cue that the rest of your green crop is at peak mature-green quality — colour break in the row means pick green now if green is what you want.

window.look: the cultivar's own finished colour carried evenly over the pod — which may be red, or yellow, gold, orange, brown or purple depending on the variety, and some varieties stop at a colour that is not red at all. The wall softens noticeably as it colours
window.gives: the sweetest state of that pod: ripening builds sugar, so a coloured pod is sweeter than the same pod picked green, and carotenoid pigments develop. In exchange the flesh goes softer, which costs you stuffing and pickling texture. Heat does not automatically rise just because a pod coloured — plenty of mild types stay mild, and the added sugar can make a ripe pod taste milder than its green self.
window.detail: Measured on Habanero, capsaicin rose 3636 → 4820 µg/g from green to yellow-ripe (Antioxidants 2019, 8(9):364, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6770197/). Vitamin C is NOT reliably directional across cultivars in that same study — Fresno fell 945 → 366 mg/100 g dry weight while CSU 256 rose 223 → 753 — so 'riper is more nutritious' does not hold per-variety.

window.at: held past full colour / drying on the plant
window.look: fully coloured pod losing gloss, going leathery and starting to wrinkle and shrivel while still attached
window.gives: for thin-walled chile types this is deliberate, not spoilage: pods can be left to dry on the plant, or cut fully ripe and hung by their stems, giving whole dried pods for flakes and powder and shelf-stable storage instead of freezer space. For thick-walled fresh-eating types it is past prime — the wall has gone soft and the pod is better used immediately.

pepper.ripe_vs_unripe: Across the crop, green is not a ripeness reading — it is either an immature pod or a deliberate mature-green pick, and only build and feel separate the two: full size for the cultivar, glossy taut skin, firm and crisp under a squeeze, and easy detachment. Colour only becomes informative once colour break starts. For a cultivar that ripens to yellow, gold, white or green, the ripe colour itself is the trap — check what colour that variety is supposed to finish at before you wait for red, because a fair share of them never turn red.
pepper.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-240 — Growing Chile Peppers in New Mexico Gardens
pepper.caveat: Assembled from NMSU H-240 (mature-green test, easy detachment, harvest at mature green or mature red, drying on the plant or hung by stems, varieties that mature yellow/orange/brown), NMSU H-230 (ideal mature-green pod build, pinto stage, type-by-type harvest colour), NMSU's Chile Pepper Institute (ripening to the red stage produces more sugar so it is sweeter; carotenoids develop), and Pepper Geek's poblano harvest guide (wait one to two weeks after growth stops; flesh softens when ripe; heat need not rise with colour and added sugar can offset it).

tomato.window_label: mature green → breaker → turning → the variety's own final colour

window.look: The fruit has stopped expanding and reached the full size that variety makes. Skin has gone from matte and faintly powdery to a first hint of gloss. Hard everywhere. No colour break yet. Cut one and the gel has formed.
window.gives: Picked here it will colour up but arrives short on flavour — sugars have not accumulated. The honest uses are fried green tomatoes, a green relish or chow-chow, and salvaging the tail of the crop ahead of a frost. Not a slicer.

window.look: Under about a tenth of the surface shows the first tint of whatever the variety's final colour is, and it almost always appears at the BLOSSOM END — the bottom — not the shoulders. Still firm all over.
window.gives: The fruit is physiologically mature and making its own ethylene, so it finishes on the counter in roughly 3-7 days at 65-85F with essentially vine-ripened flavour. It is still too firm to split, which is the real argument for picking here: rain, birds, deer, or a heat spell above 85F (which stalls ripening on the vine outright) are all bigger threats to the fruit than three days on a windowsill are to its flavour.

window.look: The break has spread up from the blossom end over a quarter or so of the fruit. Still firm enough to stack and carry.
window.gives: The practical pick for a garden that gets checked every few days rather than daily. Sugars are accumulating and it finishes indoors with good flavour development, while still being firm enough to slice cleanly and to survive being carried in a bucket with other fruit.

window.at: full ripe — 90-100% of the variety's own final colour
window.look: Colour even over the whole globe rather than patchy. Skin glossy, not dull. Heavy for its size. Sits between firm and soft under a gentle squeeze — it dents slightly at the blossom end and springs back. Grasped gently and twisted, it snaps off the vine cleanly; if it fights you, it isn't ready.
window.gives: Maximum sugar, acid and aroma, and the only stage worth eating raw straight off the plant. The trade is a short shelf life and a rising risk of splitting, insects and birds every day you leave it. Pick it, use it, and never refrigerate it — cold halts ripening and turns the texture mealy.

window.look: Colour gone dull, soft spots, weeping or failed skin, a fermented smell at the stem.
window.gives: Sugar and acid are still there but the structure is gone, so it cooks down into sauce or soup and cannot be sliced — and it has lost its keeping entirely, so it is a same-day fruit. It is also no longer any use for judging the variety, so don't taste one of these and decide whether to grow it again.

tomato.ripe_vs_unripe: One rule transfers to every tomato in this garden regardless of colour: ripening is a SHIFT IN THE COLOUR THE FRUIT ALREADY HAS, plus a change in feel — not the arrival of red. A large fraction of the varieties here never finish red at all: green, ivory, pink, peachy, dusky purple-brown. 'Is it red yet' is the wrong question almost everywhere. What is universal: (1) the colour break starts at the BLOSSOM END and spreads upward, so look at the bottom of the fruit first, every time. (2) Unripe skin is dull and slightly powdery-matte; ripening skin comes up glossy. Raking light shows this better than looking straight at the fruit. (3) The shoulders are the LEAST reliable place to look — several dark varieties keep green shoulders permanently at full ripe, and waiting for them to clear guarantees a late harvest. (4) Unripe is hard everywhere; ripe dents slightly under a thumb at the blossom end and springs back; over-ripe keeps the dent. (5) A ripe fruit detaches with a gentle twist rather than dragging the truss with it. (6) When you don't know a variety's finished colour, compare a candidate against a young fruit on the same plant — the difference in shade is the signal, and shade differences are far easier to see side by side than from memory. Then pick one and taste it. That is the calibration, and it costs exactly one fruit.
tomato.source: Penn State Extension — Is This Tomato Ready to Harvest?
tomato.caveat: Assembled from several pages read across this research run rather than one. Penn State Extension supplies the blossom-end colour break, the ethylene point, the fact that breaker-picked fruit carries vine-ripened flavour and resists cracking, the softening at pink stage, and the above-85F ripening stall. Tomato Dirt supplies the stage percentages, gel formation at green, the sweetening-and-softening at pink, and the twist-off and firm-but-giving tests. Sow Right Seeds supplies the 3-7 days at 65-85F off-vine figure, stem-side-down storage, and the observation that most people detect no flavour difference in fruit finished indoors after breaker — though some varieties do gain a little sweetness left on the vine. The Coeur d'Alene Coop and growtomato.com supply the shade-shift, dull-versus-shiny and squeeze tests as they apply to varieties that are not red when ripe. Deliberately no final colour is asserted at crop level, because a large minority of the varieties in this garden do not finish red.

window.look: skin fully coloured with a fresh chalky bloom, berry hard, no give, and it has to be pulled off the pedicel; any tinge of the pre-ripe colour still ringing the stem scar
window.gives: firmness and storage life, at the cost of flavour — acid is still high and the berry is at its smallest. Use where structure matters (baking, freezing whole)

window.look: colour slightly deeper and duller as the bloom wears, berry noticeably larger and plumper, faint give under the fingers, and it detaches on its own — a thumb-roll drops it into your palm
window.gives: the flavour stage: acid falls and sugars keep accumulating for days after the skin finishes colouring, and the berry swells as well, so waiting buys both sweetness and yield. Pay for it in shelf life

blueberry.ripe_vs_unripe: The crop mechanic to remember: blueberry skin colour completes several days before the fruit is sweet, and the berry does not ripen after picking, so nothing is recoverable in the kitchen. Judge by release and by the stem scar, not by colour — a ripe berry lets go on its own, and any trace of the unripe colour at the stem end means wait. Pick each bush on a 3–7 day rotation rather than stripping it, because within one cluster berries that look identical are at different maturities.
blueberry.source: University of Maryland Extension — Growing Blueberries in a Home Garden; NC State Extension Gardener Handbook ch. 14

blackberry.window_label: colour-complete and glossy → matte and swollen

window.look: final colour reached over the whole fruit but still shiny, drupelets tight and small, firm, and it needs a deliberate pull to detach
window.gives: handling strength and a few days of fridge life — the stage commercial fruit is shipped at. Flavour is still acid-dominant

window.look: the shine has gone flat, individual drupelets have plumped and rounded so the surface reads bumpier, and the fruit releases into your hand with barely any pull
window.gives: the sugar stage — sweetness rises as the gloss dulls. Soft, juicy, full-flavoured, and good for only two or three days

blackberry.ripe_vs_unripe: Blackberry-type fruit reaches full colour days before full sugar and does not improve after picking, so it must be finished on the cane. The colour-agnostic test is gloss plus release: shiny and gripping means wait, matte and releasing means pick. Because the receptacle stays inside the fruit in blackberry-type brambles, a ripe one comes away whole and solid-cored rather than hollow, so you cannot use the slip-off-the-core test that works on raspberries — use gloss and drupelet plumpness instead.
blackberry.source: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook — Chapter 14, Small Fruits

red_raspberry.window_label: colour partly filled in → colour complete and slip-ripe

window.look: pale, uneven colour, drupelets tight, fruit firm, and it holds its core so it will not slip
window.gives: raspberry-type fruit ripens on after picking, so an early-picked berry still reaches normal sweetness and colour indoors. That makes this a real option against weather, birds or a trip — you trade some aroma for firmness

window.look: colour even to the shoulders, slight softness, and the fruit slides off the receptacle with a light roll, leaving the pale core standing on the cane; the picked berry is hollow
window.gives: full aroma and the tender texture the fruit is grown for, with almost no shelf life — pick every 2–3 days and refrigerate immediately, since every hour before cooling costs about a day of keeping

red_raspberry.ripe_vs_unripe: The whole crop-level test is release, not colour: ripe raspberry-type fruit separates from the receptacle easily and leaves that receptacle behind on the plant, so it should be rolled off rather than squeezed or pulled. If a berry does not slip, it is not ready — and unlike blackberries that is not a lost cause, because raspberry-type fruit will finish ripening off the cane.
red_raspberry.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-320 — Raspberries for the Home Garden; Penn State Extension — Post Harvest Berry Handling

strawberry.window_label: colour complete to the shoulders → soft and matte

window.look: final colour carried all the way from the tip to the shoulders under the cap, with no pale or white patch left anywhere; glossy, scented, firm. Harvest with about a quarter-inch of stem attached instead of pulling the fruit off its cap
window.gives: the earliest legitimate pick and the practical one — sugar and flavour are at their optimum at full ripeness, and the fruit is firm enough to carry and to keep for a day or two

window.look: colour darker and duller, gloss gone, clear give under the thumb, cap parting easily, strong perfume
window.gives: maximum aroma and the best preserve fruit; no additional sugar, and shelf life falls away fast — cool it within the hour

strawberry.ripe_vs_unripe: Strawberries do not sweeten after picking, so the crop rule is that any fruit still showing white anywhere — shoulders included — is left for the next picking. Colour fills in from the tip toward the cap, and leaf cover shades the shoulders, so the shaded shoulder is where you check and the sunlit face is what fools you. Colour-agnostic cues: gloss, scent at arm's length, a slight give, and a cap that parts without tearing the flesh.
strawberry.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Harvesting strawberries; NC State Extension Gardener Handbook ch. 14

wineberry.window_label: calyx splitting open → fully exposed and slip-ripe

window.look: the bristly, sticky calyx that has enclosed the fruit peels back and shows the berry for the first time; the fruit is still hard and firmly attached to its cone
window.gives: advance warning rather than a harvest — the calyx stays shut until just before ripeness. Picking now gets you a tart, firm berry; the only reason to do it is that from this point the fruit is exposed to birds and rain

window.look: berry sitting entirely clear of the opened calyx, glossy and almost translucent, about three-quarters of an inch, and it lifts free at a touch leaving its core on the cane
window.gives: the sweet-tart, raspberry-flavoured eating stage; extremely fragile, no storage, best used the day it is picked

wineberry.ripe_vs_unripe: For this crop the calyx is the gate and release is the test: fruit still inside a closed or half-split calyx is not ready, and fruit that is out of the calyx but resists a light touch is not ready either. Since it is a raspberry-type bramble, ripe fruit slips off and leaves the core behind on the cane. Wild-foraged crop — expect thin published guidance, high variability cane to cane, and heavy bird competition in the day or two after the calyx opens.
wineberry.source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Rubus phoenicolasius (Wineberry)
wineberry.caveat: Wineberry has no extension harvest-maturity literature; the crop mechanic is assembled from the NC State plant record (calyx behaviour, colour, size, flavour, season) plus red-raspberry release guidance (NMSU H-320) applied to it as a raspberry-type Rubus.

tomatillo.window_label: fruit fills husk / husk splits → fruit drops

window.look: the papery husk stretched tight with no air space left inside; the husk drying from green toward tan; the fruit releases from the plant with a light twist or a snip and needs no force
window.gives: the opening of the window for every tomatillo regardless of colour — full size and firm flesh, maximum acidity, and the best keeping: about 1-2 weeks in the husk in a paper bag in the fridge, or 8-12 months frozen

window.look: husk brown, papery and torn along a seam with fruit skin showing through
window.gives: confirmation the fruit is done sizing; picking here is the standard commercial and home pick and gives the firmest fruit that still handles well

window.look: the ground colour moving off hard green — toward yellow, gold, or purple where sun strikes, depending entirely on the variety; skin starting to give under the thumb
window.gives: sweetness rises and tartness falls, which is the whole reason to wait on a yellow- or purple-ripening variety and the reason not to on a green one; the trade is softer flesh and a shorter shelf life

window.look: fruit lying on the ground still inside its husk
window.gives: fully ripe, not spoiled — tomatillos continue to ripen after they are separated from the plant, so windfalls left in their husks finish on the counter; check them for soil damage and use them first

tomatillo.ripe_vs_unripe: The signal is the husk, not the fruit — this is what makes tomatillos different from tomatoes. The fruit's colour reports cultivar and sugar stage, not pickability, so an entirely green tomatillo can be fully harvestable and a coloured one can be past the stage you wanted. Unready: plump green pliable husk, visible slack around a small fruit, resists twisting. Ready: fruit swelled tight against the husk wall, husk dried tan and papery, split along a seam, detaching on a light twist. Only after that does colour become a decision rather than a diagnosis.
tomatillo.source: SDSU Extension — Tomatillos: Harvest and Storage
tomatillo.caveat: The colour progression is deliberately left open-ended here because it is cultivar-determined: green types are picked before they turn and go soft and lose tang if they do, while yellow and purple types gain their sweetness only by being allowed to colour. Do not apply one variety's colour rule to another.

bean.window_label: smooth young pod → the moment seed shape shows

window.at: any stage of pod formation, pod smooth
window.look: pod sides perfectly smooth with no lumps, seeds not detectable as shapes; the pod snaps in half cleanly and audibly when bent, showing a wet break
window.gives: the entire legitimate snap window — you can pick snap beans at any stage of pod formation until seed shape appears, so this is a range and not a moment. Earlier means more tender and less fibre; picking before pods have gained size decreases total yield

window.look: pod at its variety's full length and thickness, still smooth-sided
window.gives: the most weight for the same quality, and the stage to pick for canning so the beans stay firm through processing rather than going soft

window.at: seed shape apparent, pod bulging (window closed)
window.look: individual seeds raised as distinct bumps making the pod bulge; the pod bends and tears instead of snapping
window.gives: less juicy and more fibrous — the pods go tough and stringy, and leaving them on suppresses further pod set. Redirect to shelling or dry beans; regular picking every few days is what keeps the plant producing

bean.ripe_vs_unripe: Pod colour is cultivar identity, never ripeness. Snap-bean pods come green, yellow ('wax'), purple or striped, and each of those is the colour the pod is from the day it forms — a wax bean does not turn yellow when ready and a purple bean does not turn purple when ready. Every type is judged by the same three physical cues instead: pod diameter (roughly pencil-thick for standard snaps, 1/8-1/4 in for filet types), smooth sides with no seed bumps showing, and a clean audible snap when bent. Where colour does change, it usually changes in the wrong direction for you — a deepening, dulling pod is a sign of over-maturity, not readiness.
bean.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing beans in home gardens

peach.window_label: ground colour off green, firm → soft ripe, before orange

window.at: ground colour just off green, hard
window.look: background skin behind and between any blush no longer green; fruit hard, 10-16 lb-force, at or above the variety's expected diameter
window.gives: the storage and travel pick — flesh will soften off the tree over days on the counter, but sugar stops rising the moment the fruit is cut from the tree, so it finishes soft-but-flat compared with a later pick

window.look: background colour a clear, even yellow or cream (which of the two is cultivar-determined), no green left; firm to the hand but with the stoniness gone
window.gives: nearly all the sugar the fruit will ever carry, plus enough firmness to handle and carry without bruising the tip, suture and shoulders

window.look: ground colour at its darkest before turning; a strong peachy aroma noticeable without picking it up; flesh yielding at 2-4 lb-force
window.gives: peak sweetness, juice and aroma; in exchange the fruit bruises easily and loses roughly 2 more lb of firmness for every day at room temperature, so it must be used at once

window.at: ground colour gone past to orange (window closed)
window.look: background skin orange rather than deep yellow; soft under light pressure
window.gives: overripe — the texture breaks down and it belongs in a pot or the freezer, not a fruit bowl

peach.ripe_vs_unripe: The colour-agnostic rule for stone fruit here is that only the GROUND colour reports maturity — the background skin in the areas not showing red blush, which shifts green to yellow (or cream) to eventually orange. Red blush is a response to sunlight and to cultivar and says nothing about ripeness; the degree of red coloration is not a good indicator for maturity. A red fruit with green in its background is immature. Do not rely on the ground colour alone either, and be aware that some newer solid-red cultivars are entirely red before optimal maturity, which hides the ground colour completely — for those, and as confirmation on any peach, use flesh firmness and aroma. No single maturity index is sufficient on its own.
peach.source: University of Maryland Extension FS-1182 — Are Your Peaches Ready to Harvest?; corroborated by Clemson HGIC — How to Determine Peach Ripeness and UGA CAES — Peaches: Appropriate Harvest and Postharvest Handling

sweet_potato.window_label: no colour window — test dig → frost/50°F soil, then cure

window.look: there is no above-ground ripeness cue of any kind on this crop, because the harvest is a root. The two things you can actually look at are the mound of soil heaving up at the base of the vines and one plant dug up and inspected
window.gives: the only verifiable read on size. Digging early costs yield — roots keep enlarging as long as the vines are alive — so the test dig exists to tell you whether you can afford to wait, not to declare ripeness

window.look: watch the forecast and a soil thermometer, not the plant; vines still green and growing right up to the end
window.gives: maximum size, and the last safe moment. Past it you lose rather than gain: the vines are frost-tender and must come out by the time frost kills them or soon after, a hard freeze damages roots near the surface, and soil at or below 50°F causes chilling injury that surfaces later as internal decay in storage

window.look: roots held about 10 days at 80-85°F and 85-90% relative humidity, or 2-3 weeks at 65-75°F; skins toughen and stop scuffing off under a thumb
window.gives: the actual flavour payoff, and it happens after harvest rather than in the ground — it is during curing that starch is converted to sugar, so an uncured root is starchy and a cured one is sweet. Curing also sets the skin, which is what makes the crop storable

window.look: dry, set-skinned roots in the dark at about 55-60°F
window.gives: months of keeping with flavour continuing to improve; refrigeration does the opposite — sweet potatoes prefer warm storage and decay in the cold

sweet_potato.ripe_vs_unripe: Not applicable in the usual sense, and that is the point worth stating on screen: root crops have no visible colour or ripeness window, so any colour cue offered for a sweet potato is invented. Flesh colour is variety, not stage. Size is judged by digging, timing is judged by frost and soil temperature, and sweetness is not a garden state at all — it is created by the post-harvest curing period.
sweet_potato.source: K-State Research and Extension, Johnson County — Sweet Potato Harvest; curing, chilling-injury and storage detail from Purdue Consumer Horticulture — Dig Those Sweet Potatoes

melon.window_label: mature and firm → release (slip, or colour-and-touch) → past release

window.look: Fruit at full size for its type with its surface texture finished — netting raised and well rounded on netted types, fine pubescence still detectable on smooth types. Rind colour has not yet broken from its uniform immature ground colour. Stem tight, no crack at the scar, little or no aroma.
window.gives: The firmest, best-handling, longest-keeping of the harvestable stages, and on climacteric types (netted muskmelon, Charentais, Galia) it will still soften and 'ripen' off the vine. It will not sweeten. UGA: melons ripen after harvest but do not increase in sugar content, with almost half the final sugar accumulated in the few days right before slip. Illinois: sugars are stored up to the moment the stem separates, and once picked a melon softens but does not sweeten. Every early pick is a permanent sugar cut, paid for in shelf life.

window.look: Two different mechanics, and using the wrong one loses the fruit. SLIPPING types (netted muskmelons, Charentais, Galia) form an abscission layer: a crack opens around the stem scar and the stem lifts off cleanly under a slight tug — half slip is about half the stem releasing, full slip the whole stem. NON-SLIPPING types (honeydew, Crenshaw, casaba, canary, Persian) never do this and must be cut; read instead the rind shifting away from its immature ground colour, the loss of the fine surface pubescence, and a blossom end that just gives to thumb pressure. Aroma at the stem end rises sharply in the musky group and is absent in the inodorous group.
window.gives: Peak sugar, plus full aroma on the musky types. The cost is holding time and it differs wildly by type: cantaloupe is climacteric with a very short life after picking (UMD), while the inodorous winter group can hold at room temperature for a month or more (UGA). Decide which you are picking before you pick it.

window.look: Slipping types detach on their own and lie loose on the soil; rind softens and shows brown undertones or browning along the vein tracts. Non-slipping types go from a blossom end that is 'slightly soft' to one that dents and stays dented. Aroma heavy.
window.gives: Maximum aroma, failing texture. UGA reads brown undertones and vein browning as aging and internal softness; UMD warns a melon left to full self-detachment may already be overripe. Same-day use — cut fresh, chilled soup, blended or frozen.

melon.ripe_vs_unripe: For melons the pick signal is largely NOT colour, and any colour rule has to be stated as a SHIFT rather than a target: ripe rind lands on tan, grey, cream, white or yellow depending entirely on the type, so read the move away from the immature ground colour, never a specific final colour. The universal misread is treating full size, finished netting, or days-on-the-calendar as ripeness — size and surface texture finish early, sugar finishes last. Ripeness lives at the stem (crack plus slip) on slipping types, and at rind-tone shift plus lost fuzz plus blossom-end give on non-slipping types. Aroma is the best single cue on the musky group and no cue at all on the inodorous group. And across every melon here, sugar does not rise after picking — so unlike a tomato, there is no early-pick stage that finishes properly indoors.
melon.source: University of Georgia Extension CAES Field Report B1179 — Cantaloupe and Specialty Melons; Illinois Extension — Muskmelon; University of Maryland Extension — Ripening Behaviors and Harvest Indexes

watermelon.window_label: field signals partial → all field signals agree

window.look: Fruit at or near full size, but only one or two of the four field signals present: ground spot still whitish or only part-turned, rind still glossy and reflective, tendril nearest the fruit drying rather than brown and dead, thump still bright and high.
window.gives: Firmness and handling life only, and it is a bad trade. UMD: watermelon is non-climacteric — once harvested it will not ripen any further and sugar does not increase after harvest. NC State puts the minimum for acceptable eating at 10 Brix measured by refractometer. Long-distance shippers do cut early for shelf life, and accept exactly the flavour loss you would be accepting. There is no indoor rescue for an early watermelon.

window.look: Ground/field spot has SHIFTED from whitish-green to creamy, buttery yellow (some cultivars cream to deeper yellow); the rind has gone from shiny to dull; the tendril where the fruit attaches has turned from green to brown and dried; the thump has dropped from bright to dull and hollow. Read them together, not individually.
window.gives: Full sugar, full flesh colour, best texture — and since nothing improves after cutting, this is simply the target. It also means a ripe watermelon has no ripening clock running indoors: what you carry in is what you eat. Keep it away from apples, bananas, pears, peaches and tomatoes in storage — UMD notes watermelon is ethylene-sensitive.

watermelon.ripe_vs_unripe: Watermelon is the crop where you can never see the answer, so every cue is a proxy and one wrong read costs the whole fruit. Ground spot: every watermelon has one, because that side of the fruit never saw sun — its PRESENCE is not ripeness, its COLOUR SHIFT is (whitish-green to creamy-buttery yellow). No slip: unlike cantaloupe, watermelon never forms an abscission layer, so a firmly attached stem is not evidence of an unripe melon and tugging only damages the vine — cut it. Size and calendar days: both finish before sugar does. Flesh colour as a rule (UMD: deep red ripe, pink or white immature) holds only for red-fleshed cultivars and is void on orange- and yellow-fleshed ones, where orange flesh is the cultivar, not overripeness. Minis: NC State warns that watermelons under about 9 lb often do not express these traits even when ripe, so on icebox types lean on rind gloss and rind hardness and cut the first fruit to calibrate. Because the type is non-climacteric, an early pick cannot be undone — when the signals disagree, wait.
watermelon.source: NC State Cucurbit Breeding — Choosing a Ripe Watermelon (for field harvest); ripening behaviour and indices from University of Maryland Extension — Ripening Behaviors and Harvest Indexes

squash.window_label: immature and glossy → oversized with hard seed (crop-level)

window.at: immature (the whole point of the crop)
window.look: fruit only a few days past the flower, skin glossy and easily dented by a thumbnail, blossom scar sometimes still attached, stem cuts with no effort
window.gives: summer squash is a fruit harvested deliberately immature — the eating quality is entirely in the pre-seed stage: tender skin you do not peel, seeds you cannot detect, and firm flesh. Colour is a cultivar trait here, not a ripeness signal, so pick by size, gloss and dentability rather than by shade

window.look: the size you actually want to cook, taken before the fruit thickens through the middle and while the skin still dents
window.gives: the crop has no single correct size — Extension's rule is to pick at whatever size you prefer but before large seeds, hard skin and fibrous or watery flesh appear. Frequent picking is itself a payoff: it keeps the plant setting new fruit

window.look: thick and heavy, skin dull and no longer dentable, seed outlines visible in a cut face
window.gives: the cost: hard seeds, a rind too tough to eat, and flesh that has gone fibrous or watery so it collapses in the pan. And the plant pays too — leaving very large fruit on the vine makes total yield decline, so remove oversized fruit even if you will not use it

squash.ripe_vs_unripe: Every summer squash is picked unripe, so nothing about a summer squash's colour is a ripeness cue. Bicolour and pale-tipped varieties (Zephyr among them) look permanently "half unripe" and never even out. The ripeness cues that do work are mechanical: gloss, whether a thumbnail dents the skin, thickness through the middle, and how easily the stem cuts.
squash.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing summer squash and zucchini in home gardens

cucumber.window_label: any size while dark and slender → yellowing skin and large seed (crop-level)

window.look: even dark colour to the blossom end, slender and straight-sided rather than bulging, skin taut and glossy, seed cavity invisible when cut
window.gives: cucumbers are harvested immature by definition, and Extension gives no minimum — pick at any size before large seeds and yellowish skin appear. Smaller means crisper, thinner-skinned and effectively seedless

window.look: the length the variety is described as, still uniform in width and still dark; cut the stem rather than pulling, which tears the vine
window.gives: the most fruit per pick while texture holds. Cucumbers can double in size in a couple of days, so this point is measured in days — picking every day or two both catches fruit at quality and keeps the vine producing

window.look: colour fading to pale then yellow, fruit swollen and blocky, thick tough skin, large white or tan seeds in the cut face
window.gives: the cost: seeds hardened, skin too tough to eat unpeeled, flesh pithy, and rising bitterness (which concentrates at the blossom end). Very large fruit left on the vine makes overall plant yield decline, so pull and discard them

cucumber.ripe_vs_unripe: A cucumber that looks ripe is a cucumber you left too long. Yellow is not a ripeness colour on any slicing or pickling cucumber that is dark green when good — it means seeds have set and bitterness is arriving. Judge by depth and evenness of green, slenderness, and firmness, never by colour development.
cucumber.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing cucumbers

okra.window_label: 2 in → 3-4 in tender pod, then fibre sets (crop-level)

window.look: pod 2 in, fully formed in shape but soft-tipped, skin unblemished and bright
window.gives: guaranteed tenderness with no fibre anywhere — the safe end of the window on any variety, at the cost of pod weight

window.look: roughly 3-4 in on a ridged variety (round-podded types stay tender noticeably longer), pod still snaps cleanly off the plant and the tip breaks rather than bending
window.gives: the usable size-to-tenderness trade for slicing and freezing. Okra grows very fast, so the crop must be picked every couple of days — the window is measured in days, not weeks, and pods bruise easily so handle them gently

window.look: 5 in and beyond, ribs hardened, pod bends instead of snapping and resists a thumbnail
window.gives: the cost is permanent — fibre has set in the pod walls and no amount of cooking softens it. And it costs future harvest: pods allowed to mature on the plant slow production and push the plant toward more tough pods, so cut them off and discard

okra.source: UGA Cooperative Extension C941 — Home Garden Okra (with Clemson HGIC — How to Grow Okra in South Carolina)
okra.caveat: Sourced rule is 2-3 in pods harvested every few days; the snap-versus-bend field test is the practical expression of the sourced tenderness rule, not a direct quote.

eggplant.window_label: glossy and springy under the thumb → dull with a dent that stays (crop-level)

window.look: small for the type and rock-hard — a thumb press makes no impression at all
window.gives: not worth cutting yet: a fruit with no give has not filled out, so you get thin flesh. Hardness is the immature cue, which is why size alone is not a reliable test

window.look: skin at maximum gloss and evenly coloured for the variety; pressed with a thumb the flesh gives and then springs back. Cut the stem with a knife or shears, leaving the cap attached, and wear gloves for the spines
window.gives: peak eating quality across every eggplant colour: creamy non-bitter flesh, soft unnoticeable seeds, and skin tender enough to leave on. Fruit typically reaches full size 10-20 days after flowering, and picking as fruit matures keeps quality up on later fruit

window.look: gloss gone — skin dull, matte or bronzing — and the thumb dent remains instead of springing back
window.gives: the cost, and it is not salvageable: the interior may be browning through, the seeds have gone large and tough, and the flesh is spongy and bitter. Extension's instruction is to cut these off and discard them. Colour is a cultivar trait on eggplant, so this is judged by gloss and give, never by shade

eggplant.ripe_vs_unripe: Eggplant is harvested well before botanical ripeness, so a fully ripe eggplant is a ruined one. There is no colour to wait for, and no variety improves by being left: the two cues that work are GLOSS (shiny = pick, dull = too late) and the thumb-press test (springs back = pick, dent stays = over-mature). White, green, striped and long Asian types all read the same way on those two tests.
eggplant.source: University of Illinois Extension — Eggplant (Home Vegetable Gardening)

cucamelon.window_label: grape size and firm → soft and seed-filled (crop-level)

window.look: roughly 1 in oval fruit patterned like a tiny watermelon, firm to a gentle squeeze, coming away with a light pull
window.gives: the only stage worth picking: crisp snap, tender white flesh, cucumber flavour with a lime-like tang, no seed texture. Fruits plump within a day or two of the flower dropping its petals, so daily checking is the crop mechanic — they hide under foliage and go past quickly

window.look: larger and rounder, distinctly soft rather than firm; the ripest fruit finally drops from the vine by itself
window.gives: the cost: seeds fill out and firmness goes, so the crisp texture that is the entire appeal turns soft and seedy and the flavour sours. Useful only for saving seed at that point

cucamelon.ripe_vs_unripe: The striped green-on-green pattern is the cultivar's normal look, not an unripe one, and it does not change into some riper colour — cucamelons are picked immature and judged by size (about grape size) and firmness under a gentle squeeze, never by colour.
cucamelon.source: Gardener's Path — How to Plant and Grow Cucamelons (Mexican Sour Gherkins)
cucamelon.caveat: No university extension source exists for this crop that could be found this run; crop mechanic taken from a horticultural gardening publication, corroborated on size by seed catalogues.

bitter_melon.window_label: firm shiny green → first yellow (window closes) → orange and split (crop-level)

window.look: solid green with no yellow, hard in the hand, ridges and warts sharply defined, surface shiny rather than matte
window.gives: the culinary stage for every bitter melon type — flesh firm enough to hold a slice through cooking, seeds still soft and white. Fruit reaches this roughly 50-70 days from sowing depending on variety

window.look: any yellow or orange tinge appearing, the fruit starting to soften and lose its hard feel
window.gives: the cost side: softening flesh and firming seeds. Extension guidance is to harvest before yellow or orange appears, so the first colour break is a boundary rather than a stage to aim for

window.look: soft and orange, then splitting open at the base to show light brown seeds in bright red pulp
window.gives: no cooking value left — soft flesh, hard seeds. Only the red seed pulp is of interest, and mainly for seed saving. Harvesting fruit often, before it reaches this point, is what keeps the vine producing

bitter_melon.ripe_vs_unripe: This crop is grown to be eaten unripe, so the whole colour progression is a countdown rather than a ripening cue. Green plus firm plus shiny = pick. Any yellow, any softening under a squeeze = past the cooking window. Split with red pulp showing = fully ripe and fully unusable as a vegetable.
bitter_melon.source: UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County (UC ANR) — Bitter Melon
bitter_melon.caveat: Colour, firmness and splitting progression are sourced; the cited page does not document how bitterness intensity itself shifts between stages, so no stage-to-stage bitterness claim is made here.

1884.window_label: first pink blush → even deep dark pink

window.look: Blocky 1-2 lb beefsteak, noticeably ribbed and somewhat irregular around the shoulders, still green with the first pink showing at the blossom end.
window.gives: The stage to take before a fruit this heavy splits along its own ribs or drops off the truss — and dropped fruit is the specific hazard this variety's own seller warns about. Finishes in a paper bag or wrapped in newspaper somewhere cool and dark, stem-side up.

window.look: Pink over much of the fruit; the ribs and their grooves are the last places to lose green. Still firm in the hand.
window.gives: Firm enough to slice thick and clean for a sandwich or a burger, with the sweet/acid balance already in place. On a fruit this large that firmness is what keeps a slab from folding.

window.look: An even deep, dark pink across the whole fruit and down into the ribs. Heavy, giving under a thumb.
window.gives: The full old-fashioned flavour it is grown for — very sweet, meaty and juicy with a good sweet/acid balance, ranked among the best-tasting in its seller's own trials. One fruit is a meal's worth of slices, which is the practical payoff of a two-pounder. Left past here on the vine it splits and draws insects and birds.

1884.caveat: No extension or breeder source exists for this variety — it is a rare heirloom, reportedly found by James Lyde Williamson in flood debris near Friendly, West Virginia after the 1884 Ohio River flood. The cultivar facts (dark pink, 1-2 lb, somewhat ribbed and blocky, indeterminate, heavy yields, good sweet/acid balance) come from Thresh Seed Co. and Reimer Seeds, which agree with each other. Days to maturity does not: 78 from transplant (Thresh) versus 85 (Reimer). Neither source describes 1884's own colour break, so the early points of the window use the general large-pink-beefsteak sequence; the note that ribbed grooves colour last is a reading of the fruit's shape rather than a sourced claim, so treat it as a hint and not a rule. Ripe colour is dark pink, not red.

window.look: at full cultivar size (3-4 in on a standard jalapeno), deep green rather than pale, distinctly glossy, firm with filled-out walls and even colour top to tip
window.gives: the crisp, bright vegetal stage — grassy bell-pepper flavour with clean medium heat, the firmest crunch and best-filled walls, which is what pickling, slicing and poppers want; picking here also keeps the plant setting new flowers instead of finishing the pods it has

window.look: same dark green pod now carrying tan-to-brown stretch marks (corking) running lengthwise from shoulder toward tip, from the flesh expanding faster than the skin
window.gives: a maturity signal, not a heat promise — the pod is fully developed and sound, still firm enough to roast, stuff or eat fresh; treat corking as confirmation it is ready rather than as evidence it will be hotter, since pungency tracks cultivar, air temperature, irrigation and fertility more than skin marks

window.look: green ground darkening, often through near-black or dark streaking, with the first red showing on shoulders or tip
window.gives: the sharpest heat of the whole window — pods run slightly spicier just as they begin turning, before pungency eases off with full ripening; flavour is transitional, still vegetal but starting to sweeten

window.look: evenly bright to deep red, wall giving slightly under thumb pressure rather than snapping crisp
window.gives: sweeter and fruitier, a fuller rounder flavour instead of the green grassy bite, and the only stage worth smoking for chipotle, drying, red sauce, ferments or seed saving; texture is too soft for good poppers and heat is past peak

jalapeno.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is a deliberate pick here, so the discrimination is mature green vs immature green, not ripe vs unripe. Immature: pale or light green, matte or dull, narrow and not yet filled out, walls that dent softly, clinging to the plant. Correct mature green: at the cultivar's expected length, deep and even dark green with a wet-looking gloss, firm and crisp when squeezed with the walls filled, and it detaches easily; tan corking lines, if present, confirm it. Colour alone is not the test — a filled, evenly coloured pod at size is.
jalapeno.source: Savvy Gardening — When to Harvest Jalapeños: The Secret to Better Flavor, Heat, and Bigger Harvests (with corking-vs-heat and mature-green criteria from Know The Pepper — Harvesting Jalapenos: Green, Red and Corking Signs, and stage progression from Pepper Geek — Harvesting Jalapeños)
jalapeno.caveat: Sources disagree on how heat moves across the window. This popular-horticulture source has pungency peaking as pods begin to turn and easing at full red; measured capsaicinoid data (Antioxidants 2019, 8(9):364) found capsaicin RISING with maturity in most cultivars tested. Treat the stage-by-stage heat notes as approximate and trust your own palate on this plant.

window.look: big for a jalapeno — smooth cylindrical pod about 4½ in long, deep green, notably thick-walled, skin staying smooth rather than corky
window.gives: the stage this hybrid is bred for: the most flesh per pod of any jalapeno here, thick firm walls that hold their shape for stuffing, slicing and pickling, and good shelf life after picking; smooth skin means no corking to wait for, so size and deep even green are the readiness call

window.look: fully coloured red on the same large pod, wall softening from its green firmness
window.gives: the standard jalapeno ripe-stage trade — sweeter and fruitier, rounder flavour in place of the green vegetal bite, better for sauce, drying or smoking; the thick wall that made it good for stuffing loses its snap, and it ties the plant up for one to three extra weeks

megatronf1.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is the intended pick. Because Megatron is a jumbo type, a pod that would be full size on an ordinary jalapeno is still immature here — hold out for roughly 4½ in, deep even green, glossy, and thick and heavy in the hand with no soft dent. This variety is smooth-skinned by design, so absence of corking is not evidence of immaturity.
megatronf1.source: Harris Seeds — Pepper Megatron F1 Seed
megatronf1.caveat: Harris Seeds documents the pod itself (4½ in, smooth, thick-walled, deep green ripening to red, 65 days, good shelf life); no cultivar-specific source describes what the red stage tastes like, so the red payoff is standard jalapeno-type behaviour applied to this variety.

window.look: big for a jalapeno — smooth cylindrical pod about 4½ in long, deep green, notably thick-walled, skin staying smooth rather than corky
window.gives: the stage this hybrid is bred for: the most flesh per pod of any jalapeno here, thick firm walls that hold their shape for stuffing, slicing and pickling, and good shelf life after picking; smooth skin means no corking to wait for, so size and deep even green are the readiness call

window.look: fully coloured red on the same large pod, wall softening from its green firmness
window.gives: the standard jalapeno ripe-stage trade — sweeter and fruitier, rounder flavour in place of the green vegetal bite, better for sauce, drying or smoking; the thick wall that made it good for stuffing loses its snap, and it ties the plant up for one to three extra weeks

megatronf1jumbojalapeno.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is the intended pick. Because Megatron is a jumbo type, a pod that would be full size on an ordinary jalapeno is still immature here — hold out for roughly 4½ in, deep even green, glossy, and thick and heavy in the hand with no soft dent. This variety is smooth-skinned by design, so absence of corking is not evidence of immaturity.
megatronf1jumbojalapeno.source: Harris Seeds — Pepper Megatron F1 Seed
megatronf1jumbojalapeno.caveat: Harris Seeds documents the pod itself (4½ in, smooth, thick-walled, deep green ripening to red, 65 days, good shelf life); no cultivar-specific source describes what the red stage tastes like, so the red payoff is standard jalapeno-type behaviour applied to this variety.

window.look: jalapeno-shaped pod at its full size for the variety, deep glossy green, firm with filled walls, often showing tan corking lines lengthwise
window.gives: crisp vegetal heat with the firmest walls — the stage for pickling, poppers, salsa and slicing, and the stage that keeps the plant flowering

window.look: fully coloured red, skin still glossy, wall softer under thumb pressure
window.gives: sweeter and fruitier with a rounder, fuller flavour than the green bite, and the stage to smoke, dry or cook down into red sauce; poor texture for stuffing

capeliente.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is the deliberate pick. Immature reads pale or light green, matte, slim and not filled out, with walls that dent. Mature green reads deep even dark green with a wet gloss, at the variety's expected length, firm and crisp when squeezed, detaching easily from the plant; corking lines confirm maturity.
capeliente.source: Savvy Gardening — When to Harvest Jalapeños: The Secret to Better Flavor, Heat, and Bigger Harvests
capeliente.caveat: No source for 'Capeliente' exists anywhere I could reach — a targeted search returned nothing under that name from any seed vendor or extension service. The window is derived entirely from general jalapeño-type guidance, consistent with the recorded 2,500-8,000 SHU. Trust your own eyes on this plant's actual pod size and final colour over this entry.

window.look: small jalapeno-shaped pod at full size for the variety, deep glossy green, firm with filled walls
window.gives: the crisp firm-walled stage for poppers, pickling and fresh salsa — and on this variety even the green pod carries far more heat than an ordinary jalapeno, since it runs around 25,000 Scoville

window.look: green ground going dull and lightening, first warm orange breaking on shoulders or tip
window.gives: an in-between pick — some of the green crispness left with the fruitiness starting to come up; useful when you want colour without waiting out full ripening

window.look: evenly warm deep orange over the whole pod, no green left, wall softer than at green
window.gives: the reason to grow it — distinctly fruitier than a conventional green or red jalapeno, at full 25,000 SHU heat, and the colour holds in sauces, roasted, or frozen for winter; despite the name there is no cinnamon or clove flavour

pumpkinjalapeno.ripe_vs_unripe: Orange, not red, is this pepper's finished state — an orange pod is fully ripe and not over-ripe or off. Green is also a legitimate pick, and the mature-green test is the jalapeno one: full size for the variety, deep even glossy green, firm and filled rather than slim and matte.
pumpkinjalapeno.source: John Scheepers Kitchen Garden Seeds — Pumpkin Spice Jalapeño Hot Chile Pepper
pumpkinjalapeno.caveat: Kitchen Garden Seeds is cultivar-specific for the orange ripening, the 25,000 SHU, the fruitier flavour and 65 days; it does not describe the green stage or the intermediate blush, so those two points are jalapeño-type guidance applied to this variety.

window.look: slim pod 2-4 in long, vivid green with a glossy skin, solid and plump when gently squeezed (never soft or spongy), green healthy stem, and it comes away with a clean snap when pulled gently
window.gives: the crisp fresh stage — the mildest end of this pepper's range with clean bright heat, which is what pico de gallo, guacamole and fresh salsa are built on

window.look: green fading and going yellow then orange, pod still firm, stem base beginning to turn brown or woody
window.gives: a middle setting — heat has climbed to medium and balanced, with the vegetal edge fading before the fruitiness arrives; the pick when full-red serrano would be too much

window.look: evenly bright red over the whole pod, skin glossy, wall no longer crisp-firm
window.gives: peak capsaicin — the hottest point of the window, with a bold fruity flavour; this is the stage for cooked sauces, adobos, infused oils and drying

window.look: red darkening toward brown, skin duller and starting to slacken
window.gives: the very hot, smoky and intense end of the range — worth taking only if maximum heat and a smoky note are the point; texture is gone for fresh use

serrano.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is a deliberate pick on serrano, so judge maturity by feel and size rather than colour: 2-4 in long, glossy rather than matte, solid and plump under gentle pressure with no soft or spongy give, and a clean snap at the stem. A thin, dull, flexible pod that clings to the plant is immature.
serrano.source: My Gardening Zone — When Are Serranos Ready to Pick: Color Change and Heat Signals

santafegrande.window_label: bright green → sunny yellow → orange → glossy red

window.look: conical blunt-tipped wax-type pod about 3 in long with thick flesh, still bright green rather than yellowing, firm
window.gives: the crispest, mildest pick — thick firm flesh for pickling and fresh eating before any sweetness develops

window.look: pale to sunny yellow all over — the classic chile güero (blonde chile) look, not a pale unripe green
window.gives: a mature, harvestable stage with the mildest bite of the coloured stages; this is the stage the variety is grown and pickled at, and the yellow pods are what give the plant its multi-colour display when picked selectively

window.look: yellow deepening to a strong orange, pod still thick and firm
window.gives: fuller flavour and more heat than yellow while keeping most of the wall firmness — the balanced middle of the window for salsa

window.look: deep glossy red, the finished colour, wall softer than at yellow
window.gives: the fullest flavour of the window — sweet and smoky at full maturity, at the top of its 3,000-5,000 SHU range; best cooked into salsa or sauce rather than pickled for crunch

santafegrande.ripe_vs_unripe: Pale yellow on this pepper is NOT an unripe green pepper — it is the mature wax stage the variety is named for, and it is a legitimate pick. The unripe state is bright green, before any yellow tone appears. The progression is green → yellow → orange → red, and all four colours commonly sit on the plant at once, so a plant carrying yellow, orange and red pods together is normal rather than a sign of uneven ripening.
santafegrande.source: Sandia Seed Company — Santa Fe Grande Pepper Seeds

window.look: small conical pod at full size, skin turned solid dark purple with no grass-green left in it; firm, and it snaps off the plant easily
window.gives: the earliest of the five stages, so the mildest end of this cultivar's 30,000-50,000 SHU range; thin-walled and best used fresh while the purple still shows, since the colour cooks and dries out

window.look: pod goes pale ivory-white, glossy, no green or purple cast remaining
window.gives: the short-lived middle of the sequence and the mildest-looking pod on a plant that is already hot — fresh use, thin slices, where you want a pale pepper rather than a red one

window.look: clear buttery yellow, wall still firm
window.gives: past the halfway point, so more heat than the cream stage and less than the red; a clean fresh-eating stage before the wall starts to soften

window.look: deep orange, skin beginning to lose its hard gloss
window.gives: close to full heat with the wall still sound enough to grill and peel, which is the source's own preserving method for this pepper

window.look: fully red through the shoulders, wall thinner and softer to the squeeze
window.gives: the hottest stage — allowing a hot pepper to ripen fully is what maximises capsaicin — and the only stage worth drying: this is the pod you grind for paprika/flakes, or freeze for winter sauces and stews

chinese5color.ripe_vs_unripe: The five colours the source names START at purple, so green is the only genuinely unripe state — a still-grass-green pod is pre-sequence, undersized and soft. Once a pod has gone solid purple, cream, or yellow it is a full-size, seed-mature pod, not an unripe one: check that it is at full length for the plant, firm and glossy, and that it parts from the stem without tearing the branch. Because a healthy plant carries all five colours simultaneously, colour alone tells you nothing about the pod's age — size, firmness and clean detachment do.
chinese5color.source: John Scheepers Kitchen Garden Seeds — Chile Pepper: Chinese 5-Color (colour sequence, 30,000-50,000 SHU, 85 days, harvest and preserving guidance); ripen-hotter rule from Illinois Extension — How to Grow Peppers
chinese5color.caveat: Colour sequence, heat range and preserving uses are cultivar-sourced. The per-stage heat gradient is extrapolated from the extension rule that hot peppers can be picked at any stage but are hottest fully ripe — no cultivar page rates each colour separately.

purpletiger.window_label: mature green → glossy dark purple → cream/striped → red

window.look: small plump pod near its full ~1 in, still vibrant green, firm; sits against white/green/purple variegated leaves
window.gives: the mildest pick on a 2,500-5,000 SHU pepper — roughly jalapeno-level heat at its lowest here; use fresh where you want bite without dominating the dish

window.look: deep near-black purple with a hard lacquer gloss, sometimes striped part-way through the change; pod is full-size and slightly plump
window.gives: the stage this cultivar is grown for — full-size pod, moderate heat, and the only stage where the purple survives onto the plate; snip it off with shears rather than pulling, and keep it off bare skin

window.look: purple breaking to cream with purple striping, pod still firm
window.gives: past the purple plateau and heading for full heat; still firm enough for fresh use, and the most decorative pod for a garnish

window.look: deep red throughout at about 90 days from transplant, wall softening
window.gives: the hottest and fullest-flavoured stage, and the one worth drying and grinding into chili powder — the purple is gone for good once it reddens

purpletiger.ripe_vs_unripe: The purple stage is not an unripe pod. Unripe here means green AND undersized: a pod that has not filled to its ~1 in length and still feels soft. Purple arrives after the pod has sized up, and the tell is the finish — an immature pod is matt-ish green, while the purple stage is very dark and hard-glossy, almost lacquered, with no green showing through. Striping (purple over cream) is a ripening signal, not a defect, and a full-size purple pod parts from the stem cleanly. Judge it by size, firmness and that glossy solid purple rather than by 'it isn't red yet'.
purpletiger.source: True Leaf Market — Pepper Seeds, Hot, Purple Tiger (green → dark glossy purple → red, ~1 in, 2,500-5,000 SHU, 90 days, snip with shears, dry and grind); Tradewinds Fruit — Purple Tiger Pepper Seeds (variegated white/green/purple foliage, pods ripen purple/cream/red with striped variegation)

window.look: small olive-shaped pod in tight clusters along the stems, inky glossy purple-black, set against dark purple foliage and bright purple flowers
window.gives: the stage the variety was awarded for (2012 AAS winner) — maximum contrast on the plant, and a pod firm enough to pick, though the sources describe no culinary use for it

window.look: clusters turn red over 60-85 days, standing out sharply against the still-dark foliage
window.gives: the mature stage: the strongest ornamental contrast the plant produces, and, by the general hot-pepper rule, the hottest the pods will get — but no source consulted rates this cultivar's heat, so taste one small piece before committing it to a dish

blackolive.ripe_vs_unripe: The purple-black pod reads ripe and is not — the AAS description is explicit that fruits are dark purple and turn red AS they mature, so purple-black is the pre-mature display stage and red is maturity. Because the pods are near-black rather than green, you cannot use colour to judge readiness at all here; use the pepper mechanic instead — the pod should be full-size for its cluster, firm and crisp when squeezed, and break off the plant easily rather than dragging the stem with it.
blackolive.source: All-America Selections — Ornamental Pepper Black Olive (2012 AAS winner; dark purple/black fruit maturing to red, dark purple foliage, bright purple flowers, 18-20 in upright habit); True Leaf Market — Pepper Seeds, Ornamental, Black Olive AAS (60-85 days)
blackolive.caveat: Both pages consulted (All-America Selections and True Leaf Market) describe Black Olive purely as an ornamental — neither states a Scoville rating, a flavour, or any culinary use. Treat it as ornamental-first: the colour window is cultivar-sourced, but the heat and eating quality are unsourced, so taste a small piece before cooking with it.

window.look: blunt-nosed upright pod about 2 in long by 3/8 in across, pale greenish-yellow, held above a compact 8-12 in mound
window.gives: the first stage of the display and a pod that is genuinely non-pungent — the heat was deliberately bred out of this variety, so it is the safe one to hand a curious child; use it as a garnish, not as a heat source

window.look: pods colour up to clear orange, still upright and firm above the foliage
window.gives: peak visual stage in a container or border, and still heatless; the same garnish use for salads and plated dishes with a warmer colour

window.look: matures to dark red — the terminal colour
window.gives: the finished pod: fully mature and still non-pungent, so nothing changes about eating it — its value at this stage is the deepest colour and the end of the season's display

chillychill.ripe_vs_unripe: Every stage of this pepper looks lightly unripe and none of them are dangerous or bitter to eat, because pungency was bred out rather than being a function of ripeness. A greenish-yellow pod is at its intended first colour, not an immature green one — the discriminator is that the pod has reached about 2 in with a blunt, rounded nose and stands upright and firm above the leaves. A truly immature pod is short, tapered and soft. Red is simply the last colour, not the point at which it becomes edible.
chillychill.source: All-America Selections — Ornamental Pepper Chilly Chili F1 (2002 AAS winner; fruit changes colour from yellow to orange and matures at red; non-pungent, heat bred out, safe around children; 2 in x 3/8 in pods; 8-12 in mounded plant; garnish use)
chillychill.caveat: The sourced cultivar is spelled 'Chilly Chili' F1 (AAS 2002) — almost certainly the same variety recorded here as 'Chilly Chill', but the name differs from the app record. Heatlessness is verified: AAS states the pungency was bred out in favour of colour and that it is safe around children. This is an ornamental with garnish use, not a culinary pepper.

bulgariancarrot.window_label: mature green → orange blush → full bright orange

window.look: carrot-shaped pod at close to its full 3 in, tapering, firm and crisp when squeezed, snaps off the plant without tearing
window.gives: the mildest pick on a pepper that finishes about as hot as a serrano; crisp and vegetal rather than fruity, and firm enough to hold up in a pickle jar

window.look: colour breaking unevenly from the tip and shoulders, green and orange on the same pod
window.gives: part-way to the fruity character the variety is known for while the wall is still at its crispest — the best compromise stage for frying and for salsa where you want crunch

window.look: solid bright orange end to end, no green left; still a firm, crisp-walled pod on a plant that may be toppling under 40-plus fruits
window.gives: the finished stage — full serrano-level heat with the fruity flavour the variety is grown for, and the only stage to dry: whole for hanging, or pounded into flakes. Also the stage for roasting and pickling

bulgariancarrot.ripe_vs_unripe: Bright orange IS ripe here — this variety has no red stage, so an orange pod is a finished pod, not one caught halfway. The discriminator is uniformity and depth of colour: a ripening pod carries green and orange together, usually breaking at the tip and shoulders, while a finished one is solid saturated orange from stem to point with no green cast. Do not leave orange pods on the plant waiting for red; you will only lose wall firmness. A pod picked green is a legitimate early pick, but it is the mild, non-fruity version of this pepper.
bulgariancarrot.source: Experimental Farm Network Seed Store — 'Bulgarian Carrot' ('Shipka') Hot Pepper (bright orange at maturity, ~3 in carrot-shaped pods, about as spicy as a serrano, fruity but hot, 40-55 fruits per plant, uses: drying whole, chili flakes, roasting, frying, salsa, pickling)

window.look: slender finger-long pod, 3-5 in, pale yellow-green rather than dark green, thin-walled and wrinkling slightly like a shishito; ready about 67 days after planting
window.gives: the stage the catalogue explicitly tells you to pick at — subtly smoky, sweet, and only about 200 SHU, roughly a tenth of a jalapeno. This is the blistering/roasting stage: char it with sesame, drop it in tempura, or eat it raw as a mild condiment. Expect the occasional pod that comes out unexpectedly hot

window.look: pod colours through to red, wall thinner and softer
window.gives: the catalogue's guidance is to pick before this — the pod loses the crisp texture and the smoky green character that the variety is grown for. Left this long it is sweeter and at its hottest for the variety, which for a 50-200 SHU pepper still means barely warm; usable, but not what the plant is for

dragonroll.ripe_vs_unripe: This is a pepper you pick green on purpose, so 'green' here is the finished product rather than an unripe pod. The tell is shade and shape, not colour change: a ready pod is a light chartreuse — yellow-green rather than deep grass-green — has reached a full 3-5 in finger length, feels thin-walled and slightly loose in the hand with the beginnings of shishito-type wrinkling, and breaks off the plant easily. An immature pod is short, stiff, darker green and holds on when you pull. Red is not an improvement; it is the far end of the window.
dragonroll.source: Wilson's Garden Center — Pepper, Hot 'Dragon Roll' (Shishito Type) (chartreuse-green 3-5 in pods maturing to red, Scoville 200 / about a tenth of a jalapeno, subtly smoky when young, mingling of heat and sweet, 67 days, 'Pick peppers when green before they transition to red', roasting with sesame / tempura / raw condiment)

anaheim.window_label: mature green → pinto → full red → plant-dried red

window.look: full length for the type (7–7.5 in on this cultivar), deep glossy green, flat-sided with the pod filled out, bluntly pointed; firm and crisp when squeezed, and it snaps off the plant easily instead of clinging
window.gives: this is green chile: the roasting/peeling stage. Thick, meaty flesh means more usable pepper left after you pull the blistered skin off, so it holds up for chile verde, rellenos and enchiladas. Bright, lightly sweet peppery flavour with the heat at the bottom of the pod's range.

window.look: green pod carrying its first red streaks and blush, wall still firm
window.gives: still behaves as green chile in the pan, but with the first ripening sugars showing, so it tastes rounder and less grassy than a flat green pod. NMSU uses the appearance of pinto pods in the row as the signal that the green crop has hit peak mature-green quality — so a few pintos are your cue to start picking green in earnest.

window.look: solid rich red over the whole pod, skin still smooth, flesh beginning to soften under the thumb
window.gives: sweeter — ripening puts sugar into the pod, so red reads fruity where green reads vegetal — and this is the stage red chile sauce, red chile powder and flakes are made from. Softer flesh, so it's the weaker choice for stuffing and it wants gentler roasting than a green pod.

window.at: red, dried on the plant or hung
window.look: deep red going leathery and slightly wrinkled, pod losing gloss and firmness
window.gives: the ristra stage. You can leave pods to dry on the plant, or cut them fully ripe and hang them by their stems — either way you get whole dried pods for grinding into powder or flakes, and concentrated storage that needs no freezer, unlike green chile.

anaheim.ripe_vs_unripe: You are picking this green on purpose, so the test is maturity, not colour. A correct mature-green Anaheim is at full length for the cultivar, has filled out flat-sided rather than staying skinny, is bluntly pointed rather than tapering to a soft tip, feels firm and crisp — not squashy or hollow — when you squeeze it, and detaches easily when you lift it. An immature pod is undersized, soft-walled, and hangs on the plant when you try to take it. Colour alone tells you nothing here: a young pod and a mature pod are both green.
anaheim.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-240 — Growing Chile Peppers in New Mexico Gardens
anaheim.caveat: Stage mechanics, green-vs-red use and the drying/ristra options come from NMSU H-240 and H-230 (https://pubs.nmsu.edu/_h/H230/); the sweeter-when-red point is NMSU's Chile Pepper Institute (red pods produce more sugar); the thick-flesh/easy-peel and 7.5 in size are from Sandia Seed's Anaheim listing. Heat: this cultivar sits mild (roughly 500–1,000 SHU) either way — do not expect red to make it hot.

window.look: rich near-black dark green, glossy, very firm, large and obviously full-sized — the pod reaches full size before it starts ripening, so watch for growth to stop and then give it another week or two
window.gives: the crunch-and-savour stage: firmest flesh and the best texture of the whole window, which is why this is the standard pepper for roasting and stuffing. Deep savoury, faintly grassy flavour; heat stays mild here (around 1,000 SHU or less).

window.look: colours through to red or reddish-brown, and the flesh goes noticeably softer to the squeeze
window.gives: sweeter and less grassy. The heat does not really climb — it stays around the same mild level — but the extra sugar offsets what heat there is, so it tastes milder than the green pod. Better for sauces than for stuffing now that the wall has softened.

window.look: fully red-brown pod dried down to leathery, wrinkled, dark mahogany
window.gives: this is what makes it an ancho — ancho is simply a dried ripe poblano. Drying deepens and concentrates the flavour into the sweet, raisiny, faintly smoky note you want for moles and sauces, and gives you shelf-stable storage. Sun-drying in genuinely dry conditions gives the best flavour; a dehydrator works.

ancho.ripe_vs_unripe: Ancho and poblano are one pepper at two stages, and the green stage is a deliberate pick, so judge maturity not colour. A ready green pod is full-sized (they are big enough that full size is obvious), very dark and glossy rather than pale green, and very firm. The reliable trick is to watch a pod stop growing, then wait one to two more weeks — that pod is mature green even though nothing about its colour changed.
ancho.source: Pepper Geek — When To Pick Poblano Peppers (Simple Harvesting Tips)
ancho.caveat: 'Ancho' and 'Poblano' are the same pepper — ancho is the name for the dried ripe pod, poblano the fresh one, so this one plant covers both. Cultivar-specific but sourced from a grower site rather than university extension; the crop-level firm-and-crisp maturity test cross-checks against NMSU H-240.

newmexico.window_label: mature green → pinto → full red → partially dried red

window.look: the NMSU description of an ideal mature-green pod: about 6–7 in long, flat (two-celled), smooth, thick-fleshed, bluntly pointed, and firm when squeezed. Deep green with gloss; mature pods detach easily. Roughly 35–50 days after the plant flowers
window.gives: green chile — the stage that gets roasted and peeled, then frozen or canned whole or diced. Thick, meaty walls mean more usable flesh survives peeling, so this is your stage for chile verde, stews and stuffing, with the classic bright green-chile flavour.

window.look: pods streaked and blotched red over green — NMSU's 'pinto' stage
window.gives: cooks as green chile with a rounder, slightly sweeter edge. In the field the arrival of pinto pods is the signal to make the first green harvest, so pintos on the plant mean the rest of your green crop is at peak quality right now.

window.look: solid deep red, well pigmented, wall softening
window.gives: flavour intensifies and the pod sweetens as ripening builds sugars. This is the red chile stage: red chile sauce, and the raw material for red chile powder. Same pod, different dish — you are trading green chile's fresh vegetal snap for depth and sweetness.

window.look: red pod starting to shrivel and go leathery on the plant, deeply coloured
window.gives: how red chile is actually harvested commercially — picked red, ripe and partially dried, then finished to whole dried pods, flakes or powder. Practically: string them into a ristra and you have a year of red chile with no freezer space used.

newmexico.ripe_vs_unripe: The green pick is intentional, so maturity is judged by build and feel, not colour. Mature green means full length for the cultivar (6–8 in), the pod flattened and filled out with two cells rather than round and skinny, smooth-shouldered, bluntly pointed, thick-fleshed and firm when squeezed — and it comes off the plant easily. Undersized, soft, sharply tapered pods that cling are immature and will peel badly after roasting.
newmexico.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-230 — Growing Chiles in New Mexico
newmexico.caveat: 'Hatch-type' covers the NMSU New Mexican pod cultivars (Joe E. Parker, Big Jim, NM 6-4 and kin) rather than one single cultivar, so heat varies by which one you planted — commonly mild-to-medium, roughly 1,000–3,000 SHU. Mature-green pod description and the pinto/red harvest stages are NMSU H-230 and H-240; the 'flavour intensifies at red', thick-wall/more-flesh-after-peeling, and ristra/powder points come from Sandia Seed's Joe E. Parker listing.

Parker listing.

window.look: a long curved horn-shaped pod at or near its full 8–10 in, thick-walled and heavy for its size, glossy mid-green, firm and crisp when squeezed, detaching easily
window.gives: the firmest wall of the window — the stage to take if you want pods that stay crisp in a pickle jar or hold their shape roasted or stuffed. Flavour is flatly vegetal here and the sweet-and-spice balance this type is grown for has not arrived yet.

window.look: bright red the whole length of the pod, thick flesh still substantial, skin smooth
window.gives: the stage this type is normally picked at: sweet undertones behind a medium heat (roughly 2,500–5,000 SHU on this vendor's rating, higher on others), which is what makes it work for hot sauce and roasting. Its thick flesh also makes it the pod to pickle whole, and red pods are what you dry down for flakes and powder.

cowhorn.ripe_vs_unripe: If you are taking pods green, colour cannot help you — go by build: full 8–10 in length, wall thick enough that the pod feels heavy, firm and crisp under a squeeze, and it releases from the plant with a light lift rather than needing a pull. A thin, light, short pod is immature and will be all skin and seed.
cowhorn.source: Sandia Seed Company — Cow Horn Hot Pepper Seeds (Medium Heat Heirloom)
cowhorn.caveat: 'Cowhorn' is a vendor name, not a single stable cultivar — it is a large cayenne-type hot pepper and heat ratings differ sharply between sellers (2,500–5,000 SHU on the page used here, up to 10,000–30,000 elsewhere). Red-stage character comes from that seed listing; the mature-green look and payoff are derived from cayenne-type and general chile guidance (NMSU H-230 notes cayenne types are picked in the red succulent stage, and H-240 gives the firm-and-crisp mature-green test). Treat the green pick as usable but off-label for this type.

sweetsivri.window_label: young green → mature pale green → red

window.look: long thin pod short of full length, pale green, very firm and tight-skinned
window.gives: the pickling pick, and the source is explicit about it: young green pods make crispier pickles than mature ones. You trade sweetness and size for snap and shelf texture.

window.look: full length, long and thin with the pod filled out and straightened, pale green, firm and crisp when squeezed, detaching easily
window.gives: the frying stage — a thin-walled pod at full size blisters and collapses fast in hot oil the way a Turkish frying pepper is meant to, and stays savoury rather than candy-sweet. Already sweet, but with a green edge behind it.

window.look: ripening through to red along the length of the pod; wall softens as it colours
window.gives: full maturity and the variety's intense sweetness at its peak, since ripening builds sugar in the pod. Best fresh or fried when you want the sweetness forward; the softer wall makes it a poorer pickle than the young green pod.

sweetsivri.ripe_vs_unripe: This pepper is pale green even when it is ready, and you may be picking green deliberately, so shade is a weak signal. Judge it by build and feel: full length for a long thin pod, the pod filled out and straightened rather than skinny and floppy, firm and crisp — not soft or hollow — when squeezed, and coming away from the plant easily. If a pod is still lengthening, it is young: fine for pickles, early for frying.
sweetsivri.source: Thresh Seed Co. — Tatli Kil Sivri (Sweet Sivri) Pepper Seeds
sweetsivri.caveat: Colour progression (pale green ripening to red), the intense sweetness, the fresh/frying/pickling uses and the young-green-for-crispier-pickles advice are cultivar-specific from that seed listing, which is a vendor rather than extension. The thin-walled frying-pepper handling and the firm-and-crisp mature-green test are type-level and crop-level (NMSU H-240) — the listing does not state wall thickness.

gatherersgold.window_label: pale green → full gold (gold is ripe — it never reds)

window.look: long, tapered, distinctly wrinkled pod that has reached full length but not yet coloured; firm and crisp when squeezed, detaching easily from the plant
