window.gives: a usable early pick if you need a pepper now — full size and firm wall — but you are taking it before the variety's whole point arrives. Expect a plainer, greener pepper than a coloured one.

window.look: the same long wrinkled tapered fruit gone a saturated warm gold, and that is where it stops — the breeder's own description is that it remains gold even at full maturity. Few seeds inside
window.gives: the finished pepper: this is a golden Italian frying/roasting type, so the gold pod is the one for the pan and for roasting, and the low seed count means very little cleanup for the amount of flesh you get. Waiting past gold for red gains you nothing — red never comes.

gatherersgold.ripe_vs_unripe: This is a gold-when-ripe pepper, so the usual 'wait for red' instinct will make you leave pods on the plant forever. Ripe is a saturated, warm, even gold with gloss over the whole pod, on a fruit that has finished lengthening and shows its characteristic wrinkling. Unripe is a flat, cool pale green, and the transition runs green → yellow-green → gold, so a pod that looks yellowish-green with green still in the shoulders is close but not done. If a pod is fully gold, it is ripe — pick it.
gatherersgold.source: Wild Garden Seed — Organic Gatherer's Gold Sweet Italian (Peppers) Seeds
gatherersgold.caveat: The load-bearing fact — that it stays gold at full maturity and never turns red — plus the wrinkled tapered pod, few seeds, and 102 days from transplant at Corvallis, Oregon come from the breeder (Frank Morton, Wild Garden Seed), cross-checked on the Experimental Farm Network listing. Those pages give no flavour or wall-thickness detail, so the frying/roasting payoff is type-level for a sweet Italian frying pepper (other catalogues describe it as very sweet), the green-stage payoff and the maturity test are crop-level (NMSU H-240), and the green → yellow-green → gold shade sequence is derived, not quoted.

piripiri.window_label: mature deep green → pale yellow-green → orange → full red

window.look: pod at full length for the plant (roughly 1-3 in long, about 1/2 in across), deep even green, glossy, firm and crisp when squeezed; snaps cleanly off the stem
window.gives: the coolest stage the pod ever has - sharp, grassy, vegetal bite with a faintly bitter edge and the firmest flesh; best cooked (stir-fry, sautéed into a green garlic-and-citrus piri-piri) and it keeps longest off the plant. Capsaicin is still accumulating at this point, so a green pick forfeits a large share of the pod's final heat

window.look: the deep green drains out to a pale straw-green / yellow-green while the skin stays high-gloss; chlorophyll breaking down, carotenoids not yet dominant
window.gives: the grassy, bitter note starts to fade and the first sweetness appears; heat is climbing but still well short of peak - this is the pick for someone who wants mild without the raw vegetal edge

window.look: solid orange, sometimes with a green shoulder holding on; flesh noticeably more tender than green
window.gives: the balance stage - clearly sweeter and more complex than green, the fruity/citrusy piri-piri aromatics arriving and the grassy edge gone, with heat climbing but not at the red maximum. This is the best stage for a raw or fresh sauce and for salsa, where you want piri-piri character without the full heat wall. It is a poor drying stage: still high-moisture and the powder cannot come out red from an orange pod

window.look: uniform vibrant red top to tip, gloss slightly duller, flesh softer than green; thin walls
window.gives: maximum heat plus the true fruity-citrus piri-piri flavour, and peak sugars as starches convert. This is the stage for drying and powder - the thin walls dry fast and only a red pod yields red flakes/powder - for infused oil, for traditional dried piri-piri sauce, and it is the sugar-richest stage to put into a mash or ferment. Also the only stage where saved seed is viable

piripiri.ripe_vs_unripe: Green Piri Piri is a deliberate pick, so the thing to tell apart is mature green from undersized immature green - not green from red. Mature green: pod has reached full length and width for that plant, skin is tight and high-gloss, and the pod feels firm and crisp (not rubbery) when squeezed, and detaches with a clean snap. Immature: short, narrow, matte or soft-skinned, clings to the stem. The next shift is a tone change rather than a colour change - deep leaf-green drains toward pale straw / yellow-green before any orange shows, so a pod that looks 'washed-out green' is already past mature green and on its way up.
piripiri.source: PlantNative - Piri Piri Pepper: Growing Guide, Heat Profile & Uses; corroborated by Truelove Seeds - West Park Bird's Eye (Piri Piri) Pepper and NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox - Capsicum frutescens
piripiri.caveat: Colour sequence (green → yellow/orange → red) and the green-vs-red flavour/heat contrast are cultivar-sourced, and the species-level sequence is confirmed by NC State Extension for Capsicum frutescens. The per-stage payoffs for the intermediate yellow-green and orange points are derived from general pepper colour-stage guidance (KnowThePepper - Pepper Colors), not from a Piri Piri-specific source. No source states a fermenting stage; the ferment note follows from peak sugars at full red. Truelove Seeds notes some Piri Piri lines pass through a green-purple phase - a purple cast is normal, not disease. Measured support: capsaicin rose 3636 → 4820 µg/g from green to yellow-ripe on Habanero (Antioxidants 2019, 8(9):364, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6770197/), consistent with heat still building at the green stage.

tabasco.window_label: pale yellowish-green → yellow → orange → bright red

window.look: pod at full size, about 1.5 in (4 cm) long, tapered, standing erect rather than hanging; colour is a pale yellowish-green - not a dark leaf green - firm and glossy
window.gives: the sharpest, tangiest, least hot pick with the firmest flesh and the longest keeping - use where you want acid and vegetal snap rather than heat. Capsaicin is still building, so this stage gives up much of the pod's eventual heat

window.look: pale green gone entirely to clear yellow; skin still tight and glossy
window.gives: chlorophyll is gone and the first sugars show - less grassy and slightly sweet, heat climbing, flesh still crisp; a usable pick for a bright, moderate-heat fresh sauce

window.look: solid orange, occasionally with a green-yellow shoulder; flesh more tender than green
window.gives: sweeter and rounder than yellow with fruity aromatics appearing and the grassy note gone; heat well up but short of maximum. The balance stage for raw salsa or a fresh table sauce

window.look: uniform bright red, still erect on the plant, flesh softer than at green
window.gives: peak capsaicin and peak sugars with the richest, roundest flavour - this is the traditional stage for Tabasco mash and peppered vinegar, and pods are picked at full red for exactly this reason. Also the only stage that dries or grinds to a red powder, and the only stage with viable seed

tabasco.ripe_vs_unripe: Tabasco's mature green is genuinely pale - a yellowish-green, not a deep green - so a dark green pod is usually still filling out rather than ready. Judge mature green by full length (about 4 cm), a tight glossy skin, firm/crisp feel when squeezed, and the pod sitting fully erect; a soft or matte pod that clings to the stem is immature. Because the ripe sequence goes pale green → yellow, the first real ripening signal is a warming of tone rather than a new colour: the green picking up a clear yellow cast, most visible at the tip.
tabasco.source: Wikipedia - Tabasco pepper; colour sequence corroborated by NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox - Capsicum frutescens
tabasco.caveat: Cultivar detail (pod size, erect habit, pale yellowish-green → yellow → orange → red, 30,000-50,000 SHU, mash/peppered-vinegar use) comes from Wikipedia - a last-resort source - though NC State Extension independently confirms the green → yellow → orange → red sequence for Capsicum frutescens and notes the species suits drying and grinding to powder. The stage-by-stage flavour, sweetness and texture payoffs are derived from general pepper colour-stage guidance (KnowThePepper - Pepper Colors), not from a Tabasco-specific source. Measured support: capsaicin rose 3636 → 4820 µg/g from green to yellow-ripe on Habanero (Antioxidants 2019, 8(9):364, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6770197/), consistent with heat still building at the green stage.

window.look: slender pods at full length, held in upright clusters, glossy and crisp green, firm when squeezed
window.gives: crisp, green and the least hot the pod will be, with a sharp direct bite and a clean chile finish - the firm flesh holds its shape in a stir-fry or curry and in hot oil, and green pods keep longest after picking

window.look: pods streaking or blushing from the tip as green gives way, part green and part colour on the same pod
window.gives: the grassy edge dropping away and sugars starting to build while heat is still climbing - a middle pick when you want more roundness than green but not the full ripe intensity

window.look: narrow chiles coloured fully deep red across the whole cluster; flesh drier to the touch than at green
window.gives: sweeter, richer, hotter, drier and more aromatic than the green stage - and the drier flesh is what makes this the stage for drying, flakes, powder and chile oil, where a green or part-coloured pod would neither keep nor grind red. Also the stage that carries the full 50,000-100,000 SHU

thaidragon.ripe_vs_unripe: Green Thai Dragon is a deliberate pick, so distinguish mature green from immature: mature pods have reached full length for the cluster, are glossy and tight-skinned, and feel firm and crisp rather than pliable. Undersized, matte, bendy pods are still growing and will taste thin as well as flat.
thaidragon.source: Alliance of Native Seedkeepers - Thai Dragon Pepper Seeds
thaidragon.caveat: Cultivar-specific but from a seed vendor rather than extension. The vendor states plainly that harvest stage changes flavour and texture - young pods crisp and green, fully ripe sweeter, richer, hotter, drier and more aromatic - but does not describe the intermediate colours, so the part-coloured point is derived from general pepper colour-stage guidance (KnowThePepper - Pepper Colors) and should be treated as the softest claim in this entry.

cayenneblend.window_label: mature green → part-coloured → full ripe colour

window.look: long slender pods at roughly full length for a cayenne (commonly 4-5 in), firm, with a waxy rather than matte sheen
window.gives: the milder pick - noticeably more vegetal and less intense, with firm flesh that holds up cooked; useful when you want cayenne shape and crunch without cayenne heat

window.look: colour breaking from the tip or in streaks while the shoulder stays green
window.gives: heat and sweetness both rising while the grassy note fades - the compromise pick, and a way to keep a heavily loaded plant setting new pods

window.look: pod coloured uniformly to its final colour (vibrant red on standard cayenne lines), still firm, skin waxy
window.gives: the best flavour and the full heat - and the only stage worth drying: dehydrating fully ripe pods is what produces cayenne powder and flakes, so ripeness here is not a nicety but the whole payoff. A pod picked green or half-turned cannot yield red powder

cayenneblend.ripe_vs_unripe: Green here is a deliberate pick, so judge mature green by size and feel, not colour: a cayenne at full length (about 4-5 in) with a waxy, tight skin that is firm and crisp when squeezed and detaches easily is mature; short, matte, soft pods are immature and will be thin-fleshed and flat-tasting.
cayenneblend.source: Grow Hot Peppers - When To Pick Cayenne Peppers: Best Time For Harvesting
cayenneblend.caveat: No cultivar-specific source found - 'Cayenne Blend' is a mixed packet, not a single variety, so no single description can be accurate for every plant in it. Window derived from general cayenne-type guidance. Critically: a blend may contain lines that finish a colour other than red, so do not assume red is the end point - watch the first pod on each plant all the way through and let that plant's own final colour define its late window. The part-coloured point is derived from general pepper colour-stage guidance rather than a cayenne source.

window.look: long slender pod fully developed for its length, firm and crisp when squeezed, detaching easily from the plant
window.gives: the mild, vegetal pick with the firmest flesh - fine for fresh cooking, but it forfeits both the heat and the entire dried-chile payoff this type is grown for

window.look: red breaking through from the tip while green holds at the shoulder
window.gives: heat and sweetness climbing - a usable fresh pick, but too green to string: a part-coloured pod in a ristra reads as a gap and dries unevenly

window.look: coloured uniformly deep red, skin waxy, pod firm; can be left to go leathery on the plant
window.gives: full heat and the richest flavour, and the only stage that works for the thing a ristra-type cayenne exists for - it can either be left to dry on the plant or picked fully ripe and hung by its stems in strings (ristras) to dry. Full ripeness is what gives dried pods and ground powder their red colour and concentrated flavour; a green or half-turned pod dries dull and pale

ristacayanneii.ripe_vs_unripe: For the green pick, maturity is judged by feel and size rather than colour: extension guidance for chile is that the pod should be fully developed, firm and crisp when squeezed, and most mature pods detach easily from the plant. A pod that bends, feels hollow, or has to be tugged is immature.
ristacayanneii.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-240 - Growing Chile Peppers in New Mexico Gardens (maturity and ristra drying); cayenne-type green-vs-red contrast from Grow Hot Peppers - When To Pick Cayenne Peppers
ristacayanneii.caveat: No source resolved for the exact cultivar name 'Rista Cayanne II'. Window derived from New Mexico ristra-type / cayenne-type guidance: NMSU H-240 supplies the maturity test (fully developed, firm, crisp, detaches easily) and the ristra practice (dry on the plant, or pick fully ripe and hang by the stems), and general cayenne guidance supplies the green-vs-red flavour and heat contrast. Treat pod dimensions and days-to-maturity as unverified for this specific line.

window.look: 2-3 in pods at full length, bright glossy green, standing in upright clusters of five or six at the top of the plant
window.gives: a genuinely mild pick - the Chile Pepper Institute lists green Yatsufusa as a normal harvest with mild heat - so this is the stage for fresh use in stir-fries, curries and soups where you want the pepper's shape and a light bite rather than cayenne-level heat; green pods also freeze well

window.look: green giving way unevenly within the cluster, some pods streaking red while neighbours are still green
window.gives: heat rising past the mild green stage as sugars build; usable fresh, but too moist and too pale to dry - hold these for the branch-drying pass rather than cutting the whole cluster early

window.look: pods coloured to a deep glossy lacquer red across the cluster
window.gives: the full cayenne/Thai-level heat and flavour this variety is grown for, and the only stage for the dried payoff: ripe red pods are the ones ground into shichimi togarashi, and drying is done by cutting the branches, stripping the leaves and hanging until the fruit is dry. Only a red pod grinds to a red powder - and the Institute's own suggestion is to use both, fresh green and dried red, for the fullest range

yatsufusa.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is a deliberate pick here, so what matters is mature green versus immature green: mature pods have reached 2-3 in, are bright and glossy rather than dull, and feel firm when squeezed. Because the pods stand upright in tight clusters, they ripen unevenly - a green pod beside a red one in the same cluster is normal and is not a sign the plant is behind.
yatsufusa.caveat: Green and red harvest stages, pod size, cluster habit, heat comparison and the drying/shichimi-togarashi use are all cultivar-sourced from the Chile Pepper Institute. The intermediate part-coloured point is not described by that source and is derived from general pepper colour-stage behaviour.

window.look: tiny oval to oblong pods at full size for the type - only about 1/2 to 3/4 in long and 1/4 in wide - firm and glossy green; ripe pods pop off the plant readily
window.gives: the fresh-use stage: greener, less ripe pods are the ones used fresh, and heat is at its lowest because it keeps building the longer the pod stays on the plant. Pick green when you want the pod's bite in something raw or quickly cooked rather than a dried chile

window.look: pod coloured a uniform vibrant red; comes away from the plant with almost no pressure
window.gives: hotter than green - up to the type's 30,000-60,000 SHU - with the fruity, citrusy, nutty character fully developed, and this is the stage the pepper is actually grown for: red pods are what get dried (or smoked then dried) and ground into flakes and powder, which is where the flavour concentrates. A green piquin dried gives you neither the heat nor the red

piquin.ripe_vs_unripe: The pods are so small that size is a weak cue, so use detachment and colour: fully ripe piquin pop right off the plant with almost no pull, while immature pods hold on. Green is a legitimate pick, but it is the deliberately-less-ripe pick, not the finished one.
piquin.source: Chili Pepper Madness - Pequin Peppers (Chili Pequin) - All About Them
piquin.caveat: Type-level source only, and a last-resort tier (enthusiast site, not extension or breeder) - no cultivar-specific page found for the 'Piquin' line in the packet. Piquin/pequin is a small wild-type chile with wide variation between seed lots in pod size and heat, so treat the dimensions and SHU range as typical rather than exact. Note also that at least one other online source claims green piquin are hotter than red - that contradicts the sourced 'heat keeps building on the plant' statement used here, so if your own pods taste hotter green, trust your palate over this entry.

bhutjolokia.window_label: mature green → orange → wrinkled scarlet red

window.look: full size at 3-4 in, firm flesh, skin already showing the variety's unusual puckered/pebbled structure rather than smooth immature skin
window.gives: the pickling and green-sauce stage - firmest flesh and a flatter, more vegetal heat; usable but you are picking before the fruity aroma the variety is grown for has formed

window.look: pods turn orange first, roughly 100 days after the green pods have formed, before going on to red - colour comes in unevenly over the shoulders
window.gives: the transition point: heat is close to full but the aroma is still developing, so this is the stage to take if you want fierce heat and want to slow the plant down without waiting out full red

window.look: wrinkled, scarlet, uniformly coloured with no green left under the calyx; flesh firm
window.gives: full pungency - about 1,001,304 SHU as measured at NMSU, near twice a Red Savina - and the payoff stage for drying: firm flesh that yields a lot of powder, with the subtle fruity aroma only really unfolding once dried. Fresh at this stage the sources describe an almost chemical edge from the sheer capsaicin load

bhutjolokia.source: Chili-Plant.com - Bhut Jolokia Chilliplants growing & scoville scale (colour progression, texture, aroma); Urban Farmer - Red Bhut Jolokia (Ghost) Pepper Seeds (size, SHU, 100 days, harvest when they start to turn red)

ghost.window_label: mature green → orange → wrinkled scarlet red

window.look: full size at 3-4 in, firm flesh, skin already showing the variety's unusual puckered/pebbled structure rather than smooth immature skin
window.gives: the pickling and green-sauce stage - firmest flesh and a flatter, more vegetal heat; usable but you are picking before the fruity aroma the variety is grown for has formed

window.look: pods turn orange first, roughly 100 days after the green pods have formed, before going on to red - colour comes in unevenly over the shoulders
window.gives: the transition point: heat is close to full but the aroma is still developing, so this is the stage to take if you want fierce heat and want to slow the plant down without waiting out full red

window.look: wrinkled, scarlet, uniformly coloured with no green left under the calyx; flesh firm
window.gives: full pungency - about 1,001,304 SHU as measured at NMSU - and the payoff stage for drying: firm flesh that yields a lot of powder, with the subtle fruity aroma only really unfolding once dried. Fresh at this stage the sources describe an almost chemical edge from the sheer capsaicin load

ghost.source: Chili-Plant.com - Bhut Jolokia Chilliplants growing & scoville scale (colour progression, texture, aroma); Urban Farmer - Red Bhut Jolokia (Ghost) Pepper Seeds (size, SHU, 100 days, harvest when they start to turn red)
ghost.caveat: Ghost and Bhut Jolokia are two names for the same pepper - this entry is identical to the Bhut Jolokia one on purpose. Colour-stage detail comes from a grower reference site rather than an extension or breeder page.

window.look: full-size lantern pod, wrinkled superhot skin, firm - green and glossy with no colour break yet
window.gives: a workable green-heat pod, but on a 1,300,000 SHU chinense the fruity note the variety is prized for has not arrived yet; the practical reason to pick here is to push a slow plant into setting more fruit rather than flavour

window.look: evenly dark red across the whole pod including under the shoulders, skin still taut
window.gives: the stage the variety was bred for - 1,300,000 SHU (over four times a habanero) with the fruity flavour behind it; this is the pod worth waiting for, and as an F1 bred for reduced days to maturity it should reach it earlier than open-pollinated superhots. Sow Seeds' own advice is to sow early because Armageddon takes a long time to fruit and ripen, harvest running August-October

armageddonf1.source: Sow Seeds Ltd - Chilli Pepper Armageddon F1 Seeds (SHU, fruity flavour, ripening/harvest timing); Tozer Seeds - Armageddon F1 (breeder, first F1 hybrid super-hot, reduced days to maturity, vigour and yield)
armageddonf1.caveat: Neither the breeder page (Tozer) nor the retailer page describes the intermediate colours, so only the two ends of the window are sourced - expect this pod to blush orange before red like other superhot chinense, and treat any orange stage as near-full heat rather than unripe.

window.look: wrinkled pod at full size, about 2 in x 1 1/4 in, firm and glossy green - Johnny's lists roughly 80 days from transplant to this stage
window.gives: measurably less heat: capsaicin runs about 3636 ug/g green against 4820 ug/g at ripe, so you give up roughly a third of the capsaicin. What you gain is vitamin C - 820 mg/100g dry weight green versus 349 ripe, more than double - plus firmer flesh and a sharper, greener flavour. Johnny's also advises picking the first pods promptly at full size to keep the plant setting fruit, so early pods are the ones to take green

window.look: wrinkled pod coloured right through to salmon orange with no green under the calyx; about 100 days from transplant
window.gives: the hottest stage - capsaicin up about 33% on green (4820 vs 3636 ug/g), total phenolics up ~39% and flavonoids more than doubled (204 to 467 ug/g), with the fruity citrus notes the variety is grown for. Cost of waiting: vitamin C falls by over half and the wall softens

habanero.ripe_vs_unripe: Ripe habanero here is salmon orange, not red - an orange pod is fully ripe and is the hottest state, not an unfinished red one. Read ripeness by evenness of colour rather than by hue: a finished pod is the same orange over the shoulders and right up under the calyx, with no green shadow left, and the skin has gone from hard-glossy green to a slightly softer sheen.
habanero.source: Antioxidants 2019, 8(9):364 - ripening-stage capsaicinoid and antioxidant measurements in Habanero (green vs yellow-ripe); Johnny's Selected Seeds - Habanero Organic (colour, pod size, 80/100 days, pick first pods promptly)

window.look: squat bonnet pod at full size, about 1.5 in wide and long - stouter than a habanero - firm, wrinkled and still solid green
window.gives: a firm, sharp green-heat pod for cooking down; you keep the wall firmness but you have not yet got the sweet citrus character that separates this from a plain habanero, which is the whole reason to grow it

window.look: coloured evenly to a vivid orange, skin taut and glossy with the signature wrinkling, no shrivel; about 90 days from transplant
window.gives: the jerk-and-hot-sauce stage: ~300,000 SHU with the complex sweet, citrus-like flavour, distinctly sweeter than a standard habanero. This is the pod for jerk marinade, sauce and salsa, and the stage growers dry, smoke and ferment

scotchbonnet.ripe_vs_unripe: Ripe is orange, not red - a fully orange bonnet is finished, not half-ripe. Note that Scotch Bonnet is a family of strains: yellow, orange and red-ripening lines all exist, so learn which one you planted and treat its own full colour as the endpoint. Whatever the hue, ripe reads as even colour edge to edge including under the calyx, taut glossy skin, and no wrinkling or shrivel beyond the variety's natural puckering.
scotchbonnet.source: Sandia Seed Company - Scotch Bonnet Pepper Seeds, Hot Orange Scotch

window.look: full-size, firm and crisp when squeezed, glossy green, and detaching from the plant easily - the general extension test for a mature-green chile rather than an undersized one
window.gives: a firm, thick-walled green pod carrying the jalapeno side of its parentage - good for salsa and pickling, and the stage to take if you want the wall rather than the ripe flavour

window.look: colour carried evenly over the whole pod including under the calyx; wall gives very slightly under thumb pressure
window.gives: the sauce stage the variety was bred for - it was selected over seven years from a thick-walled jalapeno crossed with ghost pepper to land at about mild-habanero heat, balanced for hot sauce, and also the stage to dehydrate for flakes

palmettopunch.ripe_vs_unripe: Ripe colour is not confirmed by any source that could be read for this entry, so do not assume red - watch your own first pods through to their endpoint and record it. In either case ripe reads the same way: colour even across the whole pod with no green left under the calyx, skin taut, wall just yielding to a thumb.
palmettopunch.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-240 - Growing Chile Peppers in New Mexico Gardens (mature-green and ripening criteria used for the derivation)
palmettopunch.caveat: No cultivar-specific page could be retrieved - the Baker Creek listing blocks fetching. Parentage and heat level come from that listing's visible summary only, and the window itself is derived from general mature-green-to-ripe chile guidance in NMSU H-240. The ripe colour is unverified; treat the endpoint as 'whatever colour your pods finish at', not red.

window.look: long pod at close to full length, about 3 in, firm and still green
window.gives: crisp, juicy flesh and heat, but almost none of the reason to grow this one - the tropical sweetness has not developed. Pick here only to thin a heavy set or to get an early crunchy, spicy pod

window.look: pod turned clear yellow - Adaptive Seeds puts this at about 60 days, a genuine named stage rather than a colour break
window.gives: the early usable stage: fruity and hot with the sweetness partway in. Twenty days earlier than full ripeness, which matters in a cool season - this baccatum ripens early for its species and sets well in cool conditions, so yellow is a reliable fallback if the season is closing

window.look: yellow warmed through to a soft peachy orange over the whole pod, about 80 days
window.gives: the payoff stage - the sweetness and almost tropical fruit undertones that make this variety, carried on 30,000-50,000 SHU. Full peach is also the stage to hold for seed saving. Crisp and juicy fresh, and this is the colour to roast, grill or pickle

sugarrushpeach.ripe_vs_unripe: Ripe is peach, and peach on this pepper is easy to misread as an unripe yellow pepper. The shift to look for is a tone change rather than a colour change: clear lemon-yellow at 60 days warms into a soft pinkish peach-orange by 80 days, first at the blossom end and spreading back toward the shoulders. A ripe pod is that warm peach right up under the calyx, not just on its sunny side, and it holds the same firm crispness - so peach plus firm means ready, and yellow with no warmth in it means twenty more days on the plant if you want the sweetness.
sugarrushpeach.source: Adaptive Seeds - Hot Pepper, Sugar Rush Peach (Organic)

window.look: 3-4 in long by 3-3½ in wide, blocky with the classic four squared lobes, glossy deep green, hard all over, walls a full ¼ in thick; cut it off with a knife or scissors leaving ¼ in of stem rather than pulling
window.gives: the benchmark thick-walled stuffing pepper — walls at their stiffest, so halves and cups hold shape under a filling and stand up to frying; flavour is mild and vegetal rather than sweet, and clearing green fruit keeps the plant setting new pods instead of pouring everything into ripening the ones it has

window.look: patchy crimson breaking through the green, usually at the blossom end first; the fruit is still hard and full-sized
window.gives: a real compromise pick — some of the ripe sweetness arriving while the wall is still firm enough to stuff, and the plant is freed sooner. Illinois Extension notes peppers may be picked at any stage of development, so this is a legitimate stop, not a mistake

window.look: vibrant crimson over the whole 6 oz fruit, blocky shape held, wall giving slightly under thumb pressure
window.gives: the flavour end — sweetness intensifies markedly as it colours, and this catalogue credits red California Wonder with more vitamin C than an orange. Best raw, roasted, or charred and peeled; a touch slack for stuffing

californiawonder.source: Underwood Gardens / Terroir Seeds — California Wonder Red Sweet Pepper Seeds (Capsicum annuum)

window.look: 4-5 in blocky four-lobed fruit at full size, mid-green, firm, flesh already thick and hearty
window.gives: the same firm-walled green bell as ordinary California Wonder — mild, vegetal, best for stuffing and frying while the wall is stiffest; picking here keeps a sturdy 2-3 ft plant setting more fruit

window.look: bright golden yellow over the whole fruit with no green left in the grooves between the lobes; flesh still thick and hearty
window.gives: the stage this variety exists for — Pepper Joe's calls it exceedingly sweet here, and it is the colour worth growing it over a red bell for. Sweet raw in salads and salsa, still firm enough to stuff

window.look: the gold deepening and flushing through to orange-red; wall a little softer under the thumb
window.gives: the true terminal ripeness — deepest, sweetest flavour and best roasted. You trade away the golden colour you grew it for, so take it here only when you want maximum sweetness over looks

goldencaliforniawonder.ripe_vs_unripe: Gold is not this pepper's last stop, which is the trap in the name. A fully gold fruit is colour-mature and sweet and is the intended harvest, but leave it on and it keeps going to orange-red — so orange creeping in is not spoilage or sunburn, it is ripening past gold. Conversely, a fruit that is still pale greenish-yellow with green lingering in the sinuses between lobes is mid-transition, not gold yet: wait for even colour edge to edge.
goldencaliforniawonder.source: Pepper Joe's — California Wonder Golden Pepper Seeds

window.look: full-size blocky fruit, firm and glossy green, ready early — Fedco rates it 70 days from transplant, the earliest of the bells here
window.gives: the guaranteed harvest in a short cool season: firm walls for frying, stuffing and freezing in halves. Flavour is green and mild, and clearing fruit keeps a variety that is prone to blossom-drop in heat working on new set

window.look: red breaking patchily over the green shoulders and blossom end, fruit still hard
window.gives: the frost-race pick — part of the ripe sweetness with the wall still firm. Illinois Extension notes peppers may be harvested at any stage of development, so a half-coloured pod is a legitimate harvest rather than a loss

window.look: fully coloured red across every lobe, blocky shape held, wall softening slightly
window.gives: the payoff this variety was picked for — Fedco chose it on Kent Whealy's advice specifically as a bell that will actually ripen red in the North, and it has been their most popular open-pollinated bell since. Sweeter and rounder than green, best raw or roasted; expect a lower total count, since every fruit you let colour occupies the plant longer

kingofthenorth.source: Fedco Seeds — King of the North Organic Sweet Bell

emeraldgreen.window_label: deep glossy green (the named stage) → red

window.look: large and blocky at roughly 4½ in long by 3½ in wide, four lobes, thick-walled, and — the actual harvest signal on the catalogue page — large, glossy and a deep green. Cut it from the plant with a sharp knife or scissors rather than twisting it off
window.gives: this is the stage the pepper is named and grown for, and the one the catalogue tells you to pick at: thick firm walls, sweet mild flesh, no heat — the best stuffing pepper of the group, and good for stir-fries and fajitas. Picking here also keeps the plant setting instead of winding down into ripening

window.look: left on the plant, the same deep green fruit blushes and finishes red; the wall gives a little more under the thumb
window.gives: the flavour end rather than the texture end — Illinois Extension notes coloured bells left on the plant develop full flavour and gain various levels of sweetness depending on the variety. Better raw, roasted or peeled than stuffed, and it costs you further set on the plant

emeraldgreen.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is a harvest stage here, not the finish line — the name describes when you pick it, not when it stops changing. Tell a correct green from a merely immature one by size and hardness, not colour: a ready pod is full-sized and blocky with squared, filled-out shoulders, skin taut and glossy, and it feels hard rather than springy when squeezed. An immature one is undersized, thin-walled, its green paler and more yellow-toned, its surface matte, and its shoulders give under thumb pressure. If you leave a correct green fruit on the plant it will blush and go red — so green is a genuine pick point you chose, not evidence you were early.
emeraldgreen.source: True Leaf Market — Pepper Seeds, Sweet, Emerald Giant
emeraldgreen.caveat: No source found for a distinct cultivar named 'Emerald Green'; the window is derived from the green-bell 'Emerald Giant' type page plus University of Illinois Extension's general bell guidance. Treat green as the intended pick stage and expect red if fruit is left on the plant.

window.look: the biggest pod on this list — blocky, up to 6 in long and 4½ in wide, deep green and hard, walls notably thick. Cut with a sharp blade leaving ½ in of stem
window.gives: the largest, firmest stuffing vessel the plant will give you; thick walls hold a savoury filling without collapsing. Flavour is mild and green at this point, and clearing fruit keeps set going on a variety that needs 75-85 days and can run out of season

window.look: red streaking over the green, most often from the blossom end up; the fruit is still hard
window.gives: picked at size and colour of your choosing, per the catalogue — some ripe sweetness with the wall still stiff. Worth taking here when the season is closing on a long-day-to-maturity Italian type

window.look: glossy candy-apple red over the whole large fruit; wall still thick but slightly yielding
window.gives: the stage the variety exists for — a rich sweet taste that deepens further when roasted, grilled or baked with a stuffing. The thick walls are what make it the classic Piedmont roaster: char it blackened, steam it in a paper bag, and the skin slips off cleanly for freezing or antipasto

quadratodastirosso.source: John Scheepers Kitchen Garden Seeds — Quadrato d'Asti Rosso Bell Pepper

window.look: blocky fruit filled out to about 3½ in by 4 in, firm and green, walls already notably thick
window.gives: a firm-walled green bell for stuffing and cooking — and the one cultivar here whose own catalogue spells out the tradeoff: Botanical Interests advises picking in both stages to boost production, so green picking is what keeps the plant cranking rather than winding down

window.look: green giving way unevenly to yellow then orange, patchy across the lobes, fruit still hard
window.gives: part of the way to the sweet end with the wall still stiff enough to stuff; Illinois Extension notes peppers may be picked at any stage of development, so this is a legitimate stop when you want the plant back to work

window.look: even bright creamsicle-orange edge to edge, thick walls, a slight give under the thumb
window.gives: the sweet end — Botanical Interests calls it very sweet with a rich flavour when left on the vine to colour fully. This is the stage worth growing an orange bell for: raw in salads, roasted, or grilled for colour on a plate. Each fruit held to full colour slows new set

orangesun.ripe_vs_unripe: Orange is easy to call once it is even, but the mid-transition fruit is what fools people. Fully ripe is uniform deep creamsicle-orange with no green left in the sinuses — the grooves between the lobes and the ring around the stem are the last places green hangs on, so check there before deciding. A fruit that reads pale or yellow-orange with green still in the grooves is still colouring and will sweeten further; it is not a yellow bell and it is not stalled.
orangesun.source: Botanical Interests — Orange Sun Sweet Pepper

window.look: a tiny three-lobed bell at full size — about 2½ in wide by 1¼ in long — glossy and firm green. Cut at the stem with a sharp tool; do not pull these off by hand
window.gives: the texture pick, not the flavour pick: walls stiffest, so the little cups hold up cored-and-stuffed or on a platter. Territorial is explicit that flavour and nutrient content are best when the fruit is fully coloured, so green here buys firmness and buys you more fruit — clearing pods keeps a very prolific 55-day plant setting

window.look: glossy red over the whole small fruit, flesh thick and juicy for its size
window.gives: what the variety is actually for — very sweet, eaten whole out of the hand, on a veggie platter, in a lunchbox or in salads. Territorial puts both peak flavour and peak nutrient content here, and at this size there is no wall-thickness penalty worth worrying about

redminibell.source: Territorial Seed Company — Miniature Red Bell Pepper Seed

pineappletomato.window_label: cream-yellow break → full gold with red marbling

window.look: the hard grass-green ground colour lifts to a pale creamy or straw yellow starting at the blossom end and spreading up; the matte bloom gives way to a faint shine; no red streaking yet and the shoulders are still green
window.gives: the vine has already stopped feeding this fruit, so picking here costs nothing in flavour and it finishes to full colour indoors in 3-7 days at 65-85F stem-side down; on a 1-2 lb fruit this is how you get it off the plant before it splits in a rain or drops and bruises

window.look: skin an even golden yellow with the first pink-red streaks bleeding up from the blossom end; still firm all over, shoulders may keep a green cast on a fruit this big
window.gives: firm enough to cut clean slices that hold their shape on a plate or a sandwich; the sweet melon-edged character is present but thinner and less rounded than it will get

window.look: deep gold to gold-orange overall, pink-red streaks well developed, fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure; a cut face shows the red-and-gold mosaic running through the yellow flesh
window.gives: the full tropical low-acid flavour with the melon note and the meaty, nearly seedless texture this variety is grown for; also the softest, so it will not stack or travel and wants using within a day or two

pineappletomato.ripe_vs_unripe: Read ripeness off the ground colour, never off the red. Unripe is hard, matte and grass-green to blue-green. Ripe is a warm gold to gold-orange with the green gone from everything but the shoulders, a low gloss instead of the dusty bloom, and a shoulder that yields a little under thumb pressure. The pink-red marbling is a variety marking, not a ripeness meter: some fruit streaks heavily while the ground colour is still pale and some barely streaks at all when fully gold, so a lightly-marbled fruit is not an unripe fruit and more red is not a thing to hold out for. A green shoulder that stays green while the body has gone gold is normal on a beefsteak this large.
pineappletomato.source: Alliance of Native Seed Keepers - Pineapple Tomato Seeds (Bicolor, Indeterminate)
pineappletomato.caveat: Colour, marbling, size, flavour and 85-95 day maturity are cultivar-specific from this seed vendor's listing (Baker Creek's own page blocked automated reading this run); the breaker-stage mechanics are the crop-level tomato rule applied to a bicolour.

tiedye.window_label: bronze break → port-wine with metallic green stripes

window.look: the flat green ground between the stripes warms to a dull bronze or muddy brown at the blossom end while the stripes stay a paler grey-green; the whole fruit stops looking green and starts looking dirty, which is the break on a dark tomato
window.gives: picks and holds unusually well for a dark beefsteak - this variety was selected to stand up in the field and after picking - so this is the stage to clear fruit ahead of weather and finish it on the counter

window.look: body has gone a dull pink-red to brick with the metallic green stripes now standing out sharply against it; still firm right across the shoulders
window.gives: firm and sliceable with the tangy, almost lightly-salted edge already up front; the sweet dark-tomato depth underneath is still building

window.at: full ripe (port wine with green stripes)
window.look: ground colour a deep port-wine, stripes still metallic green and unchanged, fruit bi-lobed and slightly ribbed at around 9 oz, giving under light pressure; interior deep brick red
window.gives: peak of the rich, sweet, smoky dark-tomato flavour with the tangy salted note it is famous for - this is the eating stage, and it is why the variety wins tastings; softer, so slice it the day you pick it

tiedye.ripe_vs_unripe: The green stripes never leave. On a fully ripe fruit they are still bright metallic green, so green on the skin is not evidence of an unripe tomato here and waiting for the stripes to colour up means waiting forever. Judge only the ground colour between the stripes: unripe is a cool flat green with a matte bloom, ripe is a deep dull port-wine or brick that looks almost dusty or smoky rather than bright. A dark tomato also never reaches the glossy bright red of a normal tomato, so the useful confirmations are the loss of any green from the ground colour, a slight give at the shoulder under the thumb, and the stem detaching easily.
tiedye.source: Fedco Seeds - Pink Berkeley Tie-Dye Organic Slicing Tomato
tiedye.caveat: Sourced as Pink Berkeley Tie-Dye, Brad Gates / Wild Boar Farms (Napa, CA), Boar Series - port-wine ground with metallic green stripes, bi-lobed, ~9 oz, 68 days. Wild Boar Farms' own page blocked automated reading this run. Note there is also a Green Berkeley Tie-Dye from the same breeder that ripens with a chartreuse-and-ruby interior; if the seed packet says Green rather than Pink, the ripe ground colour is a green-gold rather than port-wine and the window above does not apply.

speckledroman.window_label: olive-orange break → bright red with gold streaks

window.look: the dark green ground of the 3-4 in plum goes olive, then a dull orange creeps up from the blossom end; the lengthwise stripes are at this point only faintly paler green bands
window.gives: detaches cleanly and finishes indoors with no flavour loss, which matters on a paste tomato you are accumulating for one big sauce batch rather than eating one at a time - it lets you pull a whole truss ahead of rain or a cool spell and hold it

window.look: two thirds coloured, the streaks now unmistakably gold against orange-red, fruit still hard in the hand
window.gives: very firm, dry, easy to handle for dicing or halving without collapse; sauce made here is brighter and more acid, which is what you want if it is going into salsa

window.at: full ripe (bright red with gold streaks)
window.look: skin bright red with the gold streaks still plainly there, fruit just yielding to pressure; cut open the flesh is meaty red and dry with very little gel or juice
window.gives: the stage this variety is grown for - rich sweet tomatoey sauce that cooks down fast because there is so little water to boil off, and it is good enough raw at this point to eat as a slicer, which most paste tomatoes are not

speckledroman.ripe_vs_unripe: The gold streaks are the variety, not a defect and not a stage - they are just as visible on a dead-ripe fruit as on a half-coloured one, so a striped tomato is never a tomato to leave on the vine longer. Judge only the ground colour between the streaks: unripe is uniform hard dark green with green-on-green striping and a matte surface; ripe is bright red between gold stripes, faintly glossy, with a little give at the blossom end. Because the flesh is dense and dry this one always feels firmer than a slicer at the same ripeness, so do not wait for a soft fruit - a Speckled Roman that feels soft is past prime.
speckledroman.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds - Speckled Roman Organic Tomato Seed

window.look: the cool blue-green cast on the 3-4 in plum warms to a dull bronze or chocolate-brown smudge at the blossom end; from a step back the fruit reads muddy rather than green
window.gives: the fruit is physiologically finished and will darken the rest of the way indoors, so this is the pick for getting fruit off the vine intact; a dusky tomato left to hang is the one you find split or slug-holed

window.look: most of the body a dull purple-pink to burgundy, still firm end to end, shoulders holding a darker green-bronze cap
window.gives: firm enough to dice for a salsa or a salad without turning to mush, with the tangy side of the flavour forward and the sweetness only partly in

window.look: skin a smooth glossy deep burgundy-plum that reads almost black in shade, shoulders often still darker and duskier than the body; fruit yields to gentle pressure
window.gives: the full rich, full-bodied sweet-with-tang flavour and the juiciness this one is prized for, which is unusual in a plum-shaped tomato; softest stage, so eat it fresh rather than holding it

ukrainianpurple.ripe_vs_unripe: A dusky tomato never goes bright, so brightness is the wrong test. Unripe is a cool blue-green with a chalky matte bloom and a hard feel everywhere. Ripe is warm and dark - burgundy to near-black - with a smooth gloss instead of the bloom, and it gives under the thumb at the blossom end. The shoulders are the trap: on this variety the shoulder cap commonly stays darker and can hold a green or bronze-green tint while the rest of the fruit is fully coloured, and that shoulder is not a signal to keep waiting. Check the body and the blossom end, not the top. If it looks uniformly muddy brown-green rather than green, it has already broken and can come in.
ukrainianpurple.caveat: Ripe colour (deep purple nearly black), elongated 3-4 in fruit, rich sweet-tangy flavour and indeterminate habit are cultivar-specific from this vendor listing; days to maturity is listed variously as 80-90 across vendors. The persistent dark or green-tinted shoulder described is the general behaviour of dusky purple tomatoes rather than a claim from that page.

yellowbrandywine.window_label: pale amber break → deep golden amber

window.look: the flat mid-green of the big potato-leaf beefsteak lightens to a pale amber-cream at the blossom end and the dusty bloom starts to give way to a faint shine; the fruit is at full size and heavy for its bulk
window.gives: this is the practical pick point for a 1-2 lb fruit - it comes off before its own weight tears it off the truss or a heavy rain splits the shoulders - and it finishes to full colour on the counter in 3-7 days with no flavour penalty

window.look: skin an even golden yellow across the body with green retreating into the ribs and shoulders, firm all over
window.gives: firm enough to cut thick slices that hold up on a burger; the creamy texture is there and the low-acid sweetness is up front, with less of the rounded acid balance to come

window.look: deep gold with an orange cast, faint gloss, and a definite give when you cup it; a picked fruit at this stage often shows a slight softening at the blossom end first
window.gives: the intense, creamy, sweet-with-balancing-acid flavour that makes this one of the last and best fruits of the season; too soft to slice thin or transport, and one of the varieties that does gain a little sweetness from the extra days on the plant

yellowbrandywine.ripe_vs_unripe: This is the one where general advice actively misleads: vendor pages for yellow tomatoes still repeat the boilerplate to harvest when the fruit is red, shiny and firm, and this fruit is never red at any stage. The discriminator is shade and warmth, not hue change to red. Unripe is a cool, flat, slightly blue-tinged mid-green with a dusty matte bloom and no give anywhere. Ripe is a warm amber-gold to gold-orange - the green has drained out of the body and survives only in the deep ribs and the shoulder - with a low gloss, and the shoulder or blossom end yields slightly under thumb pressure. Look at the blossom end first, because the change starts there and spreads up. On a fruit this size the ribbed shoulders stay greener than the rest for days after the body is ripe; that is normal, not unripe.
yellowbrandywine.source: True Leaf Market - Yellow Brandywine Organic Tomato Seeds
yellowbrandywine.caveat: Golden-yellow ripe colour, 1-2 lb beefsteak fruit, creamy texture, balanced sweet-acid flavour, 76-90 days from transplant and late-season bearing are cultivar-specific from this vendor listing (Victory Seeds' page errored this run). Note that same page's harvest line - pick when red, shiny and firm - is generic tomato boilerplate and does not apply to a yellow cultivar.

window.look: the green ground colour pales to cream at the blossom end on a full-size, hard, glossy-skinned fruit of up to 8 oz
window.gives: picks clean and ripens the rest of the way indoors; on a heavy-setting indeterminate like this one it is the way to keep ahead of a truss that ripens all at once

window.look: an even golden yellow across the round fruit, still notably firm - this variety is a firm-fleshed slicer, so it feels harder at ripeness than a beefsteak does
window.gives: the firm slicing texture this variety is grown for, cutting neat slices that do not weep; the sweetness is already high

window.look: deep golden yellow with an orange cast, faint gloss, and a slight give at the blossom end
window.gives: the exceptionally sweet, well-balanced flavour it is known for, with the meaty firmness mostly intact - it holds better on the counter than most large yellows

sunray.ripe_vs_unripe: Nothing about this fruit turns red, so the only useful cue is the ground colour moving from a cool matte green through cream to a warm golden yellow, blossom end first. Unripe is hard and flat green with a dusty bloom; ripe is gold, faintly glossy, and yields slightly at the blossom end. Because Sunray is a deliberately firm-fleshed slicer, a fully ripe fruit still feels firmer than a ripe beefsteak - do not keep waiting for softness, because by the time it feels soft it is past prime.
sunray.source: Annie's Heirloom Seeds - Sunray Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) Indeterminate
sunray.caveat: Sunray is thinly catalogued. Only the golden colour, up-to-8 oz size, firm slicing texture, exceptional sweetness and 72-80 day maturity are cultivar-specific from this vendor page; the colour-break appearance and per-stage payoffs are derived from yellow slicing-tomato guidance plus the crop-level breaker rule.

valencia.window_label: pale apricot break → full sunny orange

window.look: the green ground colour on the round, smooth 8-10 oz fruit fades to a pale apricot or buff at the blossom end; skin is smooth and unribbed, so the change is easy to read across the whole globe
window.gives: the fruit is done taking from the vine and will colour up indoors, which lets you strip a midseason truss ahead of weather without losing anything; the smooth skin means no rib splits to worry about, so this is a convenience pick rather than a rescue

window.look: orange spreading up from the blossom end over roughly half the globe with green still holding at the shoulder; fruit firm end to end
window.gives: firm and meaty enough to slice thin without shredding; the full tomato flavour is present but flatter, with less of the roundness that finishes late in this variety

window.look: an even sunny orange over the whole smooth globe, faint gloss, slight give under gentle pressure; cut open, the interior is meaty with very few seeds
window.gives: the full tomato flavour and the texture this is selected for - Johnny's rate it among their best on both counts; the meaty low-seed interior is at its best here for slicing and for a thick orange sauce

valencia.ripe_vs_unripe: Ripe Valencia is orange, and orange arrives by way of a pale apricot stage that is easy to mistake for a sickly unripe fruit. Unripe is a cool flat green, hard everywhere, with a dusty matte bloom. Ripe is a warm even orange with the green cleared even from the shoulder - the skin is smooth and unribbed, so unlike a beefsteak it really does colour uniformly and a green patch left at the top means it genuinely is not finished. Confirm with a faint gloss replacing the bloom and a slight give under gentle pressure. Do not wait for red or for a deep blood-orange; the finish colour is a bright sunny orange and it stops there.
valencia.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds - Valencia Orange Beefsteak Tomato, Heirloom & Organic Seed

sanmarzano.window_label: breaker → deep red to the shoulders

window.look: plum is at full 4-6 oz size and rock hard; a first patch of orange-red at the blossom tip only, shoulders and stem end still green
window.gives: the hardest stage in the window, so a big pick takes stacking and jostling without bruising, and Penn State finds breaker fruit finished off the vine still eats vine-ripened; the trade is that the shoulders are still pale, so a whole-peel batch will have green ends to cut out

window.look: colour has run up from the blossom tip past the middle, shoulders still greenish, the hard-green gloss going dull
window.gives: still firm enough to handle in bulk and to hold its plum shape whole in a jar; Johnny's own guidance is to pick less ripe the further the fruit has to travel, so this is the stage for a batch you are hauling or holding a few days before you cook

window.look: vibrant deep red from blossom tip all the way up over the stem shoulders, skin taut, a slight give under the thumb
window.gives: the whole fruit is usable for sauce - skins slip easily and the flesh cooks down quickly, with no pale green core at the stem end to trim away. This is the fully-ripe pick Johnny's reserves for local and home use; the fruit is at its softest, so bring it in one shallow unstacked layer

sanmarzano.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds - San Marzano II Organic Tomato Seed
sanmarzano.caveat: Johnny's page is the San Marzano II strain (78 days, indeterminate, 4-6 oz). No blossom-end-rot or vine-holding claim appeared on the page, so none is made here.

sanmarzanoroma.window_label: breaker → deep red to the shoulders

window.look: elongated plum at full size and hard; colour break confined to the blossom tip on the underside, the rest still green
window.gives: firmest, most transportable stage, and breaker fruit finished indoors still carries vine-ripened flavour; the stem shoulders have not coloured yet, so expect pale ends when you peel

window.look: colour up past the middle of the plum, shoulders lagging, skin dulling off its green shine
window.gives: keeps enough firmness to hold shape whole in a jar and to stack in a basket - the stage for a picking you will cook later in the week rather than tonight

window.look: even deep red over the whole plum including the stem shoulders, with a little give
window.gives: the entire fruit goes into the pot - skins slip, flesh breaks down fast, no green core to cut out - and paste flavour is at its fullest; softest and shortest-keeping, handle in a single layer

sanmarzanoroma.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds - San Marzano II Organic Tomato Seed
sanmarzanoroma.caveat: No source specific to the 'San Marzano Roma' name was found; window derived from Johnny's San Marzano paste-tomato guidance plus the Penn State ripening-stage ladder. Treat the stage payoffs as paste-type behaviour, not a claim about this exact strain.

window.look: 4-6 oz round, slightly flattened fruit at full size and hard; a coin of orange at the blossom scar underneath - easy to miss on a fruit this smooth, so turn it over to check
window.gives: the pick that gets the very first fruit of an extra-early, cold-tolerant variety off the plant while it is still hard enough to carry stacked; Penn State finds breaker fruit finished indoors still eats vine-ripened, and it slices thin without weeping

window.look: colour over most of the fruit, stem shoulders still greenish, the skin losing its hard shine
window.gives: sliceable firmness with most of the flavour already built - the stage for a tomato you plan to eat over the next two or three days rather than tonight

window.look: uniform deep red over the whole flattened globe, shoulder yields to gentle thumb pressure
window.gives: the luscious, rich taste this heirloom is actually grown for, at full strength; also the softest and shortest-keeping stage, so it wants eating within a day or so and no stacking

moskvichheirloom.source: TomatoFest - Moskovich Organic Heirloom Tomato Seeds
moskvichheirloom.caveat: Cultivar-specific fruit description (deep red, 4-6 oz, smooth, round and slightly flattened, 60 days, cold-tolerant, luscious rich taste) from a seed catalogue rather than extension; Victory Seeds' own page was unreachable this run. Stage names follow Penn State's ladder.

window.look: full-size 8-16 oz slicer, still green with a colour break at the blossom end; the plants carry plenty of leaf cover, so you have to lift foliage and roll the fruit over to see it
window.gives: the lever on a determinate that ripens in one concentrated block - taking breakers staggers the flood onto the counter instead of losing the tail of it, and breaker fruit finished indoors still eats vine-ripened. Hardest stage, so it takes being picked into a full bucket

window.look: roughly 60-90% coloured, green only at the stem shoulders, still firm all over
window.gives: full-size slices that stay intact on the board and in a sandwich, and fruit that can still be carried and stacked - Johnny's harvest note is that only the softer, riper fruit needs shallow padded trays

window.look: uniform big red fruit coloured right up over the shoulders, slight give under the thumb
window.gives: the good flavour and juice this NC State slicer was bred for at its peak; softest stage, so bring it in unstacked in a single shallow layer and use it promptly

mountainfreshplus.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds - Mountain Fresh Plus (F1) Tomato Seed
mountainfreshplus.caveat: Johnny's page confirms 8-16 oz big red slicers, 75 days, determinate with concentrated ripening, heavy leaf cover, cool/wet tolerance, and Dr. Randy Gardner / NC State breeding. The crack-resistance and 'good blend of solids and gels' claims that circulate for this hybrid appear on catalogue pages that were not read this run, so they are deliberately not asserted above.

window.look: 4-6 oz flattened globe at full size and hard; first orange blush at the blossom end on the underside, where the flattened shape hides it from above
window.gives: the earliest honest pick on one of the earliest slicers there is - hardest, most bruise-proof stage, and it finishes on the counter with vine-ripened flavour, which matters on a 3-foot determinate whose crop arrives in a rush

window.look: most of the fruit red with a yellow-green ring still around the stem
window.gives: old-fashioned flavour largely developed while the flesh is still firm enough for clean, thin slices; pulling fruit here spreads a concentrated determinate set over days instead of hours

window.look: red right through to the stem ring, cut face a deep vibrant red, shoulder gives slightly
window.gives: the outstanding old-fashioned tomato flavour this variety is kept for at full strength, and its crack-resistant skin holds at this stage where thinner-skinned heirlooms split; the fruit is at its softest and keeps the least, so use it soon

newyorker.source: Sandia Seed Company - New Yorker Tomato Seeds (Early Slicer, Short Season)
newyorker.caveat: Cultivar-specific detail (red, 4-6 oz flattened globe, 65 days, determinate ~3 ft, sets reliably in cool short-season conditions, excellent crack resistance, outstanding old-fashioned flavour) from a seed catalogue rather than extension; Hudson Valley Seed's own page would not load this run. Stage names follow Penn State's ladder.

oregonspring.window_label: breaker → fully red, no yellow ring

window.look: round fruit at full size and hard, first orange-red at the blossom end only
window.gives: gets the very first fruit of a cool-spring, parthenocarpic set indoors while it is at its firmest and most handleable, and breaker fruit still finishes with vine-ripened flavour - useful given this determinate can be cropping a month either side of frost

window.at: red with a yellow ring at the stem
window.look: red over the body of the fruit with only a ring of yellow left around the stem scar
window.gives: this is Territorial's own recommended pick point - effectively all the on-vine ripening with the fruit still firm, and the meaty, seed-poor interior slices clean without flooding the board

window.look: uniform red to the stem with the yellow ring gone, slight give at the shoulder
window.gives: the maximum on-vine flavour Territorial tells you to hold for; dense meaty flesh with very few seeds, which is what makes this the stage for thick slices or for cooking down. Shortest-keeping stage of the three

oregonspring.source: Territorial Seed Company - Oregon Spring Tomato Seed
oregonspring.caveat: Territorial states 65-70 days, determinate, developed at Oregon State University, parthenocarpic, meaty interior, and gives the explicit harvest rule: 'Harvest when fully ripe; allow the fruit to ripen on the vine as long as possible. Red tomatoes should be harvested when they are fully red or with only a ring of yellow around the stem.' Fruit weight (3-7 oz depending on catalogue) was not confirmed on the page read.

window.look: medium-large fruit at full size and hard, colour break showing at the blossom end underneath
window.gives: the firmest stage on a variety already noted for keeping well, so a breaker brought inside sits for days without collapsing while it finishes with vine-ripened flavour - the way to work through a heavy set without racing it

window.look: colour across most of the fruit, stem shoulders last to turn, skin off its hard green shine
window.gives: slicing firmness with the flavour mostly built; on a high-yielding plant this is the stage to thin fruit at so a big cluster does not all come ripe on the same afternoon

window.look: uniformly red all over rather than blotchy - this variety colours evenly - with give under the thumb
window.gives: the excellent flavour it is grown for at full strength, and because it keeps well it stays usable at this stage longer than most heirlooms do; still the softest stage, so no stacking

thessaloniki.caveat: Siskiyou confirms 60-80 days, Greek heirloom introduced to the USA in the 1950s, medium-large uniform red fruit, excellent flavour, high yields, disease resistance, and that it keeps well. Victory Seeds' firm-flesh and sunburn/spot/crack-resistance claims are on a page that would not load this run and are not asserted here.

window.look: pod has reached full size — about 4 in long by 1 in wide, up to 1¼ oz — firm and glossy but still uniformly green, no flush at the shoulders yet
window.gives: juiciness and crunch without the sugar: fine chopped raw into salads or sautéed, but you are eating a snack pepper before the 'extra sweet' it was bred and awarded for has arrived

window.look: bright, even canary yellow over the whole pod, uniformly shaped and still glossy — this is the colour AAS names as the fruit colour at harvest
window.gives: extra sweet with the right amount of juiciness and crunch — the eating stage the variety won its award for; best for straight snacking off the plant, sautéing, stuffing and chopping for salads

picknpopyellow.ripe_vs_unripe: Full canary yellow IS ripe — it is the end of this pepper's colour line, not a half-way point. All-America Selections names bright canary yellow as the fruit colour at harvest, and no source describes an orange or red stage for it, so a pod holding at solid even yellow is finished and will not go on to orange. Read it by evenness rather than hue: unripe is uniformly green, then the pod pales and fills to a saturated yellow with no green left at the shoulder or tucked under the calyx, skin still glossy and the pod still firm. Leaving some green is a legitimate choice only if you specifically want the crunch without the sweetness — green costs you the sugar, it does not buy you anything the yellow stage lacks.
picknpopyellow.source: All-America Selections — Pepper Pick-N-Pop Yellow F1
picknpopyellow.caveat: AAS gives the ripe colour (bright canary yellow), size, sweetness and 65 days from transplant, but no source found describes the green stage or any orange stage for this variety. The mature-green pick point and what it costs you are derived from general sweet-pepper ripening; the no-orange conclusion rests on canary yellow being named as the harvest colour.

window.look: full length, up to 6 in long and 2 in wide with rounded blunt ends; skin an even pale yellow-green with a waxy sheen, pod firm and light in the hand
window.gives: the classic frying pepper: medium-thick sweet, fruity flesh that holds its shape in a hot pan and blisters cleanly — this is the stage the seed house explicitly tells you to pick at, for frying, roasting and sauces

window.look: the pale green breaks and deepens through to a full red over the whole pod; skin stays glossy but the wall gives a little more under the thumb
window.gives: a deeper, sweeter pepper for sauces and skillet dishes, where the flavour is doing the work rather than the structure — you trade away some of the firmness that makes the frying stage worth having

cubanelle.ripe_vs_unripe: Both stages are real harvests, so the question is not ripe-versus-unripe but which one you are after. A frying-stage Cubanelle is at FULL length — 5 to 6 in, blunt-ended, firm — and its skin is an even PALE yellow-green with a waxy gloss. An immature pod is short and still lengthening, a darker grass-green, and thin-walled. The pale, slightly yellowed cast is the tell that the pod is done growing even though it has not started to ripen. Once colour begins breaking out of the pale green you have left the frying window and committed to the red stage.
cubanelle.source: John Scheepers Kitchen Garden Seeds — Cubanelle Sweet Pepper
cubanelle.caveat: The page confirms both stages directly — 'matures from pale yellow-green to red but pick them when they're yellow-green' — plus size, medium-thick flesh, sweet fruity flavour and frying/roasting use. The red stage's specific payoff (sweeter, slightly softer wall) is general sweet-pepper ripening rather than a cultivar-specific quote.

window.look: full-size tapered bull's-horn pod, averaging 6 in long by 2½ in wide and about 5 oz, firm and still green — Johnny's clocks green pickings at 60 days from transplant
window.gives: already sweet for a green pepper and usable, and picking the first pods promptly at full size pushes the plant to set more fruit — so the trade is peak sweetness for about three weeks and a heavier total crop

window.look: deepens to an even carmine over the whole pod, around 80 days from transplant; this variety was selected for ripening red early
window.gives: notably sweet — the source is explicit that it is sweetest when fully red-ripe; this is the roasting and grilling stage the variety exists for, where the medium-thick flesh goes silky rather than staying crisp

carmen.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Carmen F1 Corno di Toro Pepper

window.look: round globe filled out to its finished 2 in width, hard and glossy, still green
window.gives: the firmest wall of the whole window — a green pod hollowed and stuffed holds its shape under the broiler with the least slump; it is also the least sweet stage of a pepper bred specifically to be sweeter than its parent

window.look: bright red 2 in globe, evenly coloured, skin glossy
window.gives: less heat and more sweet than a classic Cherry Bomb — the stage the variety was bred to be picked at, for stuffing, grilling, salads and snacking; the wall softens slightly as it colours, so stuffed pods want gentler handling

cherrystuffer.caveat: Burpee's own page would not load, so this comes from a grower listing of the same variety, which describes only the ripe stage: bright red 2 in globes, less heat and more sweet than Cherry Bomb, for stuffing, grilling, salads or snacking. The mature-green pick point and the firmer-wall-when-green payoff are derived from general sweet-pepper behaviour, not from a Cherry Stuffer source.

window.look: round globe filled out to its finished 2 in width, hard and glossy, still green
window.gives: the firmest wall of the whole window — a green pod hollowed and stuffed holds its shape under the broiler with the least slump; it is also the least sweet stage of a pepper bred specifically to be sweeter than its parent

window.look: bright red 2 in globe, evenly coloured, skin glossy
window.gives: less heat and more sweet than a classic Cherry Bomb — the stage the variety was bred to be picked at, for stuffing, grilling, salads and snacking; the wall softens slightly as it colours, so stuffed pods want gentler handling

cherrystufferburpee.caveat: Burpee's own page would not load, so this comes from a grower listing of the same variety, which describes only the ripe stage: bright red 2 in globes, less heat and more sweet than Cherry Bomb, for stuffing, grilling, salads or snacking. The mature-green pick point and the firmer-wall-when-green payoff are derived from general sweet-pepper behaviour, not from a Cherry Stuffer source.

window.look: 1 in pointed teardrop / bird's-beak pod at full size, firm, with a crisp snap when broken; still green
window.gives: tart and crunchy with only the barest touch of heat — usable, but the seedhouse's own instruction is to leave pods on the plant to change colour and sweeten up, so green is the stage before any of the sweetness has arrived

window.look: solid bright yellow over the whole 1 in pointed pod, still glossy and firm
window.gives: the sweetened, marginally tart pod with its almost fruity tang and delightful crunch — the stage it is pickled in vinegar for, and the one to use raw or cooked if you want the fruit character rather than just the crunch

biquinhoyellowf1.ripe_vs_unripe: Bright yellow is the END of this pepper's ripening, not a stop on the way to red — do not stand around waiting for a colour that never comes. Because ripe and unripe are both bright-ish and the pod is tiny, read it by evenness rather than hue: unripe pods are uniformly green, then pale, then go a saturated even yellow with no green left at the shoulder or hidden under the calyx. A ripe Biquinho is still firm and glossy and still snaps — softness or a dull skin means you have gone past ripe, not that ripeness is still coming.
biquinhoyellowf1.source: Pinetree Garden Seeds — Biquinho Yellow Pepper (55 days)
biquinhoyellowf1.caveat: The listing gives the ripe pod as a 1 in pointed yellow pepper, marginally tart with a tiny bit of heat, fruity tang and crunch, usually pickled in vinegar, and advises leaving pods on the plant to change colour and sweeten up. It does not name intermediate stages and no source found describes a red stage, so yellow is treated as the end of the window. The gloss and firmness discriminators are general pepper cues.

window.look: blocky bell filled out to roughly 5 in across with squared shoulders and 3-4 lobes, hard to the squeeze and glossy dark green
window.gives: the crisp thick-walled green-bell stage — the best structural wall in the window for stuffing, grilling and roasting halves, at the cost of the sweetness that only comes with the colour

window.look: the dark green pales, then the shoulders and the ridges between the lobes flush first, and the pod finishes an even bright golden yellow with the skin still high-gloss
window.gives: the thick sweet flesh the variety is grown for — peak sweetness raw for salads, dip and pizza, and it still has enough wall to grill or stuff

sunbright.ripe_vs_unripe: Golden yellow is the finished colour, not an under-ripe red — a Sunbright will not go on to red, so don't hold pods waiting for it. What you are watching for is a shift, not a hue change: the deep dark green pales, the shoulders and lobe creases yellow first, and the pod ends an even bright gold with no green left in the creases or under the calyx. A ripe Sunbright is still HARD and still glossy — softness means past prime, not almost-there. Even gold plus a firm wall equals ripe.
sunbright.source: True Leaf Market — Sweet Pepper Seeds, Sunbright
sunbright.caveat: Sourced from a seed retailer listing rather than the breeder or an extension service. It gives green → bright yellow, roughly 5 in blocky bell, thick sweet flesh, no heat, 75 days from transplant, and names no red stage. The order in which the pod colours (shoulders and lobe ridges first) is general bell-pepper behaviour, not a cultivar-specific claim.

window.look: blocky pod filled out to 4-6 in with 3-4 lobes, hard-walled and high-gloss green
window.gives: the fresh-use stage the source names for green pods — thick crisp flesh and a plain green-pepper flavour; you are trading away the full flavour that only develops once it browns

window.look: the green goes dull and a muddy bronze-olive creeps down from the shoulders; the pod is still firm and the skin still tight
window.gives: part of the way to the ripe flavour with the green stage's firmness mostly intact — mainly useful as your signal that the pod is days from finished, so start checking it daily

window.look: deep even chocolate-brown skin, still glossy and drum-tight; cut one open and the flesh under the skin is brick red to dark red
window.gives: full flavour — sweet, richer and earthier than a red bell, with thick crisp flesh; the stage for raw eating, stuffing, grilling and sautéing, and where the striking red interior shows on a cut face

sweetchocolate.ripe_vs_unripe: Ripe brown reads as spoiled to most eyes, so check three things before you throw a pod away. (1) Gloss and tension — ripe chocolate skin is glossy and drum-tight over a hard wall; rot is dull and slack, and dents or weeps under thumb pressure. (2) Evenness — ripeness browns the whole pod evenly, working down from the shoulders; spoilage starts as a defined soft patch, usually at the blossom end or over a bruise, with a wet or darker margin around it and healthy firm skin beside it. (3) The cut face — a ripe Sweet Chocolate is brick red to dark red inside beneath the brown skin. That red interior is the variety's signature and decay does not produce it; rot shows as brown or grey mush and often a smell. A ripe pod also still snaps when you break it.
sweetchocolate.caveat: The listing supplies both ends directly — pods can be picked at glossy green for fresh use, but full flavour develops once they ripen to the signature chocolate-brown — plus the brick-red flesh beneath the skin, 4-6 in blocky 3-4 lobe fruit, thick crisp flesh, and a richer, earthier sweetness than a common bell. The intermediate bronze-olive turning stage and the ripe-versus-rot feel tests are general pepper cues, not cultivar-specific claims.

window.look: fruit already at full size for the variety (about 1/2 oz, round), still mostly pale green, with the first creamy-gold colour showing at the blossom end
window.gives: the plant has stopped feeding the fruit by breaker, so it finishes to full colour off the vine with vine-ripened flavour while escaping the cracking that excess moisture causes in coloured fruit, plus sunscald and further insect damage (Penn State Extension)

window.look: roughly a third to half the skin turned pale gold, green still held in the shoulders and around the stem scar, flesh firm with no give
window.gives: firmest handling stage — the fruit stays whole in a packed lunch or a tossed salad instead of bursting, and it eats tangier and thinner, because the candy sweetness this hybrid is bred for is a full-colour trait

window.look: saturated deep golden-orange right over the shoulders and around the stem scar, no green cast left, thin high-gloss skin, slight give under the thumb
window.gives: the 'sweeter than candy' stage the variety exists for, and about three times the vitamin A of a red cherry; the thin skin is crack-resistant, so unlike most cherries it can sit at full colour through a weather swing rather than splitting the first wet night

sunsugar.ripe_vs_unripe: Golden-orange IS the finished state on this one — there is no red stage coming. Unripe reads hard pale green shading to creamy white-green, greenest in the shoulders and right around the stem scar, which colour last. Ripe is an even, saturated deep golden-orange carried through those shoulders, skin thin and high-gloss, with a slight give under thumb pressure. A fruit that is still lemon-pale, or holds any green cast at the shoulder, is short of finished; one that is deep orange and gives slightly is done.
sunsugar.caveat: Cultivar facts (orange when ripe, 0.5 oz, 62 days, crack-resistant, vitamin A, indeterminate) are from Urban Farmer's catalogue listing; the stage-by-stage colour points and the breaker payoffs are Penn State Extension's tomato ripening stages applied to this cultivar.

window.look: full-size cherry, still green over nearly all the fruit with the first pink just visible at the blossom end
window.gives: the pick that beats a coming rain — at breaker the fruit is not yet taking up the excess moisture that splits coloured cherries, and it still finishes to full colour with vine-ripened flavour off the plant (Penn State Extension)
