window.look: a third to half the skin pink-red working up from the blossom end, shoulders still greenish, flesh only just starting to soften
window.gives: firmest stage for handling — skin still tight, so it halves cleanly and rides in a bowl or lunchbox without squashing; flavour is short of the sweetness the variety is grown for

window.look: even deep red over the shoulders and round the stem scar, high gloss, slight give under thumb pressure
window.gives: the full sweet-red flavour this cherry is grown for; it is also the most fragile stage — coloured fruit draws in water and cracks, so once a truss is at full colour it wants picking daily rather than holding

window.look: gloss gone dull, fine ring cracks around the stem scar, soft or watery spots
window.gives: same-day cooking only — roasting or a quick sauce; the skin has stretched and the fruit will not store or travel

supersweet100.source: Penn State Extension — Is This Tomato Ready to Harvest?
supersweet100.caveat: No cultivar-specific ripeness source found: Johnny's lists Supersweet 100 only as 'the classic sweet red cherry tomato'. The window and the per-stage payoffs here are derived from Penn State Extension's six tomato ripening stages applied to a red cherry type.

window.look: full-size grape-shaped fruit, uniform for size and shape, still green with the first red showing at the blossom end
window.gives: the storm pick — it finishes to colour off the vine with vine-ripened flavour and is not yet drawing in the water that cracks coloured fruit, and it skips sunscald and further insect damage (Penn State Extension)

window.look: red over roughly half the fruit, shoulders still pale green, flesh distinctly hard to the squeeze
window.gives: peak firmness on an already-firm type — stays intact whole through packing and tossing, and reads more tart than sweet, since the sweetness is a full-colour trait

window.look: even shiny red over the whole fruit including the shoulders, and — unlike a round cherry at the same stage — the flesh is still noticeably firm rather than slack
window.gives: the good sweetness grape types are known for, arriving while the firm texture holds; you get the sweet stage without losing bite, which is why this one survives being picked into a bowl at full colour

window.look: red dulls, fine cracks appear at the stem end, flesh finally softens
window.gives: cook it the same day; past this the skin has stretched and the fruit will not hold or travel

redgrape.source: Harris Seeds — Tomato Red Grape F1
redgrape.caveat: Harris Seeds supplies the cultivar facts (shiny red, 70 days, firm texture, good sweetness, intermediate late-blight resistance, large indeterminate plants) but gives no ripeness guidance and makes no crack-resistance claim; the stage points and their payoffs are Penn State Extension's ripening stages applied to a firm grape type.

window.look: 1-2 in pear-shaped fruit at full size, still green with the first cream-yellow break at the blossom end (the fat end, away from the stem)
window.gives: the pick that beats weather damage — at breaker the fruit is not taking up the excess moisture that cracks coloured fruit, and it still ripens to full colour and vine-ripened flavour off the plant (Penn State Extension)

window.look: greenish-yellow overall, with green still held in the narrow neck by the stem and across the shoulders, flesh hard with no give
window.gives: firmest stage — holds its pear shape whole in a salad or a jar of preserves without collapsing, and eats thin and green-tasting, because a tomato's flavour is not fully developed before colour completes

window.look: even bright yellow all the way through the neck and over the shoulders, skin glossy and waxy, slight give under the thumb
window.gives: the mild, sweet, low-acid flavour this pre-1800 heirloom is kept for — the stage Territorial says to hold for, since on a yellow variety completed colour is the flavour signal; from here coloured fruit splits after rain, so pick daily rather than holding

yellowpear.ripe_vs_unripe: Yellow IS the finished state — there is no red stage coming. Unripe fruit is hard and green-tinged ivory, and the green sits longest in the narrow neck beside the stem and across the shoulders, which colour last. Ripe fruit is an even, bright, clear yellow carried right through that neck, with a glossy, almost waxy finish and a slight give under thumb pressure. Any green cast still held in the neck means it is climbing; even bright yellow plus a little give means it is done.
yellowpear.source: Territorial Seed — Yellow Pear Tomato Seed
yellowpear.caveat: Territorial supplies the cultivar facts (bright yellow, pear-shaped 1-2 in cherry, 75-80 days, indeterminate, harvest when fruit has fully reached its expected colour) and Baker Creek's listing the mild, low-acid, pre-1800 heirloom character; the stage-by-stage points come from Penn State Extension's ripening stages applied to a yellow cherry type.

window.look: deeply ribbed, almost pleated, slightly flattened fruit at full size, still green with the first pink at the blossom end
window.gives: the plant has finished feeding the fruit, so it ripens the rest of the way indoors with vine-ripened flavour and escapes the moisture cracking, sunscald and insect damage that catch coloured fruit still hanging (Penn State Extension)

window.look: pink spreading over the lower half, green still in the ribbed shoulders, fruit firm with no give at all
window.gives: firmest for slicing — the lobes hold their pleated edge on the board instead of slumping, and the flavour is still short of the bright, full old-world tang the variety is grown for

window.look: rosy red-pink over the whole fruit including the ribbed shoulders; feels firm with a slight amount of give — the grower's own stated harvest test
window.gives: richest flavour, per the catalogue's own note that fully coloured fruit is where the flavour is; this is the stage for slow-simmered sauce, and sliced, the pleated folds catch oil and sauce

rosasicilian.source: Bucktown Seed Company — Rosa Sicilian Heirloom Tomato Seeds
rosasicilian.caveat: Rosa Sicilian is thinly catalogued and searches mostly return the red 'Rosso Sicilian', a different variety — the only description found was Bucktown Seed Company's (rosy red-pink, deeply ribbed, 80-90 days from transplant, indeterminate, harvest at mature colour when firm with slight give). The intermediate stage points are derived from Penn State Extension's ripening stages applied to a ribbed pink heirloom.

stupice.window_label: breaker (blossom-end blush) → full red and slightly soft

window.look: 2-3 in slightly oval fruit at full size, green with the first red at the blossom end — often early and in cool weather, since this cold-tolerant potato-leaf sets and colours at about 65 days
window.gives: a genuine pick point on a cold-season tomato: the fruit finishes indoors with vine-ripened flavour, so a cold wet spell banks fruit instead of splitting it, and it escapes sunscald and further insect damage (Penn State Extension)

window.look: red over roughly half, shoulders still green, flesh hard to the squeeze with no give
window.gives: firmest for slicing and the only stage that really travels; flavour has not reached the sweetness Stupice is grown for, since a tomato's flavour is not fully developed before colour completes

window.look: even red through the shoulders and — the test the catalogue actually names — slightly soft when squeezed
window.gives: the sweet, excellent flavour this early northern heirloom is kept for; note that the squeeze, not the colour, is the signal here, because a Stupice can read fully red while still hard, and holding a soft ripe fruit through rain is what cracks it

stupice.caveat: Urban Farmer supplies the cultivar facts (2-3 in slightly oval red fruit, 65 days, cold tolerant, does well in northern climates, sweet excellent flavour, indeterminate potato-leaf, pick at proper red colour when slightly soft to the squeeze). No source was found addressing whether cool-weather fruit colours up ahead of flavour on this variety, so nothing is claimed about that; the intermediate stage comes from Penn State Extension's ripening stages.

window.look: small round fruit, up to 2 oz, at full size and still green with the first red at the blossom end — this can arrive around 50 days from transplant, the earliest fruit in the garden
window.gives: on a determinate that concentrates its whole crop into a short window, breaker picking spreads that crop out: the fruit ripens the rest of the way indoors with vine-ripened flavour instead of the entire set going ripe together and splitting on the plant (Penn State Extension)

window.look: a third to half red from the blossom end, shoulders still green, fruit firm with no give
window.gives: firm all-purpose fruit that will sit and finish on the counter for several days — the practical stage when a determinate sets more at once than you can eat

window.look: even red round fruit through the shoulders, glossy, slight give under the thumb
window.gives: the full all-purpose flavour with the sharp acidity this Canadian cold-climate early is known for — good raw and worth cooking down; from here coloured fruit takes up water and cracks, so pick at colour rather than holding

subarcticplenty.caveat: MIgardener supplies the cultivar facts (red round fruit up to 2 oz, 50 days, determinate, bred in Canada, extremely tolerant of cold climates, all-purpose, high yields) but no ripeness or harvest guidance, and no source was found describing whether cool-weather fruit colours ahead of flavour on this variety — nothing is claimed about that. Stage points are Penn State Extension's ripening stages applied to a small red determinate.

window.look: the fruit has reached full size for its variety and the skin is glossy, and colour has just appeared at the blossom end — on a variety that does not ripen red, this shows as a shade and tone shift there rather than a new colour
window.gives: the plant stops sending nutrients into the fruit at breaker, so it ripens the rest of the way off the vine and still eats as vine-ripened; picking here also takes the fruit out of reach of moisture cracking, sunscald and further insect damage

window.look: colour spreading upward from the blossom end; the shoulders and the ring around the stem scar are the last to change; past about 30% the fruit begins to soften
window.gives: firmest handling stage — halves and slices cleanly, packs and travels without bruising; flavour is still short of finished. Above about 85°F on-vine ripening slows or stops, so in a heat wave a part-coloured fruit finishes faster indoors than out

window.look: colour even over the shoulders and around the stem scar with no lingering green cast, gloss at its highest, and the fruit gives slightly under thumb pressure and parts easily from the stem
window.gives: the finished flavour of whatever colour that variety ripens to, and its highest sugars; also its most fragile state — fully coloured fruit takes up water and splits, so daily picking beats holding, and small-fruited types need checking every day once the first fruit colours

window.look: gloss dulls, ring or radial cracks open around the stem scar, soft or watery patches appear
window.gives: same-day cooking only — sauce or roasting; the skin has stretched past holding and the fruit will neither store nor travel

croptypetomato.ripe_vs_unripe: Across the crop, three things separate a finished fruit from an unfinished one regardless of what colour it ripens to: colour reaches the shoulders and the ring around the stem scar (always the last areas to change, so a coloured blossom end with green shoulders is not done); gloss peaks and the skin looks taut rather than matte; and the shoulder gives slightly under thumb pressure where an unripe fruit is rigid. On green-, yellow-, ivory- or bicolour-ripening varieties, colour alone cannot be read — use the tone shift at the blossom end plus the shoulder give.
croptypetomato.source: Penn State Extension — Is This Tomato Ready to Harvest?

window.look: Fruit has stopped enlarging at a pound or more and the skin has gone glossy; the first colour is a yellowish-green fading toward salmon at the blossom end, under 10% of the surface, shoulders still green. Still rock hard.
window.gives: Texas A&M reports no taste or tenderness difference between fruit pulled at colour break and fruit left to full red on the vine, and it finishes on a room-temperature counter in five to seven days. The fruit is at its hardest here, so a pound-plus tomato survives being carried in and slices thin without collapsing — and it is off the vine before the radial-crack window and before birds and stinkbugs, which target red.

window.look: Colour has swept up from the blossom end across 10–60%, then 60–90% of the surface; shoulders are last to go. A bit softer to the touch, but the thick meaty wall keeps it solid.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish. The thick wall means slices hold a clean edge on a sandwich instead of weeping, and most of the season's split risk is already behind the fruit.

window.look: 90%+ deep bright red over smooth, blemish-free skin; firm under the thumb and parts from the stem with a slight twist.
window.gives: Clemson puts best flavour exactly here — fully vine-ripened but still firm. The catalogue's crack-free, blemish-resistant skin lets this one sit at full colour through a rain that would split a thin-skinned heirloom. Holds 4–7 days at room temperature; refrigerating costs flavour and turns the flesh mealy.

bigboy.source: Totally Tomatoes — Tomato, Burpee's Big Boy® Hybrid
bigboy.caveat: Fruit traits (1 lb+, firm, meaty, blemish-resistant, crack-free, indeterminate, 78 days) are from this reseller catalogue page — Burpee's own page blocks fetching. Stage boundaries, breaker location and the counter-ripening claims are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Clemson), not measured on this cultivar.

window.look: 8 oz deep-globe fruit at full 3½ in size, skin glossy; a yellowish-green then salmon break at the blossom end on 10% or less of the surface, shoulders still green, flesh hard.
window.gives: Finishes on the counter in five to seven days with no taste or tenderness penalty versus vine-ripening (Texas A&M). More useful on a determinate: the whole crop comes in one flush, so pulling fruit at breaker spreads the ripening across two or three weeks of counter instead of dumping eight-ounce tomatoes on you in the same week. Also puts the fruit past radial cracking and out of reach of birds, which go for red.

window.look: 10–60% then 60–90% coloured, working up from the blossom end; the oblate shoulders colour last. Slightly softer but the firm flesh still resists a thumb.
window.gives: Two to three days to finish indoors, and the firmness that this variety is known for is still intact — clean even slices for sandwiches, no collapse under a knife.

window.look: 90%+ deep red across a smooth oblate globe, still firm, comes away with a slight twist.
window.gives: The exceptional flavour the 1984 AAS award was given for, and Clemson's best-flavour point: fully vine-ripened but still firm. Because the fruit is bred crack-resistant it can hold at full colour longer than a thin-skinned variety before a rain splits it. Room temperature, 4–7 days; refrigeration flattens the flavour.

celebrity.caveat: AAS supplies size, shape, firmness, flavour, 75 days and determinate habit; the crack-resistance and 3½ in oblate detail come from NE Seed's Celebrity F1 page. Stage boundaries and breaker location are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Clemson).

window.look: Smooth 7–8 oz globe at full size and glossy; colour breaks yellowish-green to salmon at the blossom end over 10% or less of the skin, shoulders still green, fruit hard.
window.gives: No taste or tenderness difference from vine-ripened fruit and five to seven days on the counter to finish (Texas A&M). This is the firmest the fruit will be, so it takes handling and slices thin cleanly, and it is off the vine before the radial-crack window and before birds start working on red fruit.

window.look: Colour climbing from the blossom end over 10–60% then 60–90% of the globe, shoulders last; a bit softer to the touch but still smooth and firm.
window.gives: Two to three days to finish indoors. Fedco's note that these "almost never scar or crack" is doing its work in this stretch — the fruit rides through the moisture swings that split other varieties at this stage.

window.look: 90%+ bright red with the interior colouring to match the exterior; firm, parts with a slight twist.
window.gives: The low-acid, mild flavour this variety is bought for — the late end is where that mellow character actually arrives, and Clemson's best-flavour point is here, fully ripe but still firm. Interior colour matching exterior means cut slices are evenly red rather than pale-cored. Because it barely cracks, it tolerates sitting at full colour longer than most.

jetstar.source: Fedco Seeds — Jet Star Slicing Tomato
jetstar.caveat: Fedco supplies 7–8 oz, smooth and firm, "almost never scar or crack", low acid, interior/exterior colour, 72 days, compact indeterminate. Stage boundaries, breaker location and counter-ripening are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Clemson).

window.look: A 1–2 lb beefsteak that has stopped growing and gone glossy; the break is a yellowish-green to salmon patch at the blossom end, 10% of the surface or less. Nearly solid flesh, so it feels dense and hard for its size.
window.gives: Texas A&M found no taste or tenderness loss versus vine-ripening, and five to seven days on the counter finishes it. On a two-pound fruit that matters more than on a small one: the nearly-solid, tiny-seed-cavity flesh is at its most rigid here, so it carries in without bruising against its own weight and a full slice holds together edge to edge on the board.

window.look: Colour spreading up from the blossom end over 10–60% then 60–90%; the broad shoulders of a beefsteak are the last to change. Softens slightly, but the solid interior means far less give than a juicy heirloom of the same size.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish, with the structure still there for thick sandwich slices. Tiny seed cavities mean very little juice runs when you cut it at this stage.

window.look: 90%+ red over a smooth, huge, near-solid fruit; firm, and it takes a deliberate twist to part it.
window.gives: The excellent old-fashioned beefsteak flavour, at Clemson's best-flavour point — fully ripe and still firm. Catalogue reports "very little cracking", so unlike most fruit this size it can hold at full colour without splitting across the shoulders. Room temperature only, 4–7 days.

delicious.source: Tomato Growers Supply Company — Delicious Tomato
delicious.caveat: Fruit traits (huge red, 2 lb+, nearly solid, tiny seed cavities, very little cracking, excellent flavour, 77 days, indeterminate) come from this catalogue plus Seeds 'n Such's Delicious page; no extension source is cultivar-specific for Delicious. Stage boundaries and breaker location are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Clemson).

window.look: Firm, smooth, slightly deep globe at full 5–7 oz size; the first change is a lighter yellowish green shading to salmon at the blossom end, on 10% of the surface or less. Rock hard.
window.gives: Finishes on the counter in five to seven days with no taste or tenderness difference from vine-ripened (Texas A&M) — and on this cultivar there is a second reason it matters: above 85°F the fruit stops making the pigments that colour it (Purdue), so in the heat this variety was bred to set fruit in, colour stalls on the plant. A 60–70°F counter is where it actually finishes. Firmest state, so it holds shape and takes handling.

window.look: Colour working up from the blossom end across 10–60% then 60–90% of the globe; the stem-end shoulders lag well behind. Softer to the touch but the flesh stays firm and low-moisture.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish. Firm, lower-water flesh means it holds its shape through slicing and through canning at this stage rather than going to mush.

window.look: The lower two-thirds fully red, the fruit firm but yielding slightly to gentle pressure, and — per the catalogue description of this variety — a green cast that may persist at the shoulders.
window.gives: Sweet, rich, tangy flavour at its fullest, and the firm flesh means it still slices and cans cleanly rather than collapsing. Sources report Floradade holding market quality 7–10 days, so it sits at full colour better than a soft-fleshed variety.

floradade.ripe_vs_unripe: Catalogues describe ripe Floradade as "red with green shoulder fruits" — so on this one, waiting for uniform all-over red may never pay off. Judge the bottom of the fruit, not the top: colour arrives at the blossom end and the shoulders are last everywhere, but here a green ring at the stem end can be part of the ripe fruit rather than a sign it needs longer. Use full red across the lower two-thirds plus a slight give under the thumb, not a green-free shoulder. Not every catalogue mentions the green shoulder, so check it against your own first ripe fruit before trusting it on the rest.
floradade.source: True Leaf Market — Floradade Tomato Seeds
floradade.caveat: Green-shoulder claim is catalogue-level and sources disagree: True Leaf Market describes the fruit as "red with green shoulder", while Underwood Gardens' Floradade page calls it simply "luscious red fruit" and says to pick when fully coloured with a slight give. Treat the green shoulder as a possibility to verify on your own fruit. University of Florida release (1976), heat tolerance, 5–7 oz, firm/smooth, determinate and 74 days are catalogue-sourced; stage boundaries, breaker location and the 85°F pigment cutoff are extension (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Purdue).

window.look: 4–5 oz plum at full size and glossy; a yellowish-green to salmon break at the blossom end on 10% or less of the surface, shoulders still green. Very hard — thick-walled paste fruit feels solid rather than heavy.
window.gives: Finishes on the counter in five to seven days with no taste or tenderness difference from vine-ripened (Texas A&M). Johnny's notes that on this variety any fruit breaking colour will still ripen after picking, and to pick less ripe the further the fruit has to travel. Thick walls at their firmest here means it dices without weeping — the difference between salsa and soup.

window.look: Colour running up from the blossom end over 10–60% then 60–90%; Johnny's notes clusters ripen from the base toward the tips, so the lowest fruit on a truss is ahead of the rest. Slightly softer, walls still thick.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish. Still firm enough that halves hold their shape roasting or on a tray instead of slumping.

window.look: 90%+ even bright red — Johnny's calls the fruit uniform and attractive at maturity — firm, thick-walled, parts with a slight twist.
window.gives: Peak flavour at Clemson's best-flavour point, ripe but still firm, and the stage the thick walls pay off in: high solids and little juice, so sauce and salsa cook down with less water and less time. Low blossom-end-rot susceptibility means fewer fruit lost while waiting for the last of them to colour.

granadero.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Granadero (F1) Tomato Seed
granadero.caveat: Johnny's supplies the 4–5 oz uniform bright red, thick-walled, low-blossom-end-rot, 75-day indeterminate traits. The blossom-end-to-shoulders and base-of-cluster-to-tip ripening pattern and the "any fruit breaking color will still ripen post-harvest" line are Johnny's standard tomato harvest guidance (read on their Estiva F1 page); stage boundaries are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Clemson).

window.look: Oblate 6–7 oz fruit at full size on a compact determinate plant; first colour is yellowish-green to salmon at the blossom end, 10% of the surface or less, shoulders still green, flesh hard.
window.gives: Finishes on a counter in five to seven days with no taste or tenderness difference from vine-ripening (Texas A&M). On the earliest variety in the garden that buys the thing that actually matters — the first tomato of the season lands on the counter roughly a week sooner. It also staggers the single determinate flush instead of ripening the whole plant at once, and gets fruit out of reach of birds, which target red.

window.look: Colour climbing from the blossom end across 10–60% then 60–90% of the oblate fruit, shoulders last; softens a little under the thumb.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish, still firm enough to slice cleanly. On a 3–4 ft determinate the low fruit is the most exposed to soil splash and rain, so this is the stage where taking it in avoids the splitting that follows a downpour.

window.look: 90%+ deep red on the outside with matching deep red interior; firm, parts with a slight twist.
window.gives: Clemson's best-flavour point — fully ripe but still firm — and, per Harris, excellent flavour for something this early, which is what a 63-day variety trades away when picked green. Deep interior colour means cut slices are red through rather than pale-cored. Room temperature, 4–7 days; refrigeration costs flavour and texture.

bushearlygirl.source: Harris Seeds — Tomato Bush Early Girl F1
bushearlygirl.caveat: Harris supplies 6–7 oz oblate, deep red exterior and interior, excellent flavour for the early class, 63 days and compact determinate habit; other catalogues list 54 days, so first harvest may run earlier than 63. No extension or breeder page is cultivar-specific. Stage boundaries, breaker location and counter-ripening are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Clemson).

window.look: Fruit at full size for a cherry, roughly 1 in and round, skin gone glossy; the first colour is a lighter yellowish green then a salmon flush at the blossom end. Hard all over.
window.gives: Finishes on the counter in five to seven days with no taste or tenderness difference from vine-ripened fruit (Texas A&M), and on a small thin-skinned fruit that is the whole difference between a whole tomato and a burst one after rain — Maryland Extension recommends harvesting as soon as colour begins to change specifically to head off cracking, splitting, insect feeding and disease.

window.look: Colour has spread from the blossom end up toward the shoulders and, on a truss, from the base of the cluster toward the tip — so the bottom fruit on a cluster runs several days ahead of the tip. Slight softening.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish. This is the stage where a whole cluster can be taken at once rather than picked over daily, and where the fruit is still firm enough to go into a bag or tray without the skins scuffing.

window.look: Evenly coloured to the shoulder, glossy, with a slight give when gently squeezed; the ripest come off by hand while firmer ones need shears.
window.gives: Full sugar — the sweetness a cherry type is grown for, at Clemson's best-flavour point: fully ripe but still firm. This is also the end of the window rather than the middle of it: Missouri Extension notes ripe fruit splits vertically and that fruit left on the vine too long cracks concentrically at the stem end, and a small fruit with a thin skin gets there fast. After any rain following a dry spell, split fruit needs using immediately before rot.

cherry.source: University of Maryland Extension — Growing Tomatoes in a Home Garden
cherry.caveat: "Cherry" is not a cultivar name, so nothing here is cultivar-specific: the window is derived from general cherry-tomato-type guidance plus extension crop-level tomato harvest science (Maryland, Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Missouri, Clemson) and Johnny's cluster-ripening pattern. Size, sweetness and how fast it splits will vary by whatever cherry variety this actually is — check it against your own first ripe fruit.

cherryfalls.window_label: breaker → bright red with a slight give

window.look: 1–1½ in round fruit at full size, glossy, hanging over the rim of the basket; first colour is a lighter yellowish green then salmon at the blossom end. Hard.
window.gives: Finishes on the counter in five to seven days with no taste or tenderness difference from vine-ripened (Texas A&M). This one lives in a container or hanging basket, where soil moisture swings hardest between waterings — and uneven moisture is the exact trigger for the swelling that splits skins (Missouri Extension). Taking fruit at breaker is how you keep a basket's worth from splitting after one heavy watering.

window.look: Colour running up from the blossom end and, along the trailing 3 ft of vine, working through the abundant clusters unevenly. Softening slightly, skin still tight.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish. Firm enough to handle without scuffing, which matters on a cascading plant where fruit sits against the basket and the foliage.

window.look: Evenly bright red and, per Botanical Interests, with a slight give when gently squeezed.
window.gives: The sweet, juicy flavour the variety is grown for, at its peak. It is also a determinate — the whole plant ripens in one flush at 55–65 days — so at this end the crop arrives together and holds only briefly: Missouri notes ripe fruit splits vertically and long-held fruit cracks at the stem end. Daily picking through the flush is what keeps the yield off the ground.

cherryfalls.source: Botanical Interests — Cherry Falls Bush Cherry Tomato Seeds
cherryfalls.caveat: Botanical Interests supplies the 1–1½ in bright red fruit, 55–65 days, determinate container/basket habit and the "red with a slight give" ripeness cue; John Scheepers Kitchen Garden Seeds adds the 6 in tall / 3 ft cascade and the sweet flavour. No extension or breeder page is cultivar-specific. Stage boundaries, breaker location, the splitting mechanism and counter-ripening are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Missouri, Clemson).

window.look: Round fruit at its full 1 in, roughly 1 oz, skin glossy; colour breaks as a lighter yellowish green then salmon at the blossom end. Hard to the finger.
window.gives: Finishes off the plant with no taste or tenderness difference from vine-ripened fruit (Texas A&M) — five to seven days on the counter, or faster in a paper bag with a banana, which the catalogue recommends for this variety specifically. Hardest state, so a 1 oz fruit does not bruise or scuff in the pail, and it is out of the way of the splitting and insect feeding that Maryland Extension says early picking prevents.

window.look: Colour climbing from the blossom end toward the shoulders; within a cluster of about five, the fruit nearest the base colours first and the tip lags. Slight softening.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish, and clusters can be taken part-coloured as a unit instead of picked over every day. Firm fruit is best clipped with shears at this stage — pulling it risks tearing the truss the rest of the cluster is still ripening on.

window.look: Evenly bright red to the shoulder; the ripest pull free by hand, firmer ones still need shears.
window.gives: Extra sweet and juicy with minimal acid compared with a large slicer — that low-acid sweetness is what the late end of the window is actually buying, and it is the reason this one is grown for snacking rather than slicing. It is also the end of the safe window: ripe fruit splits vertically and fruit held too long cracks at the stem end (Missouri Extension), and this variety carries these over a long season, so picking runs weekly rather than once.

largeredcherry.source: True Leaf Market — Tomato Seeds, Large Red Cherry
largeredcherry.caveat: True Leaf Market supplies the 1 in fruit, extra-sweet minimal-acid flavour, cluster habit, 75–80 days indeterminate, and the harvest guidance (ripest pull by hand, firmer clipped with shears, early-picked fruit finished in a paper bag with a banana). "Large Red Cherry" is used loosely across catalogues, so fruit size and sweetness may vary from the strain you are growing. Stage boundaries, breaker location and the splitting mechanism are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Maryland, Missouri).

window.look: Smooth-skinned, slightly flattened 6–6½ oz fruit at full size and glossy; the break is a lighter yellowish green shading to salmon at the blossom end, 10% of the surface or less, shoulders still green. Hard, and dense for its size.
window.gives: Finishes on the counter in five to seven days with no taste or tenderness difference from vine-ripening (Texas A&M). On a very early determinate bred for short cool seasons, this is what gets the whole flush processed in shifts rather than in one overwhelming week — and it takes fruit off the plant before the crack window and before birds work on red fruit.

window.look: Colour spreading up from the blossom end over 10–60% then 60–90% of the flattened fruit, shoulders last. Softens slightly; the firm meaty flesh gives less than a juicy variety would.
window.gives: Two to three days indoors to finish. Firm meaty flesh at this stage holds up to being cut and cooked down — the reason this variety reads as a preserving tomato as much as a slicer.

window.look: 90%+ even brick-red over smooth skin; firm, meaty, parts with a slight twist.
window.gives: The refreshing tangy flavour this Morden-bred variety is known for — a real acid edge, unlike the low-acid hybrids, and the late end is the only place that tang fully arrives. Clemson's best-flavour point: fully ripe and still firm. Firm meaty flesh means good yield and body when canned. Room temperature, 4–7 days; refrigeration costs flavour.

manitoba.source: West Coast Seeds — Manitoba Tomato Seeds
manitoba.caveat: West Coast Seeds supplies the 170 g (6 oz) bright red fruit, smooth skin, firm meaty flesh, refreshing tangy taste, 60-day determinate habit, short-cool-season adaptation and the Morden Experimental Farm origin (mid-1950s); Tomato Growers Supply adds brick-red colour, 6½ oz and the slightly flattened shape. No extension source is cultivar-specific. Stage boundaries, breaker location and counter-ripening are extension crop-level (Penn State, Texas A&M AgriLife, Clemson).

highbush.window_label: first full blue → dull-ripe blue, 3–6 days later

window.look: 100% of the skin blue with a heavy pale waxy bloom, no reddish tinge left at the stem end, berry hard and still needs a real pull to come off the pedicel
window.gives: the firmest berry and the longest fridge life, but acid is still high and it eats sharp and bright rather than sweet — the stage for freezing whole, muffins and anything where you want the berry to hold its shape instead of collapsing

window.at: dull-ripe blue (3–6 days after full blue)
window.look: the same blue gone slightly deeper and duller as the bloom wears, berry visibly larger and plumper, gives a little under the fingers, and it rolls off into your palm under a thumb-roll with no pull at all
window.gives: maximum sweetness and flavour: acid keeps falling while sugars keep climbing after the skin is already fully blue (in a measured 'Legacy' trial titratable acidity fell from 0.62% to 0.44% in the five days after full blue, with soluble solids holding at ~14.7%), so the same sugar tastes far sweeter — and the berry swells in that window. Softer, so it is a two-or-three-day fruit, not a week one

highbush.ripe_vs_unripe: Blue is not ripe on a blueberry — full colour arrives 3 to 6 days before maximum sweetness and flavour, and the berry does not ripen at all after picking, so the whole flavour decision is made on the bush. Three discriminators the eye and thumb can use: (1) stem end — any reddish or pink tinge around the stem scar means under-ripe, leave it; (2) bloom and depth — an under-ripe berry is a brighter, bluer blue under a fresh chalky bloom, a ripe one is duller and deeper as that bloom wears; (3) release, which is the real test — a ripe berry detaches from the pedicel on its own and drops into your hand when you roll it with your thumb, while an under-ripe one holds on and has to be pulled. Also size: the tempting berry is the one that just turned blue and looks finished, but it is still up to a size class smaller than it will be in a few days.
highbush.source: University of Maryland Extension — Growing Blueberries in a Home Garden

window.look: every drupelet fully black but the whole berry still glossy, drupelets tight and small, the fruit firm and it takes a definite pull to break it off
window.gives: the firm, transportable stage — this is what survives a walk back through brush and several days in the fridge. It eats tart and acidic with the sugar not yet in; take it only if you are carrying fruit any distance or racing birds

window.look: the gloss has gone matte and slightly powdery-looking, drupelets swollen and rounded so the surface looks bumpier, and the berry comes away with almost no pull
window.gives: the eating stage — sugar levels rise as the berry goes from shiny to dull, so this is where the flavour is; the trade is that a dull-ripe blackberry is soft and juicy and will leak within a couple of days

alleghenyblackberry.ripe_vs_unripe: A blackberry turns fully black several days before it is sweet, and it does not improve after picking — a blackberry must reach full colour on the cane, so a berry taken early stays sour forever. The tempting berry is the shiny one: full black, plump-looking, obviously 'done', and it is the one that will make you think you dislike wild blackberries. Look at the shine, not the colour — glossy means wait, matte/dull means pick. Second cue is the drupelets: on an unripe berry they are tight, small and clearly separate; on a ripe one they plump up and round over. Third is release — a shiny berry resists and tears, a dull-ripe one falls into your fingers. Anything with red or purple drupelets is nowhere near ready.
alleghenyblackberry.source: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook — Chapter 14, Small Fruits
alleghenyblackberry.caveat: No source specific to the wild native Allegheny blackberry (Rubus allegheniensis) was found; the window is derived from NC State's blackberry harvest guidance, plus Penn State's post-harvest rule that blackberries must reach full colour before picking. The shiny-versus-dull test is shared across blackberry types.

window.look: colour not yet filled in — drupelets pale pink to washed red, berry firm, and it still grips its core so it has to be pulled
window.gives: raspberries are the one bramble that finishes off the cane: picked at the light pink stage they will ripen on to normal sweetness and colour indoors. So this is the stage to take when rain, heat or birds are about to cost you the crop, or when the fruit has to travel — you keep the sugar and gain the firmness

window.look: even deep red right out to the shoulders, slightly soft, and the berry slides off with a gentle roll leaving the white core standing on the cane — the fruit in your hand is hollow
window.gives: peak aroma and the melting texture the berry is actually grown for; in exchange it has almost no shelf life, so this is eat-now, freeze-now or jam fruit. Pick every 2–3 days at this stage or you lose fruit to over-ripeness

redraspberry.ripe_vs_unripe: Colour is the weaker signal here and release is the whole test: ripe fruit separates from the receptacle easily, so a ripe raspberry lifts off with a gentle roll and leaves the white core behind on the plant, while an under-ripe one holds on, needs a pull, and tears or comes away with the core still inside it. The tempting berry is the one that has gone fully red on the sunny side but is still pale at the shoulder and refuses to let go — that resistance is the answer. Because raspberries do keep ripening after picking, a firm pink berry is a legitimate pick; a berry that will not slip is simply telling you it is a pink berry and will finish on the counter, not the cane.
redraspberry.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-320 — Raspberries for the Home Garden

cavendish.window_label: full red to the shoulders → deep soft red

window.at: full red to tip and shoulders
window.look: no white or pale green anywhere, including the shoulders under the cap; glossy, strongly scented, still firm to the thumb. Snip or pinch with about a quarter-inch of stem attached rather than pulling the berry off its cap
window.gives: the main pick — full sugar and aroma with enough firmness to hold a day or two in the fridge. Cavendish is a large-fruited, excellent-flavoured variety that holds its flavour, so this stage is genuinely dessert-grade, not a compromise

window.look: colour darker and duller, surface losing its shine, the berry yielding under light thumb pressure and the cap parting easily
window.gives: the most aromatic eating and the best jam and freezer fruit. No extra sugar arrives at this point — sugar and flavour are already optimal at full ripeness — what you are buying is aroma and softness, and paying for it in shelf life: get soft berries cold within the hour or you lose most of their keeping

cavendish.ripe_vs_unripe: Strawberries do not sweeten after picking, so any berry showing white anywhere — including the shoulders under the cap — should be left for the next picking; a white-shouldered berry picked today is a sour berry tomorrow. The confusable case for Cavendish specifically is heat: this variety has a known tendency to ripen unevenly in hot weather, so in a heat wave you can get a berry with a dead-ripe soft tip and shoulders that stay pale. In that situation judge by softness, scent and gloss as well as colour, and expect uneven fruit rather than assuming a few more days will fix the shoulders. Under-ripe strawberry at its most tempting: bright red on the exposed face, hard to the thumb, no smell, and a green-white ring under the cap.
cavendish.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Harvesting strawberries; cultivar detail from Nourse Farms — Cavendish Strawberry Plant

earlyjune.window_label: full red to the shoulders → deep soft red

window.at: full red to tip and shoulders
window.look: red all over with no white or pale patch left at the shoulders or under the cap, glossy and fragrant, firm to the thumb; pick with about a quarter-inch of stem still on the berry
window.gives: the main pick and the earliest stage worth taking — flavour and sugar are already optimal at full ripeness, and the berry is still firm enough to carry and to hold a day or two chilled

window.look: darker, duller red, gloss going, soft under light pressure, cap detaching with almost no effort
window.gives: peak aroma and the best jam/freezing fruit; it will not survive handling or a warm kitchen — cool it fast, since delaying refrigeration by hours costs most of the shelf life

earlyjune.ripe_vs_unripe: The trap is the same as for any strawberry and it is a shoulder problem, not a tip problem: the berry reddens from the tip toward the cap, so the most tempting fruit is bright red down the front, hard to the thumb, scentless, and still carrying a white or green-white ring on the shoulders under the leaves. Because strawberries gain no sugar after picking, that berry never recovers — it will colour up on the counter and stay sour. Ripe reads as: red into the shoulder, gloss, real smell at arm's length, and a slight give.
earlyjune.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Harvesting strawberries
earlyjune.caveat: No source specific to the 'Early June' cultivar was found; window derived from general June-bearing strawberry harvest guidance (University of Minnesota Extension, with post-harvest handling from Penn State). Treat the timing as type-level and the colour/feel cues as reliable.

strawberry.window_label: full red to the shoulders → deep soft red

window.at: full red to tip and shoulders
window.look: fully red with nothing white left anywhere on the fruit, shoulders included; glossy, scented, firm; harvested with roughly a quarter-inch of stem attached
window.gives: the standard pick: flavour and sugar are at their optimum at full ripeness, and the berry is firm enough to move and to keep briefly. Best for slicing, shortcake and anything that needs the berry to hold together

window.look: dark dull red, matte, soft to a light press, cap comes free easily, strongly perfumed
window.gives: maximum aroma; the jam, smoothie and eat-in-the-row stage. Nothing more is gained in sugar, and shelf life collapses — unrefrigerated for eight hours after picking costs roughly 70% of a strawberry's remaining shelf life

strawberry.ripe_vs_unripe: Only pick berries that are red all over: a berry still showing white anywhere, including the shoulders, should be left for the next picking, because strawberries do not sweeten off the plant. The most tempting under-ripe berry is the one facing the sun — brilliant red on the exposed cheek, hard, odourless, and pale green-white where the cap and leaves shaded it. Ripe: colour carried into the shoulder, gloss rather than shine, obvious scent, and a faint give under the thumb.
strawberry.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Harvesting strawberries

wildwineberry.window_label: calyx just splitting open → bright ruby red, slip-ripe

window.look: the sticky, red-bristled calyx that has been wrapped around the fruit all season splits back and exposes the berry for the first time; the fruit underneath is not yet full ruby and still holds firmly to its cone
window.gives: the calyx opening is your countdown signal, not the pick signal — the fruit is enclosed in its calyx until just before it is ripe. Taken here it is tart and firm; worth doing only to beat birds, a rain or a heat spell, since the fruit is exposed and unprotected from this moment on

window.look: glossy bright ruby red, about three-quarters of an inch across, sitting fully clear of the opened calyx, and it lifts off its cone at the lightest touch leaving the pale core behind on the cane
window.gives: sweet-tart with a raspberry-like flavour, juicy and thin-walled — the eating and jelly stage. Essentially zero keeping quality; a full container crushes itself, so pick shallow and use the same day

wildwineberry.ripe_vs_unripe: Red is the ripe colour here, and an unripe wineberry is also reddish, so the two states are easy to confuse. The under-ripe berry is the tempting one: the calyx has only just split or is still half-closed, the fruit beneath is orange-toned rather than ruby and looks slightly dry rather than glassy, it is hard to the finger, and it resists — it tears or drags its core rather than releasing. Ripe reads as glossy, almost translucent bright red, fully clear of the calyx, and above all it comes free with no pull at all. Two extra points for a wild bramble: only fruit that is completely out of its calyx is worth testing, and a berry that falls off as you reach for it is past prime rather than perfect.
wildwineberry.source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Rubus phoenicolasius (Wineberry)
wildwineberry.caveat: Wineberry is a wild-foraged, potentially invasive Asian bramble with thin horticultural coverage — no harvest-maturity extension guidance exists for it. Colour, calyx behaviour, size, flavour and season are from the NC State plant record; the slip-off-the-core release test is derived from red raspberry harvest guidance (NMSU H-320), which wineberry shares as a raspberry-type Rubus.

window.look: large fruit ~2 1/2 in across, still bright apple-green, filling the husk so tightly the papery husk has dried toward tan and started to split; the fruit twists off with almost no pull
window.gives: peak tartness and firm flesh — the sour-side salsa stage, holds its shape when roasted and keeps 1-2 weeks in the husk in a paper bag in the fridge

window.at: husk fully papery, fruit bulging out of the split
window.look: husk brown and shredded, green skin taut and glossy where it pushes through, fruit sometimes already dropped and lying under the plant in its husk
window.gives: the fullest green-tomatillo body — still tangy but rounder; dropped fruit keeps ripening in the husk on the counter, so windfalls are not losses

window.look: the apple-green ground colour warming toward a soft yellow-green, skin giving slightly under the thumb
window.gives: sweetness arrives and the sour drops — better raw or in a fruit-forward salsa, but the flesh softens and the sharp tang that makes green salsa taste like green salsa is largely gone

cisneros.ripe_vs_unripe: A green tomatillo that is ready looks almost identical in colour to one that is not — the fruit is the wrong thing to read. Read the husk: unready fruit sits loose inside a plump, green, wholly intact husk with visible air space, and resists when twisted. Ready fruit has swelled until it is pressed flat against the husk wall with no slack, and the husk has gone from green and pliable to dry, tan and papery, then split along a seam so green skin shows through; at that point it detaches with a light twist. A separate, later shift — apple-green drifting to yellow-green with a slight softening — means it has gone past the tart green stage into the sweet one, not that it has only just become pickable.
cisneros.source: Adaptive Seeds — Tomatillo, Cisineros (Organic); husk and stage behaviour from SDSU Extension — Tomatillos: Harvest and Storage
cisneros.caveat: The two sources pull in opposite directions on the last point: Adaptive names the yellow-green stage as the sweet one, while SDSU says green cultivars should be picked before they turn and otherwise 'become soft and lose their tangy flavor'. Both are true — it is a choice between tang and sweetness, not a right and wrong pick.

pineappletomatillo.window_label: husk-split pale green → full golden yellow

window.look: cherry-sized fruit about 1 in, skin still green to pale green, husk drying from green toward brown and just beginning to split; fruit filling the husk out
window.gives: the earliest legitimate pick — firm and clean-tasting but distinctly tart, with the pineapple note only hinted at; you trade most of the variety's reason for existing to beat the birds and the ground

window.look: green washing out to yellow, gold showing first on the shoulders through the split husk, husk fully brown and papery
window.gives: the balance point — sweet and tangy together, which is what makes it work in a fruit salsa; still firm enough to handle without bruising

window.look: uniformly yellow-gold right to the stem, skin slightly soft, husk brown and shredded; many fruits will already have dropped and be lying under the compact 1.5 ft plants in their husks
window.gives: this is where the sweetness and the actual pineapple flavour arrive — a marked jump in sugar and fruitiness over the green pick, and the only stage worth using in jam or dessert. The cost is fragile skin, a short shelf life, and having to pick off the ground; dropped fruit is still good and keeps ripening in the husk.

pineappletomatillo.ripe_vs_unripe: Husk-split comes before colour on this variety, so a split husk alone proves pickable, not ripe — the fruit inside can still be green. The colour tells you the rest: unready fruit is a flat, uniform green with the husk plump and loose around it; the sweet stage is a warm gold that starts on the shoulders and spreads to cover the whole fruit, with the husk brown and papery rather than green. Two independent confirmations of full ripeness: the fruit gives slightly under thumb pressure instead of feeling hard, and it abscisses on its own — a fruit found already dropped inside its husk is fully ripe, not spoiled.
pineappletomatillo.source: Grow Organic — Pineapple Tomatillo Seeds (Organic); husk/stage and green-vs-coloured flavour behaviour from SDSU Extension — Tomatillos: Harvest and Storage
pineappletomatillo.caveat: Cultivar-specific detail comes from a retail catalogue rather than extension or the breeder; the extension source names the 'Pineapple' type as cherry-sized with a sweet, citrussy flavour, which agrees, but the intermediate part-coloured stage is inferred from the green-to-gold progression both sources describe rather than named as a stage by either.

window.at: husk split, green, blush not yet showing
window.look: large 2 in-plus fruit, green skin, husk dried toward tan and split, fruit tight against the husk and twisting off easily; shaded fruit low in the sprawling 5 ft plant may show no purple at all
window.gives: full tomatillo tang and firm flesh for green salsa; picking here costs you the sweetness and the colour, and on a shaded fruit it is the only stage you will ever get

window.look: purple appearing as a patch or wash on the side and bottom that the sun actually reaches, over green ground colour — patchy and asymmetric, deeper on the exposed face
window.gives: sweeter and fruitier than the plain green pick while keeping enough acid to carry a salsa; the purple skin also survives roasting as visible colour

window.look: a large purple blush over a ground colour that has warmed off hard green, skin softening under the thumb, husk brown and shredded
window.gives: the sweet, fruity end of the range — testers reached for 'sweet' and 'fruity' at this stage — at the cost of tang, firmness and shelf life; roasted with pumpkin seeds and chile this is the stage that carries the dish

purpleblush.ripe_vs_unripe: Purple is sun exposure, not ripeness — the fruits blush purple only where they are kissed by the sun, so an interior or leaf-shaded fruit can be fully mature and still entirely green, and a purple fruit picked from the outside of the plant is not automatically further along than a green one beside it. Judge pickability from the husk exactly as for a green tomatillo: plump green intact husk with air space around a loose fruit means wait; husk dried tan and papery, split, with the fruit swelled tight against it and detaching on a light twist means pick. Use purple only to decide which mature fruit you want — blushed for sweeter and fruitier, green for tangier — and read softening plus a lightening ground colour, not the purple itself, as the signal that it has moved into the sweet stage.
purpleblush.source: Fedco Seeds — Purple Blush Organic Tomatillo; husk and stage behaviour from SDSU Extension — Tomatillos: Harvest and Storage
purpleblush.caveat: Fedco names the colour behaviour, size, 68 days and the flavour verdict but gives no harvest instruction; the husk-split window, the detachment test and the sweeter-but-softer tradeoff at the late stage are the SDSU Extension tomatillo rules applied to it.

contender.window_label: slender pencil-thick pods → just before seed bulge

window.look: smooth green pods, no bumps at all along the sides, roughly pencil-thick; pod snaps cleanly in half with an audible break and a wet cut face
window.gives: the most tender and juiciest eating, no fibre; the cost is yield — picking pods before they have gained more size decreases total pounds off the plant

window.look: pods at full length and thickness but still smooth-sided, seeds inside detectable only as a faint line, not as shapes
window.gives: the best combination of weight in the basket and quality on the plate — still snaps, still juicy, and this is the stage that stays firm through canning rather than going limp

window.look: individual seeds showing as distinct bumps that make the pod bulge, pod wall dulling and going leathery, pod bends rather than snapping
window.gives: less juicy and more fibrous — the pods turn tough and stringy, and leaving them on also signals the plant to stop setting new pods; shell them for the seed or leave them to dry rather than eating them as snaps

contender.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing beans in home gardens
contender.caveat: No cultivar-specific source found for Contender; window derived from extension snap-bean guidance for the green bush snap class. Contender is simply an early one — commonly listed at 45-55 days — so the same stages arrive sooner, not differently.

goldrush.window_label: slender pencil-thick yellow pods → just before seed bulge

window.at: slender yellow pods, about 2 weeks after bloom
window.look: lemon-yellow pods short of the full 5 1/2 in, thinner than a pencil, sides perfectly smooth; snaps easily when bent
window.gives: the most delicate texture and the cleanest snap; picking this early costs pounds, since the pod has not finished filling

window.at: nearly full size, pencil-thick, seeds still small
window.look: lemon-yellow pods at or near 5 1/2 in long and about as thick as a pencil, sides still smooth, white seeds inside small and not raised; pod snaps easily
window.gives: the prime pick — buttery flavour and crisp texture at full weight, and this variety holds that tender texture and delicate flavour on the plant longer than most snap beans, so the pencil-thick stage is forgiving rather than knife-edge

window.look: deeper gold, dulling pods with the white seeds raised as visible lumps; the pod flexes and tears instead of snapping
window.gives: the bean goes tough once seeds mature and start bulging — fibrous and dry to eat; pick every 3-5 days to stay ahead of it, and picking regularly is also what keeps yields coming

goldrush.ripe_vs_unripe: Yellow is what this cultivar IS, not a sign that it is ready — a Gold Rush pod is lemon-yellow from the day it forms, so waiting for it to 'turn yellow' means waiting for something that already happened and picking tough beans. Ignore colour entirely and read the pod: prime is nearly full size at roughly 5 1/2 in, about as thick as a pencil, sides smooth with no lumps, and snapping easily and cleanly when you bend it. Over-mature is the opposite set of cues — a deeper, duller gold, seed shapes standing up as bumps along the pod, and a pod that bends and tears rather than snapping. The other direction is real too: a very slender, pale, short pod is genuinely under-filled and light, so you are giving up yield rather than gaining tenderness past a point. Judged the same way, a yellow wax bean and a green snap bean are picked at exactly the same stage.
goldrush.source: Territorial Seed — Gold Rush Wax Beans; over-maturity/seed-bulge rule corroborated by University of Minnesota Extension — Growing beans in home gardens

window.look: very slender medium-dark green round pods, well short of the 4-5 in finished length, no seed detectable at all
window.gives: the true French extra-fine grade — the tender, nutty, restaurant-quality eating the variety was bred for, needing no trimming and barely any cooking; the cost is very low weight per pod, so you pick a lot of pods for a little dinner

window.at: fine filet, up to 1/4 in diameter
window.look: round pods 4-5 in long, still uniformly slender at about 1/4 in through, straight and smooth, medium-dark green
window.gives: the practical pick — full filet length and the variety's uniformity and eating quality at usable weight, still tender-crisp rather than fibrous; this is the last point that is still a filet bean

window.look: pods thicker than 1/4 in, losing their round cross-section and their straightness, seed shapes starting to show
window.gives: oversized, tough beans — the tenderness that justified growing a filet type over an ordinary snap bean is gone and does not come back; not worth freezing or canning either, since Tavera is not recommended for those

tavera.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Tavera, Organic Bush Bean (filet)
tavera.caveat: The narrower window is explicit in the source, not an inference: filet beans must be picked very slender at 1/8-1/4 in diameter and Johnny's specifies picking every 36-48 hours to hold the extra-fine grade, with delays of only 2 days in hot weather or 4 days in cool weather producing oversized, tough beans. A standard snap bean tolerates a 3-5 day interval; Tavera does not.

peach.window_label: yellow ground colour, firm → dark yellow, soft ripe

window.at: ground colour breaking green to yellow, hard
window.look: the background skin between and behind the red blush losing its green and turning yellow (cream on a white-fleshed cultivar); fruit still rock-hard, in the 10-16 lb-force range a packing house picks at
window.gives: the shipping and storage pick — travels and keeps without bruising, and the flesh will soften off the tree. What it cannot do is get sweeter: sugar in a peach rises until full maturity on the tree and then stays constant after harvest, so this fruit will end up soft but permanently less sweet than one left hanging.

window.look: no green left anywhere in the background colour, clear yellow or cream under and around the blush; fruit still firm to the hand but no longer stony; 2 1/2 in or more across
window.gives: the honest home-garden compromise — a few days of counter life to finish softening, and it arrives with nearly all the sugar it will ever have because it was on the tree to full maturity. Bruises much less on the walk back to the kitchen than a tree-ripe peach.

window.look: deep dark yellow ground colour, strong peachy aroma standing off the fruit, flesh yielding at 2-4 lb-force — the pressure a farmers-market ready-to-eat peach is picked at
window.gives: maximum sweetness and juice, with the acid balance the cultivar is supposed to have — tangy on a yellow-fleshed peach, honey-sweet with little acid on a white-fleshed one. The cost is fragility: the tip, suture and shoulders bruise from handling, and a fruit at room temperature loses roughly another 2 lb of firmness per day, so it must be eaten or processed almost immediately.

window.look: the background colour gone past dark yellow into orange, flesh soft under light pressure
window.gives: past prime — mealy, leaking texture; the fruit is only worth cooking, freezing or jamming at this point, not eating out of hand

peach.ripe_vs_unripe: The red is not the ripeness. The degree of red coloration is not a good indicator for maturity — the blush comes from sun exposure during the season and from the cultivar, so the shaded side of a perfectly ripe peach can be barely blushed at all, and a hard, green-shouldered peach on the sunny outside of the tree can be almost entirely red. What you read instead is the GROUND colour: the background skin, in the areas not showing red blush, moving green to yellow to eventually orange. Green anywhere in that background means immature no matter how red the rest is. Yellow or cream (which of the two depends on the cultivar) means genuinely mature. Dark yellow means fully ripe; orange means overripe. Two warnings: some newer solid-red cultivars are completely red before optimal maturity, so on those the ground colour is hidden and you must go by firmness and aroma; and background colour cannot be used entirely alone — pair it with give in the flesh and a strong peachy smell.
peach.source: University of Maryland Extension FS-1182 — Are Your Peaches Ready to Harvest?; aroma, flavour-by-flesh-colour and the solid-red-cultivar caution from Clemson HGIC — How to Determine Peach Ripeness
peach.caveat: Both sources are extension and both are specific about ground colour versus blush, but neither is cultivar-specific — no cultivar name was recorded for this planting, so the window is the yellow-fleshed peach standard. Colour thresholds shift by cultivar (the mature ground colour is cream rather than yellow on white-fleshed types), so calibrate against the first fruit you cut.

sweetpotato.window_label: test-dig size → before frost or 50°F soil (no colour cue)

window.look: nothing on the plant tells you — the crop is a root and there is no colour, size or ripeness cue above ground. Judge by the height of the mound of soil heaving up at the base of the vines, then dig one whole plant and look at what is actually on it
window.gives: the earliest honest pick, and the only one you can verify. Digging now means smaller roots, because they keep growing right up until the vines are killed, so every week you leave them is weight you keep — traded against the risk below.

window.at: late season, vines still alive, before frost
window.look: still no visible cue; you are watching the forecast and the soil thermometer rather than the plant. Roots at this point run from baby-baker size up to full size on the same plant
window.gives: the maximum size the season will give. Oversized roots are not a quality problem — size does not affect taste — but football-sized ones are awkward in the kitchen

window.at: at or just after frost kills the vines (hard limit)
window.look: blackened, collapsed vines; roots must come out by the time frost kills the vines or soon after
window.gives: the end of the window, and past it you lose the crop rather than gain anything. The plant is incredibly tender and will not respond well to frost, a hard freeze damages roots sitting near the surface, and chilling injury sets in once soil temperature drops to 50°F or lower — which shows up not in the garden but as internal decay weeks into storage. Cold wet soil also rots roots left waiting.

window.at: after curing (where the sweetness actually happens)
window.look: skins set and toughened, no longer skinning off under a thumb; held about 10 days at 80-85°F and 85-90% relative humidity, or 2-3 weeks at 65-75°F if you have no warm room
window.gives: this is the payoff stage, not the dig — it is during curing that starch is converted to sugar, so a freshly dug sweet potato is comparatively bland and a cured one is sweet. Curing also sets the skin and is what makes them storable at all; hold them at 55-60°F in the dark afterward, never in the fridge, since they take chilling injury in cold storage.

sweetpotato.ripe_vs_unripe: There is no visible ripeness signal, and no colour window — say so plainly rather than looking for one. Nothing about the leaves, stems or flowers reports what the roots are doing, and the flesh colour of a variety is fixed identity, not a stage. The only real reads are: the mound of soil lifting at the base of the vines, an actual test dig of one plant, and the calendar/frost/soil-temperature limit at the far end. Just as important, sweetness is not a field state at all — an uncured root dug at perfect size tastes starchy, and the sugar you are after appears during the curing period after harvest, so 'is it sweet yet' cannot be answered by digging earlier or later.
sweetpotato.source: K-State Research and Extension, Johnson County — Sweet Potato Harvest; curing, chilling-injury and storage detail from Purdue Consumer Horticulture — Dig Those Sweet Potatoes
sweetpotato.caveat: Neither source is cultivar-specific and neither gives a days-from-planting number, so the timing anchor here is frost and test digging rather than a date; K-State's mid-September to mid-October window is for Kansas and should be read as 'the few weeks before your first frost' at Mathews Ridge.

window.look: round to slightly flattened pod at its full 1.5-2 in across, glossy mid-green, firm and crisp when squeezed, and it snaps off the plant easily
window.gives: the firmest, thickest wall of the whole window - this is the stage that holds its shape pickled whole or stuffed, and the flavour is straight vegetal bite with the least sweetness. Picking the first pods here also pushes the plant to set more fruit.

window.look: patchy red creeping over the shoulders and cheeks while the rest stays green; the pod is still hard under thumb pressure
window.gives: still nearly full wall firmness, so it still pickles and stuffs well, with the first of the sweetness coming in behind the bite. The practical compromise pick if you want colour in the jar without losing crunch.

window.look: evenly deep crimson, still glossy, wall giving very slightly to a squeeze
window.gives: the bold, distinctly sweeter flavour these are grown for - fullest heat and best raw eating, salsa, relish and chutney. Wall has softened enough that stuffed pods slump more than green ones do.

cherryhot.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is a real pick stage here, so the thing to judge is mature green vs undersized green. A mature green cherry pepper is at its full width (1.5-2 in across, as wide as it is tall), glossy rather than matte, hard and crisp when you squeeze it, and it detaches from the plant with a light tug. An immature pod is narrower, softer, duller, and clings to the stem - leave it, the wall is still thin.
cherryhot.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds - Capperino (F1) Hot Cherry Pepper
cherryhot.caveat: "Cherry Hot" is a market-class name, not a single cultivar, so no cultivar-specific source exists. This window is derived from cherry-hot type guidance: Johnny's Capperino F1 (1.5 in round-to-flattened pods, 60 days to green and 85 days to red - so roughly three to four weeks of legitimate picking between the two ends) and a Red Cherry Hot listing giving thick walls, 1.5-2 in pods and 3,000-5,000 SHU. Your own record puts this one at 5,000-8,000 SHU, hotter than typical cherry hots, so expect more heat than the type average. Wall thickness and the green-to-red progression are reliable for any cherry hot; exact pod size and days will vary with whichever strain you actually have.

window.look: pod has stopped lengthening and is glossy bright green, firm and crisp when squeezed, and comes away from the plant easily. Note the length and which way it points - see the caveat.
window.gives: the mildest and grassiest this pepper will ever taste, with a slightly bitter vegetative edge and less heat than the ripe pod. Best used fresh where you want the pepper's bite without its full burn.

window.look: colour lifting off green toward orange-red, usually starting at the tip or along one side
window.gives: the identification stage as much as an eating stage - the bitterness starts dropping out and heat starts climbing. If you are trying to work out what this plant is, this is the point to stop picking and let a few pods run all the way through.

window.look: evenly red the whole length, still smooth and glossy
window.gives: peak heat - capsaicin tops out just after full colour - plus the fruity sweetness green pods lack. This is the stage worth using for sauce, flakes and anything where you want the heat to read.

window.look: red gone matte, skin wrinkling and shrinking against the seeds
window.gives: pods that are already part-dried and ready to finish for flakes or powder. Once the fully red pods start to wrinkle you have waited as long as you can - pick them now rather than let them go further.

chilired.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is a legitimate pick, so judge mature green against undersized green: a mature pod has stopped growing longer, is glossy rather than dull, is firm and crisp when squeezed, and detaches with a light tug. A pod that is still soft, matte or clinging is not done growing.
chilired.source: Botanical Interests - Thai Hot Chile Pepper Seeds
chilired.caveat: "Chili Red" is a garden-centre label, not a cultivar - there is no source for it and your own notes flag it as one label over two plants, with pods left to ripen specifically so the plant could be identified. At the recorded 50,000-100,000 SHU it is almost certainly a Thai/bird's-eye type or a hot cayenne, and the ripening itself will tell you which. Thai-type: pods 1.5-3 in, thin, pointed, standing UPRIGHT in clusters on a low bushy plant, green and red pods on the plant at the same time, thin-fleshed, 50,000-100,000 SHU - this matches the recorded heat exactly. Cayenne-type: pods much longer and slender, hanging DOWN, thin-walled, prone to drying on the plant before they finish colouring, on a 2-4 ft plant, and normally cooler than the recorded range. So: short upright pods in clusters means Thai; long pendant pods means cayenne. The colour window above holds for either, since both go green to red - the stages and payoffs are type-derived, and no pod dimensions, days to maturity or final colour should be trusted for this entry until the plant is identified.

korisitakame.window_label: mature green → red → dried on the plant

window.look: roughly 3 in, triangular tapering pod at full length, smooth glossy skin, firm and crisp when squeezed, and it detaches from the plant easily
window.gives: the fresh-cooking stage - use it green for frying and cooked dishes. Thin flesh means it will never be a stuffing pepper, but green pods carry a cleaner, less sweet flavour and less heat than the ripe ones.

window.look: red running up from the tip over the smooth skin while the shoulders hold green
window.gives: heat climbing toward its peak and the fruity sweetness coming in. Still firm enough to use fresh, and the earliest point at which the pod will finish colouring off the plant if frost is coming.

window.look: evenly deep red, smooth and glossy, pod still firm despite the thin wall
window.gives: full medium-to-hot burn - the heat on this one builds a few seconds after the first bite rather than hitting immediately - with the fullest flavour. This is the stage to pick for fresh Mexican cooking or to hang and dry.

window.look: red skin gone papery and shrunken, the thin wall drying almost translucent so you can see the seed shadow through it
window.gives: pods ready to store whole, string up, or grind for flakes and powder. The thin flesh is the reason this one dries so well - it loses water fast and rarely rots on the plant.

korisitakame.ripe_vs_unripe: Green is a real pick stage, so tell mature green from immature: a mature pod has finished lengthening to about 3 in, is glossy rather than dull, feels firm and crisp when squeezed, and comes off with a light tug. Anything shorter, softer or still clinging is not done.
korisitakame.caveat: A real named landrace, not a vendor invention: Kori Sitakame comes from Norogachi, a Raramuri (Tarahumara) pueblo at about 7,500 ft in highland Chihuahua, and Native Seeds/SEARCH holds it in their seed-bank collection. Cultivar-sourced facts: 3 in triangular pod, smooth skin, thin wall, almost translucent when dried, medium-to-hot with a heat that builds a few seconds in, green to red, about 85 days, and it does better in its second year if overwintered than replanted. The per-stage payoffs above are type-derived from thin-walled red-chile guidance - green for fresh cooking, red for drying whole or grinding - because no source gives stage-by-stage picking advice for this chile specifically. Your recorded 5,000-30,000 SHU is a wide band, so treat the first pods of the season as a heat test before committing a batch to anything.

cherokeegreen.window_label: first yellow hint at the bottom → chartreuse with amber blossom end

window.at: breaker — the bottom just hints yellow
window.look: Fruit at or near full size (8-12 oz, oblate beefsteak) and still reading as an overall dark-to-medium green, but the very bottom — the blossom end — carries the first faint yellow-amber tint. Skin has begun to gloss up instead of looking dull and matte. Still hard everywhere, including the base.
window.gives: It is physiologically mature at this point and finishes on the counter in a few days at room temperature with essentially the vine flavour. This is the stage to take if rain, birds, or a heat spell are coming — it has not started to soften, so it will not split, and it still slices cleanly. On a variety this prone to going to mush, picking here is the low-risk play.

window.at: ripe — chartreuse with an amber blossom end
window.look: Overall skin has lightened and warmed from dark green to a yellow-green / chartreuse. A distinct warm amber blush — on some fruit going as far as orange-red — has spread up from the blossom end. The bottom yields to gentle thumb pressure while the shoulders are still firm. Interior is bright green.
window.gives: Peak eating. Bold, complex, acidic flavour with a real sweet-tart balance on the dense meaty Cherokee-type flesh — several catalogues that carry a lot of green tomatoes rate it the best-flavoured of the green-when-ripe class. This is the stage to slice raw.

window.look: Amber gone dull, the sides give with no resistance, blossom end keeps the dent when pressed.
window.gives: This is the documented failure mode of this specific variety, and it arrives fast: growers report that a few days past ripe it liquefies into pure pulp and collapses into a puddle rather than slicing. Cook it that day or compost it. The practical consequence is that Cherokee Green wants checking daily, and when in doubt you pick early rather than late.

cherokeegreen.ripe_vs_unripe: Unripe is one flat, dull, dark green over the whole fruit — matte, almost powdery-looking — and rock hard everywhere including the blossom end. Ripe is three changes happening together, and you want all three rather than any one. (1) SHADE: the overall green lightens and warms, dark green toward yellow-green / chartreuse. It is a shift in the tone of the green you already have, not the appearance of a new colour — this is why it reads as 'nothing has happened' if you glance at one fruit in isolation. Hold a candidate up against a young fruit on the same truss; the difference in shade is the signal. (2) BLOSSOM END: the bottom picks up a warm amber tint, sometimes running to orange-red. On this variety that is the single most reliable thing your eye can use, and it is at the BOTTOM. Every source that gives a rule gives it as some version of 'harvest when the bottom just hints yellow.' (3) FEEL: press the blossom end with your thumb — unripe is hard, ripe gives slightly and springs back, over-ripe keeps the dent. Gloss is a fourth, weaker cue: unripe skin is dull and matte, ripening skin comes up shiny, and that is easier to see in raking light than looking straight at the fruit. One thing that does NOT help: the interior stays bright green right through full ripeness, so cutting one open tells you nothing about whether the next one is ready.
cherokeegreen.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Cherokee Green Organic Tomato Seed
cherokeegreen.caveat: Every source read agrees on the three things above — the shade shift, the amber blossom-end blush, and the thumb test. Two honest gaps. FIRST: nothing I could read describes what the SHOULDERS do. No source says whether they hold a deeper green at full ripe the way Black Krim's do or lighten with the rest of the fruit. Because all the colour guidance points at the blossom end, treat the shoulders as uninformative — do not read green shoulders on this variety as 'not ready.' SECOND: the amber itself is described across a real spread — 'the bottom just hints yellow' (Bucktown Seed), 'blushed amber' (Pinetree Garden Seeds), 'a warm amber to orange-red blush' (Survival Garden Seeds), 'yellowish-orange' (Johnny's). That is probably a difference in how far past first-blush each grower picks rather than a disagreement about the fruit, so calibrate on your own first two or three and then trust that. Corroborating pages read this run: Pinetree Garden Seeds, Sow Right Seeds, Survival Garden Seeds, Bucktown Seed Co., The Coeur d'Alene Coop and growtomato.com on green-when-ripe shade and gloss, a Houzz growers' thread on the narrow window and the pulp failure, and Craig LeHoullier's A Way To Garden interview for its origin as a chance green fruit in a Cherokee Chocolate planting in his garden.

blackkrim.window_label: first warm colour low on the fruit → mahogany body, green shoulders

window.look: Full-size fruit with the first visible warm colour on less than about a tenth of the surface, low down rather than at the top. Shoulders hard olive-green. Firm all over.
