window.gives: The stage to take when heavy rain or animal pressure is coming. Black Krim splits, and picking here removes that risk entirely — it finishes indoors and you give up very little flavour. It also buys you a fruit firm enough to handle without bruising a soft heirloom skin.

window.look: The lower and side surfaces have shifted off hard green toward brick red or red-brown. The olive shoulders are unchanged. Still firm in the hand.
window.gives: Firm enough to slice cleanly and to travel, with most of the flavour already built. This is the realistic pick for a garden that gets looked at every few days rather than daily.

window.look: Body a dusky red-brown to mahogany, near-black through a hot sunny spell, over a rust-red base. Shoulders STILL olive-green. Yields slightly to a thumb without feeling watery or collapsed. Smells strongly of tomato at the stem end, and feels dense and heavy for its size.
window.gives: The whole reason to grow it — rich, sweet, smoky and full-bodied with the distinctive savoury, almost salty note that puts it near the top of taste trials. A fresh-slicing tomato at this stage; the flavour is wasted cooked.

window.look: Soft spots, leaking, skin failure, a fermented smell at the stem.
window.gives: Past use for eating and past use for judging the line if you are saving seed. Worth naming because this is exactly where you land if you wait for the green shoulders to colour up — they never will, so waiting for them means arriving here every time.

blackkrim.ripe_vs_unripe: The trap is the shoulders. Green or olive shoulders persist right through full ripeness on Black Krim — that is the variety, not a signal — so waiting for a uniform finish means harvesting too late every single time. Judge from the BODY: look at the bottom and the sides, not the top. Unripe reads as hard, uniform green everywhere. Ripe reads as a dusky red-brown to mahogany body — a rust-red base darkening to brownish-maroon — capped by shoulders that are still greenish-brown. Then confirm with two things that are not colour, because colour on a dark tomato is genuinely hard to read in garden light: it should yield slightly under a thumb without feeling watery or collapsed, and it should smell strongly of tomato near the stem. It should also feel dense and heavy for its size. Do not wait for it to go uniformly black or uniformly red. It will not.
blackkrim.source: Alliance of Native Seedkeepers — Black Krim Tomato Guide: Ripeness, Growing and Cracking
blackkrim.caveat: One genuine disagreement worth knowing about: how soft is 'ripe.' The field guide above says 'slight give without collapse or leakage,' while Plantura's Black Krim page says to harvest once the skin is 'very soft.' Those are different fruit. Given that this variety splits and that over-ripe on a dark tomato is hard to see, the safer of the two is the slight-give version — a Black Krim that feels very soft is at or past the edge. The 'salty' flavour descriptor is catalogue language (Hudson Valley Seed, Baker Creek) rather than anything measured, but it is consistent across sellers and matches what growers report.

window.look: Full 1-1.5 in size, mostly still green, with the first purple-brown wash showing — it usually reads first as a darkening at the SHOULDERS rather than at the bottom, unlike most tomatoes. Hard to the touch.
window.gives: Fruit showing breaking colour will continue ripening after harvest, so this is the stage to strip a truss before a storm or a few days away. Firmest skin and least likely to split — and on a cherry, the difference between picking here and picking ripe is measured in a couple of days on the windowsill.

window.look: Deep dark red carrying a distinct purple-brown cast, darkest at the shoulders. Still quite firm but with a little give when gently squeezed.
window.gives: The target. Intense old-fashioned tomato flavour — more sweet than tart with a clear acid edge and a hint of smokiness, the complex fruity richness the good black tomatoes are grown for. Pick in the morning for the best of it.

window.look: As dark as it gets — almost black-purple in strong sun. Skin taut and glossy, fruit noticeably soft under light pressure.
window.gives: The sweetest and most complex it will be; the seller's own advice for this variety is explicitly to leave it on the vine 'till nice and dark.' The trade is a short window and real split risk — the skin is crack-resistant but not crack-proof, and one heavy watering after a dry stretch at this stage will burst a whole truss.

blackcherry.ripe_vs_unripe: A ripe Black Cherry never looks red, so 'not red yet' is simply the wrong test — it is a black tomato and it holds chlorophyll underneath the red pigment, which is precisely why it reads dusky and muddy rather than bright. Unripe: uniform green, hard, no warm tone anywhere. Ripening: the purple-brown arrives first as a DARKENING AT THE SHOULDERS and works its way down, which is the opposite of the blossom-end-first pattern you use on most tomatoes. Ripe: an overall dusky mahogany-purple peel — deep dark red with a purple or brown tint — that still feels quite firm but gives a little under a gentle squeeze. The bigger practical problem with this variety is not confusion with unripe but invisibility: the dusky fruit vanish against the foliage and ripe ones simply get missed, which is a documented complaint from people picking them commercially. Look at the plant deliberately, from more than one angle and from underneath, instead of scanning for red.
blackcherry.source: Home for the Harvest — Black Cherry Tomato
blackcherry.caveat: Days to first harvest spread widely across the sources read — 64 days from transplant (Johnny's), about 65 (Home for the Harvest), 75 (Fedco) — so treat any of them as a rough marker rather than a date to plan against. Johnny's adds a useful shipping rule that translates directly to a garden: pick less ripe the further the fruit has to travel and the longer before it gets eaten. Bred by Vince Sapp of Tomato Growers Supply, released 2003.

evapurpleball.window_label: first pink blush → even deep dark pink (never red)

window.look: Round, tennis-ball-shaped 4-6 oz fruit at full size, skin still green but a pink tint coming up. Skin is thin and completely blemish-free — no catfacing, no shoulder cracks, no ribbing to read anything from.
window.gives: The safest stage on a variety that extension trial gardeners report DROPS from the vine once ripe. Picked here it finishes indoors and you do not lose fruit onto the ground. Firmest, too, which matters on a thin-skinned tomato.

window.look: Roughly a third to two-thirds of the ball turned, and the colour comes on evenly because the skin is smooth and unbroken. Sweetening and starting to soften but still firm in the hand.
window.gives: Firm enough to hold a slice and to sit on the counter a few days. This is the compromise pick if you can only get to the plant twice a week — which on this variety is the realistic choice, because ripe fruit do not wait.

window.look: The whole ball an even dark pink — more pink than purple despite the name, and never true red. Thin skin, still uncracked, gives to gentle pressure.
window.gives: Full flavour, which trial gardeners describe on the acidic and tart side of sweet, with several noting it gets better as the season goes on and comparing it favourably to Brandywine. Good sliced, and it cans and sauces well — the thin skin peels off easily, which is a real advantage for putting up a batch. It also keeps producing well through heat and humidity when other varieties quit, so this stage recurs all season rather than in one flush.

evapurpleball.ripe_vs_unripe: The name is the problem. 'Purple' here is nineteenth-century seed-catalogue language for PINK, not for a Black Krim-style dusky tomato — Cornell's trial gardeners put it plainly: it is more pink than purple. Ripe Eva Purple Ball is an even dark pink, and it does not turn red. If you wait for red you will be waiting past ripe, and on this variety past ripe means on the ground: growers report the fruit dropping from the vine when ready and not holding long once mature, so it needs daily scouting rather than a weekly look. The variety also takes away the cues you would normally use on an heirloom — the skin is thin, genuinely blemish-free and crack-resistant, so there are no shoulder cracks and no catfacing to read. That leaves you two things: colour EVENNESS across the whole ball, and a gentle squeeze. Even dark pink all over with a slight give — pick it now, not tomorrow.
evapurpleball.source: Cornell Cooperative Extension — Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners: Eva Purple Ball
evapurpleball.caveat: One source read contradicts the pink call: Giving Ground Seeds describes 'dark red fruits' and instructs 'harvest tomatoes at full red.' Everything else — Cornell's extension trial reports, TomatoFest ('pink-purple'), Southern Exposure, Experimental Farm Network — points at deep pink. I have gone with the extension reports, but if your own fruit finish genuinely red rather than dark pink, believe your eyes over this entry. Flavour reports also genuinely split: some trial gardeners called it sweet with good tart balance and great tomato flavour, others 'sourish, thin and uninteresting' — that spread looks like a season and site effect, and several noted improvement later in the year. Late-1800s heirloom from the Black Forest region of Germany, brought to New Jersey by the Bratka family, introduced through the Seed Savers 1991 yearbook by Carolyn Male.

bananacreme.window_label: half-changed cream blush → ivory / soft creamy yellow

window.at: first blush — about half the colour changed
window.look: Elongated sausage-shaped fruit at full length (around 3 in, 2-5 oz), still pale green overall but the green draining toward off-white over roughly half the fruit. Hard to the touch.
window.gives: A legitimate pick on this type, not a compromise — it finishes to full ivory indoors. On a determinate bush that sets its whole crop at once, picking frequently at this stage measurably raises total yield and cuts cracking, so staggering the harvest here is the right way to work the plant.

window.look: The pale green has gone to a soft ivory-to-light-creamy-yellow with no green cast left anywhere. A slight give when gently squeezed. Cut one and the interior is the same creamy white to pale yellow as the skin, very meaty with little gel.
window.gives: The target. Smooth, buttery, mildly sweet and notably low-acid — a paste tomato's density rather than a slicer's juice. This is the stage for a pale yellow sauce or a yellow ketchup, for a salsa where you want the colour contrast, or sliced into a salad. The low acidity is worth knowing if you are water-bath canning: it is the wrong tomato to can unacidified.

window.look: Colour warmed past ivory into a fuller yellow; the whole fruit gives under light pressure.
window.gives: Sweetest and easiest to cook down, but the meaty, low-water texture that is the entire reason to grow a paste tomato has started to go. Use it the day you pick it, and use it in a pot rather than on a board.

bananacreme.ripe_vs_unripe: Pale IS the ripe state here, so the instinct — 'it hasn't coloured up yet' — is exactly backwards. What you are watching for is not the arrival of a colour but the DEPARTURE of the green. Unripe: a cool, slightly grey-green, hard, and matte. Ripe: a warm ivory to light creamy yellow with the green completely gone, skin come up glossy instead of dull. Read it at the shoulder and at the blossom end, where the last green hangs on longest — if there is still a green cast up by the stem, it is not there yet. Confirm by feel: a slight give when gently squeezed. And calibrate once by cutting one open — a ripe one is creamy white to pale yellow all the way through and very meaty, so if you find bright green gel inside you picked early and can adjust. Note that the half-changed stage, when a definite cream cast has taken over about half the fruit, is a real and recommended pick point on this type, not a mistake: it finishes ripening indoors.
bananacreme.source: Botanical Interests — Cream Sausage Bush Tomato Seeds
bananacreme.caveat: 'Banana Creme' is the same Tom Wagner variety sold as Cream Sausage and as Banana Cream — Tradewinds Fruit and Grow Your Health Gardening both list the names as synonyms for one line. The ripeness detail above comes from Botanical Interests' Cream Sausage page rather than from a page headed 'Banana Creme', so the colour endpoint should be right and the fine detail is close but not cultivar-verified. Two live disagreements: HABIT — determinate bush (Botanical Interests, Tradewinds) versus semi-determinate (Grow Your Health Gardening), which decides whether the crop arrives in one flush or trickles; and DAYS — 75-80 versus 80. Also worth knowing: Grow Your Health Gardening describes the ripe interior as creamy white and pale yellow, which is what makes the cut-one-open calibration above safe to rely on.

deltonet.window_label: under-ripe by the truss → even peachy-pink (a keeper)

window.at: just under-ripe — cut the whole truss
window.look: Golfball-sized fruit with a pointed blossom end, carried in big broad multiflora trusses. Colour just short of finished — a peach cast rather than a settled pink. Flesh already firm and dense.
window.gives: This is the INTENDED harvest for a hanging long-keeper, not an early pick. Cut the truss whole, slightly under-ripe, and hang it: the fruit keep three months or more without much effort and finish slowly in storage. Picking singly at full ripe forfeits the entire point of the variety.

window.look: An even peachy-pink over the whole fruit, with a deep red interior the skin colour does not predict. Firm, almost crisp, low-juice flesh that barely softens the way an ordinary tomato does.
window.gives: The fresh-eating stage — high acid, bright, genuinely good flavour, and firm enough to hold a diced shape in a salad or to grate onto pa amb tomàquet without turning to slurry. Crack-resistant, so it will sit on the vine without splitting. The cost is that anything you eat now is not in the winter store.

window.at: in storage, weeks to months on
window.look: Same peachy-pink, still firm and thick-fleshed, no collapse. Some fruit in this class deepen from peach toward red over storage, as though blushing.
window.gives: A real tomato on the table in midwinter. The firm, thick, low-water flesh is exactly what buys the keeping, so accept dense-and-crisp rather than juicy — this is a sauce, soup and grating tomato out of season, not a beefsteak substitute. Three-plus months is routine and longer is likely in good conditions.

deltonet.ripe_vs_unripe: Two things make this one hard to read, and neither is obvious. FIRST: the ripe skin is a peachy-PINK, not red, while the interior is a contrasting deep red — so the outside always looks less ripe than the fruit actually is. Cut one open the first time to calibrate your eye; the gap between skin and flesh colour is the single most useful thing you can learn about this variety. SECOND: it is a long-keeper bred for firm, thick, low-water flesh, so it does NOT go soft when it ripens the way a slicer does. The thumb test that works on everything else in the garden barely registers here, and a fruit that feels firm is not therefore unripe. Go by colour evenness over the whole fruit, and judge the TRUSS as a unit rather than fruit by fruit. And note the deliberate inversion: for storage you actively WANT it slightly under-ripe at harvest. On this variety, 'not quite there' is the correct picking state.
deltonet.caveat: The sources disagree on the ripe colour, and it matters. Uprising Seeds, who trialled it in 2025 and describe it in most detail, call the fruit peachy-pink with a contrasting deep red interior. Meraki Seeds simply list it as red. Both agree on everything else — Catalan 'tomate de colgar' hanging long-keeper from Preixens, small round fruit with a pointed end, firm flesh, high acid, crack-resistant, indeterminate, 70-75 days. If your fruit finish red rather than peach you are almost certainly still on-type; either way, treat the peach-or-just-under stage as the storage-harvest signal. No extension or university source covers this variety, and no source describes an over-ripe state — which is consistent with a tomato bred not to have one on any normal timescale, but it does mean the late end of this window is unmapped.

margaretcurtain.window_label: first dark blush → dusky black-red body, permanent green shoulders

window.look: Large beefsteak at full size (6-12 oz and up), still green but with the first dark wash coming up low on the fruit. Shoulders green — and staying that way.
window.gives: Picks and finishes indoors like any large heirloom. The sensible stage to take a heavy fruit off a big indeterminate vine before its own weight splits it or pulls the truss down.

window.look: The body darkening off green, through brick, toward the deep dark finish. Shoulders unchanged green. Still firm enough to handle without bruising.
window.gives: Firm enough to slice cleanly and to carry — this is the stage that gives you the sturdy slices the variety is known for, rather than a fruit that slumps on the board.

window.look: Body a deep dark 'black tomato' colour over deep brick-coloured flesh, shoulders still clearly green. Gives under a gentle thumb at the base.
window.gives: The full payoff, and it is a flavour payoff rather than a keeping one: the collection that holds the line calls it absolutely delicious, low-acid and more sweet than acidic — noticeably rounder and less sharp than a Black Krim of the same darkness. Dark-fleshed tomatoes also scored high in Mark Christensen's nutritional trials, which is part of why this one was kept. Slice it fresh; don't cook it.

margaretcurtain.ripe_vs_unripe: Same problem as Black Krim, and Kōanga — the New Zealand collection that holds the line — says it outright: it looks very like Black Krim but bigger if anything, with a green shoulder. The green shoulder is PERMANENT. It is a variety trait, not a ripeness signal, and if you wait for it to clear you will be late every time. Read the BODY and the base of the fruit: unripe is uniform hard green all over; ripe is the dark black-tomato colouring over deep brick-red flesh, with green confined to a ring around the stem. Because dark skin makes colour genuinely hard to judge in garden light, confirm with a gentle thumb at the base — slight give, no collapse — rather than trying to decide from ten feet away whether the top half looks green.
margaretcurtain.caveat: Thinly catalogued, and I want to be clear about which parts are the variety and which are read across. CULTIVAR-SPECIFIC and reliable: the green shoulders, the dark 'black tomato' body, the Black Krim resemblance, large beefsteak, indeterminate, regular leaf, mid-season, New Zealand heirloom from Southland reportedly grown over 100 years, held in Kōanga's Henry's collection (Kōanga); deep brick-coloured flesh, sweeter than acidic, sturdy slices (Secret Seed Cartel). DERIVED: neither source describes its breaker appearance or its over-ripe behaviour, so the first two points of the window above use the general dark-beefsteak colour-break sequence rather than anything observed on this variety. No days-to-maturity figure exists in either source — 'mid season' is all you get. Calibrate on your own first fruit, and if it behaves like a big Black Krim you are probably reading it right.

dester.window_label: first pink blush → even deep pink, smooth shoulders

window.look: Big oblate beefsteak, anywhere from 6 oz to a full 2 lb, with smooth shoulders and no ribbing or catfacing. Still green but the first pink showing at the blossom end.
window.gives: The stage to take a 1-2 lb fruit off before its own weight or a rain event splits it. It finishes in a paper bag in a cool dark place with little loss — and on a variety this late (80-92 days depending who you ask), being able to bring the tail of the crop indoors at breaker is what makes it worth growing in a short season at all.

window.look: Pink over a third to two-thirds of the fruit, sweetening and softening but still firm in the hand.
window.gives: Firm enough that the slices hold their shape — with this variety's very meaty flesh and unusually small seed locules that is the whole selling point, so this is the sandwich and burger pick. A slice cut here covers a bun and does not weep through the bread.

window.look: An even deep pink across the whole oblate fruit, shoulders smooth and fully coloured, clear give under a thumb, heavy for its size.
window.gives: Peak flavour, and by consensus a very high ceiling: excellent, intense and balanced, sweet without being flat. It finished in the top two of Seed Savers Exchange's tasting trials — memorable enough that visitors voted for it forty-odd samples later — and sits in Craig LeHoullier's top ten. This is a slicing tomato at its best; there is no reason to cook it.

dester.source: Thresh Seed Co. — Dester Pink Heirloom Slicing Tomato
dester.caveat: Ripe colour is a deep PINK, not red — don't wait for red on this one either, though it is far less ambiguous than the dark and green varieties in this group, which is why the ripe-vs-unripe field is left empty. Flavour ranking, the Seed Savers tasting-trial result and the origin story (brought from Germany by Dr Herbert Edgar Dester's family, passed to their Amish housekeeper Anna in Missouri, donated to SSE by farmer Larry Pierce) come from Craig LeHoullier's A Way To Garden interview and Thresh Seed Co.; harvest and off-vine ripening guidance from Thresh, who also warn against refrigerating it — it goes mealy. Neither source describes Dester's own breaker appearance, so the first two points use the general large-pink-beefsteak colour-break sequence. Days to maturity is reported anywhere from 80 to 92: treat it as a late variety and plan to finish the last fruit indoors.

czechsbush.window_label: breaker (first pink at the blossom end) → full red

window.look: Medium round fruit at full 4-6 oz size on a stocky 30-36 in bush with rugose foliage. Under about a tenth of the surface showing the first pink break at the blossom end. Still hard.
window.gives: Physiologically mature and will finish off the vine. Genuinely useful on a determinate that ripens a whole flush at once — staggering the picking spreads the crop over more days and takes weight off a heavily-laden dwarf that is already leaning enough to want a stake.

window.look: Roughly 10-60% coloured. Sweetening and beginning to soften, but still firm in the hand.
window.gives: Firm enough to sit in a bowl for a few days, and already past the point where a bird peck or a split costs you the fruit. Good sliced at this stage, and the extra firmness helps if you are dicing.

window.look: 90-100% an even red, glossy rather than dull, sitting between firm and soft under a gentle squeeze, and it snaps off the vine with a twist instead of dragging the truss.
window.gives: Best flavour and the stage to cook from — this is a heavy-yielding early dwarf sold for slicing and for sauce, and full ripe is where the sugar and acid actually are. Don't leave it past here: red-stage fruit left on the plant splits and draws insects and birds, and on a determinate the whole flush arrives together, so a few days of hesitation costs a lot of fruit at once.

czechsbush.source: Tim's Tomatoes — Czech Bush Tomato Seeds (Heirloom)
czechsbush.caveat: Czech's Bush ripens plain red, so ripeness is not ambiguous here — but nothing I could read describes ITS ripening specifically, so the window and the per-stage payoffs above are the standard red-tomato breaker-turning-red sequence (Tomato Dirt's stage percentages and firmness, Penn State Extension on breaker and ethylene, Tomato Dirt on the twist-off test), applied to a fruit of this size and habit. The cultivar facts are sourced: dwarf-determinate topping out at 30-36 in, round red 4-6 oz fruit, heavy early yields, stocky plants with rugose foliage that may still want a small stake, sent to Ben Quisenberry in 1976 by Milan Sodomka from Czechoslovakia with the original Czech name lost along the way (Tim's Tomatoes, Mary's Heirloom Seeds, Tatiana's TOMATOBase via search). Days to maturity is reported 70-75 (Tim's) or 85 (Mary's) — a wide spread for something sold as early; assume the shorter figure is from transplant. Being determinate, expect the crop inside a couple of weeks rather than as a long trickle.

window.look: The signal is at the STEM, not the colour. Netting is raised and well rounded over the whole fruit (except the vein tracts), and the rind has just broken from deep uniform green to tan-yellow between the netting. A crack has opened partway around the stem scar; a light tug releases about half to three-quarters of the stem and the rest tears rather than letting go. Musk smell faint or absent.
window.gives: The keeper of the harvestable stages: firmest flesh, much less bruising and decay in handling, and it does finish ripening off the vine. What it does not do is finish sweetening. UGA: cantaloupes ripen after harvest but do not increase in sugar content, and almost half the final sugar concentration is laid down in the few days right before three-quarter-to-full slip. Illinois is blunter — a picked muskmelon softens but never sweetens further. Whatever sugar is missing at half slip is missing for good.

window.look: Rind fully tan-yellow between the net. The whole stem lifts off cleanly with a slight tug, leaving a smooth round scar — that is the abscission layer fully formed. Sweet musk aroma at the stem end, rind slightly softer under the thumb.
window.gives: Peak sugar and full musk aroma: sugars are stored right up to the moment the stem separates (Illinois), so this is the sweetest the fruit is capable of being. The cost is shelf life — cantaloupe is climacteric and ripens very fast after harvest with a very short life (UMD). Eat or process within a couple of days; this is not the one to pick before a trip.

window.look: Fruit is lying loose off the vine on its own, aroma heavy, rind soft to the thumb and showing brown undertones or browning along the vein tracts.
window.gives: Loudest aroma but the texture is going — UGA reads brown undertones and vein browning as aging and internal softness, and UMD warns that a melon taken at full self-detachment may already be overripe. Same-day use: cut fresh, blended, or frozen. It will not survive a few days in the fridge intact.

cantaloupe.ripe_vs_unripe: For a melon the pick signal is largely NOT colour, and this is where people lose fruit. Full size and full netting arrive early; sugar arrives last, so a big, beautifully netted melon can still be days short. Two things actually discriminate. (1) Under the netting: unripe rind is a flat, uniform deep green between the net; ripe has warmed to tan-yellow. (2) The stem, not the fruit: ripe shows a crack opening around the stem scar and gives the stem up to a light tug; unripe holds it tight so you have to cut or tear it. A muskmelon cut off a firm green stem is finished — it will soften on the counter and read 'ripe' to the thumb while never gaining a point of sugar.
cantaloupe.source: University of Georgia Extension CAES Field Report B1179 — Cantaloupe and Specialty Melons; corroborated by Illinois Extension — Muskmelon and University of Maryland Extension — Ripening Behaviors and Harvest Indexes

charentais.window_label: green rind → grey colour break with slip and aroma → soft-ended and over

window.look: Smooth rind with clear sutures, just lifting off green toward grey-buff with the sutures staying darker grey; netting on the sutures becoming pronounced. Ends still firm, stem tight, almost no smell. Full size is only about 2 lb — small is not the same as unripe here.
window.gives: The only stage you can pick and still keep it a couple of days. Orange flesh, sweet enough, but the perfume — the entire reason to grow a Charentais — is only part built, and no melon builds sugar or aroma after cutting.

window.look: Rind grey with dark grey sutures over the whole fruit, a crack around the stem scar, the tendril nearest the fruit dried, both ends softening to the thumb, and a strong sweet aroma you can smell standing over the plant. A gentle tug slips it off the vine — Charentais is a slipping type (UGA).
window.gives: Peak: full sugar and the intoxicating aromatic stage this type is famous for. It is also essentially the whole window — Charentais colour-breaks, perfumes and softens in quick succession, so plan to eat it within a day or two, not to store it. Check the patch daily once the first fruit greys.

window.look: Already separated from the vine and lying on the soil, ends distinctly soft, aroma very heavy, rind dulling.
window.gives: UMD's warning stage: cantaloupe-group melons left to full self-detachment are often already past it — flesh watery and soft rather than melting. Same-day eating, chilled soup or sorbet only.

charentais.ripe_vs_unripe: A ripe Charentais looks wrong to eyes trained on an orange netted cantaloupe, and that is how it gets left on the vine until it is over. It stays small (about 2 lb at full size) and it never goes orange on the outside — the ripe rind is grey to grey-buff with darker grey sutures, so the shift you are reading is green → grey, not green → tan/orange. Because the colour change is subtle, use the other three together: aroma strong at the stem end, both ends giving to thumb pressure, and the stem cracking and slipping under a gentle tug. Unripe: flat green rind, tight stem, no smell, firm ends. Nose first on this one — it is the most reliable cue and it goes over fast.
charentais.source: Pinetree Garden Seeds — True Charentais Melon (Heirloom, 80 Days); slip behaviour and rind type corroborated by UGA CAES Field Report B1179

greenflesh.window_label: rind breaking off green → creamy white with fuzz gone and blossom end giving (cut, never tug)

window.at: colour break — rind turning off green
window.look: The fine pubescence — hairs you feel rather than see — is still present in patches, and the rind is moving off green toward greenish-white. The stem is still firmly attached, and that tells you nothing: a honeydew-type melon never forms a slip layer (UGA, UMD), so waiting for it to loosen means waiting forever.
window.gives: The long keeper. UGA puts honeydew types in the inodorous group, which holds at room temperature for a month or more — an early-cut one is your storage melon. The tradeoff is sugar: UMD classes honeydew as non-climacteric and states it will not continue to ripen or increase in sweetness after being detached, so an under-mature cut is permanently under-sweet.

window.at: full maturity — creamy white rind, fuzz gone, blossom end just giving
window.look: Rind completely creamy white to pale yellow, with a faint waxy slickness where the fuzz has gone — UGA's actual test is that the pubescence is no longer detectable. The blossom end gives slightly to thumb pressure. Illinois: cut it off the vine once it has turned completely, because the stem will not separate on its own.
window.gives: Peak sweetness and the best texture, plus this type still stores unusually well for a ripe melon. Illinois reports honeydews continue improving at room temperature for several days after cutting, with complete ripeness marked by the blossom end being slightly soft to pressure — so a just-cut one can be finished on the counter.

greenflesh.ripe_vs_unripe: This is the hardest melon in the garden to read, because a pale ivory fruit looks under-ripe to the last day and there is no slip to tell you. Discriminators the eye can actually use: TONE, not colour — unripe is a cool greenish-white (green undertone, matte); ripe has drifted warm to creamy white or pale yellow with no green left in it. TEXTURE — run a palm over it: an immature honeydew still has fine fuzz you can feel, and a mature one is bare and slightly waxy-slick. FEEL — press the blossom end (opposite the stem): unripe is rock firm, ripe gives slightly and springs back. What is NOT a signal: the stem. It stays tight at full ripeness, so a firm stem is not evidence of an unripe melon, and tugging one only tears the vine. Cut it.
greenflesh.source: Illinois Extension — Muskmelon (honeydew and Crenshaw harvest guidance) and UGA CAES Field Report B1179 — Cantaloupe and Specialty Melons (inodorous group, pubescence test, no slip)
greenflesh.caveat: No cultivar-specific source: the Victory Seeds page for 'Green Flesh' honeydew failed to load this run, so the window is derived from honeydew-type extension guidance. Two sources also disagree on one point worth knowing at the plant — Illinois says a cut honeydew keeps improving on the counter for several days, while UMD classes the type as non-climacteric and says it will not sweeten after cutting. They agree completely on the mechanics: it never slips, so cut the stem, and read rind tone plus lost fuzz plus blossom-end give.

window.look: Netting raised and finished over the fruit, rind just breaking from uniform green to tan-yellow between the net, and a crack starting around the stem scar — a light tug takes part of the stem and tears the rest. On a small-fruited melon the size cue is worthless: it reaches full size well before it reaches sugar.
window.gives: Firmer flesh and a couple of days of shelf life on a type that otherwise has almost none. But UGA's number applies: nearly half the final sugar is banked in the few days just before slip, and Illinois notes a picked muskmelon softens without sweetening — so an early pick on a small melon gives up a large share of the sugar in a fruit that was only ever going to hold a little.

window.look: Rind tan-yellow between the netting, sweet musk aroma at the stem end, and the entire stem lifting off cleanly with a slight tug, leaving a round scar.
window.gives: Full sugar and full aroma — the reason to grow a short-season melon at all. Being climacteric and small, it goes from perfect to soft in days, so this is an eat-now pick. Check the patch daily once the first fruit shows colour under the net (Illinois).

minnesotamini.ripe_vs_unripe: Do not read a small melon's size as immaturity, and do not read full netting as ripeness — both finish early. The real discriminators are the same as any netted muskmelon: rind between the netting shifting from flat uniform green to tan-yellow, a crack opening at the stem scar, the stem releasing to a light tug, and musk aroma at the stem end. Unripe: green between the net, tight stem, no smell. If you have to cut the stem, you picked early, and it will soften on the counter while staying under-sweet.
minnesotamini.source: Illinois Extension — Muskmelon; corroborated by UGA CAES Field Report B1179 — Cantaloupe and Specialty Melons
minnesotamini.caveat: No source for 'Minnesota Mini' itself loaded this run, so the window is derived from netted-muskmelon (cantaloupe-type) extension guidance. This cultivar is also sold as 'Minnesota Midget' — check the packet confirms a netted muskmelon rather than a honeydew/winter type, because the two have opposite harvest rules: muskmelons slip and must be tugged, honeydews never slip and must be cut.

crimsonsweet.window_label: ground spot greenish-white and rind glossy → ground spot creamy yellow, tendril brown, rind dull

window.at: signals partial — one or two of three
window.look: Ground spot moving off greenish-white toward pale cream, rind still fairly glossy and reflective, tendril at the fruit's stem drying but not yet brown and dead. Fruit may already be at full 15–25 lb size — size is not one of the signals.
window.gives: Buys a few days of extra firmness and handling life, and that is the entire benefit. Watermelon is non-climacteric: UMD states that once harvested they will not ripen any further, and sugar does not increase after harvest. NC State's floor for acceptable eating is 10 Brix, and a melon cut short of ripe will never reach it in the kitchen. This is the point of no return in the garden — a Crimson Sweet taken a week early is a wasted 20 lb fruit.

window.look: Ground spot fully creamy yellow through orange-yellow (Johnny's), the rind shifted from shiny to dull so it no longer mirrors the sky (NC State), the tendril nearest the fruit brown and dry, and the thump gone from a bright high pitch to a dull hollow one.
window.gives: Crisp, fine-grained, sweet flesh at full sugar — and because the type is non-climacteric, this is exactly as sweet as it will ever be, so there is nothing to gain by waiting and nothing to gain by resting it on the counter. Cut it with a stub of stem left on and get it out of the sun.

crimsonsweet.ripe_vs_unripe: You cannot see the flesh, so every cue is indirect and the misread costs a whole fruit. The trap is the ground spot: EVERY watermelon has one from the moment it starts sizing, because that side never saw sun — a pale patch is not ripeness. The COLOUR SHIFT in it is the signal: greenish-white or chalk white = not yet; creamy, buttery yellow to orange-yellow = ripe. Size is the second trap: Crimson Sweet hits 15–25 lb well before it hits sugar. And unlike a cantaloupe there is no slip — the stem stays firmly attached at full ripeness, so a tight stem is not evidence of anything. Read all three real signals together (ground-spot colour shift, brown dried tendril at the fruit, glossy rind gone dull) because any one alone will lie, and remember there is no recovery: cut it a week early and it stays a week early.
crimsonsweet.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Crimson Sweet Watermelon; ripening behaviour from University of Maryland Extension — Ripening Behaviors and Harvest Indexes; gloss and Brix from NC State Cucurbit Breeding — Choosing a Ripe Watermelon (for field harvest)

sugarbaby.window_label: stripes still distinct and rind glossy → stripes darkened to near-solid dark green, rind dull and hard

window.at: striping still readable, ground spot just turning
window.look: You can still make out light-against-dark striping, the rind is still glossy and just soft enough to indent with a fingernail, the spot on the bottom is going from white toward pale yellow, and the tendril at the stem is starting to shrivel.
window.gives: A firmer melon with the storage edge Sow True Seed credits Sugar Baby for — genuinely useful in an icebox type you may want to hold. The cost is unrecoverable sugar: sugar does not rise after harvest in watermelon (UMD), so an early 8 lb Sugar Baby is simply a less sweet 8 lb Sugar Baby forever.

window.look: This one really does have a colour progression: the stripes darken and merge toward near-solid dark green, and the surface turns dull. The rind also strengthens — it resists a fingernail where it used to dent. Bottom spot bright yellow, tendril at the stem shrivelled, thump hollow.
window.gives: Full, extra-sweet red-orange flesh in a thin-rinded 6–10 lb melon: the best flesh-to-rind ratio of the watermelons here and the only one that fits a fridge shelf whole. Still the type's best keeper, so ripe-and-held is a workable state rather than an emergency.

sugarbaby.ripe_vs_unripe: Sugar Baby's ripe colour is the counter-intuitive one: it gets DARKER and duller, not brighter. Unripe reads as clear light/dark striping on a glossy rind that dents under a fingernail. Ripe reads as stripes swallowed into a near-solid dark green, the shine gone flat, and a rind that pushes back against a fingernail. So the two mistakes are opposite in shape — reading crisp stripes as 'good markings' when they mean not yet, and reading a dark dull melon as sunburnt or old when that is exactly the pick point. Confirm with the bottom spot (white = no, bright yellow = yes) and the shrivelled tendril, and remember it never slips: the stem stays tight at ripeness. Icebox melons are also the size class NC State flags as often failing to show the standard field signals clearly, so cut the first one to calibrate your eye for the rest of the patch.
sugarbaby.source: Sow True Seed — Sugar Baby Watermelon; ripening behaviour from University of Maryland Extension — Ripening Behaviors and Harvest Indexes; mini-melon caution from NC State Cucurbit Breeding

tendersweetorange.window_label: belly spot pale and rind glossy → belly spot yellow, tendril brown, thump dull → held ripe on the vine

window.look: Belly spot lifting off pale green-white toward cream, rind still glossy, tendril near the fruit drying but not brown through. At 35–40 lb the fruit looks emphatically finished long before it is — size is not a cue on a large oblong melon.
window.gives: Only firmness for handling a very heavy melon. Holmes states plainly that sugar levels do not increase post-harvest and sets a 10% sugar minimum for good eating, so an early cut on a 35 lb fruit is the single most expensive mistake available in this patch.

window.at: ripe — yellow belly spot, brown tendril, dull hollow thump
window.look: Belly spot clearly yellow, the tendrils nearest the fruit brown, the rind gone from shiny to dull, and a hollow, soft, low sound on the thump instead of a bright ring.
window.gives: Deep orange flesh at its crisp, sweet, high-sugar best — this is the peak and, being non-climacteric, the ceiling. Thin-to-tough dark green striped rind over an enormous amount of usable flesh.

window.look: Belly spot deepening past yellow, rind fully dull and dead-looking, tendril dry and brittle, fruit still firm and sound.
window.gives: Holmes rates Tendersweet Orange as holding well on the vine, so a ripe one is not an emergency — genuinely useful when a 35–40 lb melon is more than you can deal with today. Nothing further is gained in sugar, so this is a scheduling stage, not a flavour stage.

tendersweetorange.ripe_vs_unripe: The trap here is flesh colour, and it is worth being explicit: the flesh of this cultivar is supposed to be deep orange. Orange flesh means you grew Tendersweet Orange, NOT that the melon is overripe — and you will never see the deep red that UMD gives as the ripeness marker for watermelon generally, nor should you wait for it. UMD's other half of that rule (pink or white flesh means immature) still applies in spirit, but on an orange-fleshed cultivar the whole flesh-colour test is void, so do not use it. Judge from the outside only: pale green-white belly spot = not yet; yellow belly spot plus brown tendril plus dull rind plus a low hollow thump = ripe, no matter how big or how long the melon has been sitting there. And there is no second chance — watermelon does not ripen or sweeten after cutting, so a 35 lb fruit cut a week early is 35 lb of bland.
tendersweetorange.source: Holmes Seed Company — Tendersweet Orange Watermelon; flesh-colour and ripening-behaviour rule from University of Maryland Extension — Ripening Behaviors and Harvest Indexes

darkgreenzucchini.window_label: baby (4-6 in) → full-size tender (6-8 in), closing hard as seeds set

window.look: 4-6 in and slim, skin very dark glossy green, blossom scar often still soft, fruit bends nothing and cuts with no resistance
window.gives: the tenderest eating of the whole range — dense flesh, no perceptible seed, skin thin enough to eat whole; grill, saute or eat raw. Costs you weight per fruit, but cutting at this size is also what keeps the plant setting new fruit

window.look: 6-8 in long, 1-2 in across, still uniformly glossy dark green, thumbnail dents the skin easily, stem cuts cleanly
window.gives: the best yield-to-quality trade: firm flesh, seeds still soft and invisible in the slice, skin tender. Standard stage for rounds, planks and bread. Fruit reaches this in only a few days from flower, so this point lasts days, not weeks

window.look: over ~10 in and thickening, skin dulls and stops denting under a thumbnail, cut face shows a pale seed cavity with distinct white seeds
window.gives: a real cost, not just a bigger squash: seeds have hardened, the skin has toughened past eating, and the flesh has gone fibrous or watery so it collapses when cooked. Worse, leaving big fruit on the vine pulls the plant's energy into seed and plant yield declines — remove oversized fruit even if you will not eat it

darkgreenzucchini.source: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing summer squash and zucchini in home gardens
darkgreenzucchini.caveat: No cultivar-specific source found; window derived from Extension guidance for dark-green zucchini-type summer squash, which Dark Green Zucchini is the standard example of. The 6-8 in prime range and the seed/skin/watery-flesh failure mode are the sourced parts.

zephyr.window_label: young 4-6 in bicolour → over-size (green tip is the cultivar, not unripeness)

window.look: slender fruit 4-6 in, yellow over the stem two-thirds with faint white striping, and a distinctly light-green blossom end; skin glossy and dents under a thumbnail
window.gives: the stage the variety was bred for — unusually nutty flavour and a firm, non-watery texture that holds up sliced and grilled. Picking here 2-3 times a week is what keeps the plant in production

window.look: past 6 in and filling out; the yellow deepens, the green blossom end may cover more or less of the fruit depending on heat stress
window.gives: more weight per fruit but the firm nutty character that distinguishes Zephyr from a plain yellow squash starts to dilute toward ordinary summer-squash blandness

window.look: thick through the middle, skin gone dull and no longer dentable, seed outlines visible in a cut face
window.gives: the cost: hardened seeds, toughened skin, and fibrous or watery flesh. Oversized fruit left on the vine also drops the plant's further yield, so cut and discard rather than leave

zephyr.ripe_vs_unripe: The green blossom end is the cultivar, NOT unripeness. Zephyr is bicolour by design — yellow with faint white stripes at the stem end and a light-green tip. Do not wait for it to turn fully yellow; it never will, and waiting only pushes the fruit into hard seeds and tough skin. Heat stress makes the amount of green vary fruit to fruit, and the first one or two fruits of the season can come out green-striped overall — both are normal and not a ripeness signal. Judge Zephyr by size (4-6 in) and gloss, never by how much green is on the tip.
zephyr.source: Johnny's Selected Seeds (breeder) — Zephyr (F1) Yellow Summer Squash Seed

clemsonspineless80.window_label: 2 in → 3-4 in tender pod (closes within about two days)

window.look: ridged, angular, medium-to-dark green spineless pod about 2 in long, the whole pod bends slightly and the tip is soft
window.gives: the most tender pod of the range — no fibre anywhere, good whole for roasting, grilling or pickling. Small pods weigh little, so this stage costs yield

window.look: 3-4 in, dark green, still glossy and unpuckered; a pod at this stage snaps off cleanly and the tip breaks with an audible snap rather than bending or resisting a thumbnail
window.gives: the best size-to-tenderness trade for slicing, gumbo and freezing. Pods can pass through this in a day or two, so on a healthy plant the field test matters more than the ruler: if it snaps, it is still good

window.look: 5 in and up, ribs hardening and often paling or drying at the tip; the pod refuses to snap — it bends, or a thumbnail will not press in
window.gives: the cost is unrecoverable: fibre has set through the pod walls so it stays tough and woody however long you cook it, and the seeds inside have gone hard. It also costs the rest of the season — pods allowed to mature on the plant slow further pod production, so cut them off and discard even if you will not eat them

clemsonspineless80.source: UGA Cooperative Extension C941 — Home Garden Okra (with Clemson HGIC — How to Grow Okra in South Carolina)
clemsonspineless80.caveat: The sourced rule is pods at 2-3 in (up to about 4 in on vigorous plants), harvested every few days, with larger pods going tough and fibrous and maturing pods slowing production. The snap / thumbnail test in the look field is the standard field expression of that tenderness rule rather than a direct quote from the cited pages.

pingtunglong.window_label: glossy and springy (any usable length) → dull skin and lasting dent

window.look: long thin fruit, deep glossy purple, hard and unyielding to a thumb — flesh does not press in at all
window.gives: too young rather than too early: a hard fruit that gives nothing under the thumb has not filled, so you get little flesh for the cut. Firmness with no give is the immature signal, not the ripe one

window.at: prime — glossy and springy (the pick point)
window.look: skin bright, mirror-glossy and evenly coloured; hold the fruit in your palm and press with your thumb — the flesh presses in and springs back. Full length for a long Asian type (roughly 10-18 in) but size alone is not the test
window.gives: the whole reason to grow this type: creamy flesh with no bitterness, seeds still soft and unnoticeable, thin skin that needs no peeling and holds together when grilled or stir-fried. Cut with the cap and a bit of stem attached; do not twist it off

window.look: skin has gone dull, matte or bronze/brown-cast rather than shining; the thumb dent stays put instead of springing back
window.gives: the cost, and it is a hard stop: the interior can be browning through, the seeds have gone large and tough, and the flesh turns spongy and bitter — Extension's advice is to cut these off and discard them rather than try to cook them. Leaving them on also gives the plant no reason to set more fruit

pingtunglong.source: University of Illinois Extension — Eggplant (Home Vegetable Gardening)
pingtunglong.caveat: No cultivar-specific source found; window derived from University of Illinois Extension general eggplant guidance — the gloss test, the thumb-press spring-back test and the over-mature description are all sourced, but the length range for Ping Tung Long specifically is not, so judge by gloss and thumb press rather than by inches.

bittermelon.window_label: firm shiny green → light green → first yellow tinge (culinary window closes here) → orange, then split

window.look: firm, shiny, warty-ridged fruit in solid green with no yellow anywhere; the fruit feels hard in the hand and the ridges are sharply defined
window.gives: the stage the fruit is grown for — dense crisp flesh that holds its shape sliced and stir-fried, seeds still soft and white, and the clean assertive bitterness that carries the dish rather than overwhelming it

window.look: still firm and unsplit but the ground colour has lightened toward pale green, warts a little rounder
window.gives: a milder plate than solid green — this is the point to pick if you want the vegetable to read as bitter-but-approachable rather than sharp. Still fully usable; the sourced boundary is the first yellow, not this

window.look: a blush of yellow at the blossom end or along a ridge, the fruit beginning to lose its hardness under a squeeze
window.gives: the cost begins here: the flesh softens and the seeds start to firm up, so it no longer holds a slice. Extension guidance is to harvest before any yellow or orange shows, so treat the first yellow as the close of the cooking window

window.look: skin gone orange and soft, and finally the fruit splits open at the base to reveal light brown seeds wrapped in bright red pulp
window.gives: no longer a cooking vegetable — the flesh has gone soft and the seeds hard. The red seed coating is the only part worth taking at this stage, and only as a curiosity or for seed saving. Ripening fruit left on the vine also stops the plant setting more, so harvest often to keep it producing

bittermelon.ripe_vs_unripe: Bitter melon is eaten unripe on purpose, so "ripe" is the failure state, not the target. There is no colour break to wait for — the pick signal is solid green with zero yellow, plus firmness: the fruit should feel hard in the hand, with sharply defined ridges and a shiny rather than matte surface. Any yellow blush, any softening under a squeeze, or a fruit that has begun to look inflated means you are past the cooking window. Splitting at the base with red pulp showing is fully ripe and fully past use.
bittermelon.source: UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County (UC ANR) — Bitter Melon
bittermelon.caveat: Species-level Extension guidance, not cultivar-specific, and the cited page documents the colour and texture progression (firm shiny green at harvest, softening and orange with ripeness, splitting to red seed pulp) but does NOT document how the bitterness itself changes stage to stage — the green-vs-pale-green flavour difference in this entry is the widely-reported pattern, not a sourced claim, so trust your own palate over it.

cucamelon.window_label: grape-size and firm (only real stage) → soft and seedy

window.look: about 1 in, oval, marked like a miniature watermelon in pale green over darker green; firm when gently squeezed, and it detaches with a light pull
window.gives: everything the fruit is for — crisp snap, tender white interior, cucumber flavour with a lime-like tang, no seed texture at all. Eaten whole, raw or pickled

window.look: over about 1 in and rounding out, noticeably soft to a squeeze rather than firm; fully mature fruit eventually drops off the vine on its own
window.gives: the cost: the seeds inside fill out and the fruit loses its firmness, so the crisp snap that is the whole point goes flabby and the interior turns seedy and sourer. Fruit at this stage is worth keeping only for seed saving. Fruits go from perfect to past in a day or two, and they hide under the foliage, so check daily once they start

cucamelon.source: Gardener's Path — How to Plant and Grow Cucamelons (Mexican Sour Gherkins)
cucamelon.caveat: No university extension source found for this crop; window taken from a horticultural gardening publication rather than Extension or a breeder. The firm/grape-size pick point and the softening-and-seed-fill failure mode are what that page documents; the 1 in figure is corroborated by seed catalogues but not by an Extension page.

suyolong.window_label: 8-10 in slender → 12-15 in (18 in max) → yellowing and seedy

window.look: 8-10 in, narrow, deeply ribbed, uniformly dark green, skin thin and glossy, seed cavity invisible when cut
window.gives: peak crisp texture and the mild sweet burpless flavour the variety is grown for, with essentially no seed to notice and no need to peel

window.look: 12-15 in and still slender for its length, ribs pronounced, colour still dark green all the way to the blossom end
window.gives: the most cucumber per pick while the flesh is still crisp and the seeds still soft. This variety can reach 18 in, but fruit can double in size in a couple of days, so it passes through this point fast — cut, do not pull, and pick before the seeds get large inside

window.look: skin losing its dark green and going pale then yellowish, fruit thickening and bulging rather than staying slender, cut face shows large white seeds
window.gives: the cost: seeds have gone large and hard, skin has toughened past eating unpeeled, the flesh turns pithy, and the flavour picks up the bitterness that concentrates at the blossom end — so the one trait the variety was chosen for is what you lose first. Large fruit left on the vine also drops the plant's remaining yield

suyolong.source: Urban Farmer Seeds — Suyo Long Cucumber (length, ribbing, burpless, pick-daily) + University of Minnesota Extension — Growing cucumbers (over-mature yellowing, seed size, yield decline)
suyolong.caveat: Cultivar traits and length come from seed-catalogue sources (Urban Farmer, Renee's Garden); the over-maturity failure mode (yellowing skin, large seeds, declining plant yield) is species-level guidance from U. Minnesota Extension applied to this cultivar.

pepper-jalapeno-variant.window_label: mature green → the cultivar's own final colour

window.look: the pod is fully developed for its cultivar — filled out to expected size and shape, firm and crisp when squeezed, glossy rather than matte, evenly coloured, and it detaches easily from the plant. Under good conditions a mature green pod is ready roughly 45-55 days after that flower was pollinated
window.gives: the firmest walls and crispest texture of the whole window, a clean vegetal flavour, and the longest handling life — the stage for pickling, stuffing and anything that needs the flesh to hold its shape. Picking here also keeps the plant setting new flowers rather than pouring resources into finishing pods

window.look: the green ground dulling and lightening while the cultivar's ripe colour appears first on shoulders or tip; some cultivars pass through a dark, near-black or intermediate shade on the way
window.gives: an intermediate pick with some green firmness retained and ripe flavour beginning — and often the sharpest heat, since pungency in hot types tends to run high as the pod starts turning and can ease once fully ripe

window.look: the pod evenly carries the cultivar's finished colour with no green ground left, skin glossy, and the wall gives under thumb pressure instead of snapping crisp
window.gives: maximum sweetness and the fullest, roundest flavour, and the only stage worth drying, smoking or ristra-hanging — ripe pods can be dried on the plant or hung by their stems. Costs one to three extra weeks of plant time, a softer wall, and shorter fresh-keeping

pepper-jalapeno-variant.ripe_vs_unripe: The crop-level trap is mistaking an undersized pod for a mature green one. Immature: pale or light green, matte, slim, walls that dent under pressure, clinging to the plant. Mature green: full cultivar size, deep even colour with a wet-looking gloss, firm and crisp when squeezed, detaching easily. The finished colour is cultivar-specific — green, yellow, orange, brown, purple and red are all legitimate final states — so never treat 'not red yet' as evidence a pepper is unripe. On hot types, tan corking lines mark that the flesh outgrew its skin and the pod is mature; treat corking as a maturity clue, not a promise of extra heat, since pungency varies with cultivar, air temperature, irrigation and fertility.
pepper-jalapeno-variant.source: NMSU Cooperative Extension Guide H-240 — Growing Chiles in New Mexico (crop harvest mechanics and 45-55 days after pollination), with the corking-as-maturity qualifier from Know The Pepper — Harvesting Jalapenos: Green, Red and Corking Signs

pepper-illinois-variant.window_label: mature green (full size) → colour break → full mature colour → dried on the plant

window.look: pod has reached the full length and girth that variety is supposed to reach, feels firm and crisp when squeezed, skin taut and glossy, and it breaks off the plant easily when picked — that clean snap is the maturity test, not the colour
window.gives: the firmest wall and the crispest texture of the whole window, and the mildest version of a hot variety's heat; this is the stage for pickling, stuffing and anywhere you need the pod to hold its shape. A pod that is still short, soft, or clings when you pull it is genuinely immature and worth leaving

window.look: colour arriving unevenly, usually from the tip or the shoulders, with green and the mature colour on the same pod; wall still firm
window.gives: a genuine middle option: some of the ripe flavour with most of the green stage's firmness. Best when you want a pod that still grills, fries or roasts without collapsing

window.look: the pod is uniformly at its own final colour — which is variety-specific and may be red, orange, yellow, purple-to-red, brown or ivory, not necessarily red — with the hard gloss dulling and the wall softening under the thumb
window.gives: the fullest flavour of the window and, on a hot variety, the hottest stage: peppers can be picked at any colour stage but are hottest when allowed to ripen fully. The trade is texture — softer wall, poorer for stuffing and pickling

window.look: fully coloured pods left in place until the skin shrivels and the flesh loses water
window.gives: concentrated heat and flavour with no processing, and the form to store: dry them on the plant, or cut them at full colour and hang them by their stems (the ristra method) for flakes and powder

pepper-illinois-variant.ripe_vs_unripe: Colour alone never decides a pepper, because each variety has its own final colour and several finish green, orange, purple or ivory. Look up what that variety is supposed to end at, then judge readiness three ways that hold for every pepper: full size for the variety, firm and crisp when squeezed, and a pod that breaks cleanly off the plant instead of dragging the branch. An immature pod fails all three regardless of what colour it is.
pepper-illinois-variant.source: Illinois Extension (Good Growing) — How to Grow Peppers (mature size and firmness; 'they will easily break off of plants when picked'; hot peppers can be picked at any stage but are hottest fully ripe; find out what the variety is supposed to look like); NMSU Extension Guide H-240 — Growing Chile Peppers in New Mexico Gardens ('fruit should be fully developed, firm, and crisp when squeezed'; green crop harvested before colour change; mature colour may be red, yellow, orange or brown by variety; drying on the plant and ristras)

pepper-frutescens-variant.window_label: mature green → intermediate colour → final ripe colour

window.look: colour-agnostic test: the pod is fully developed for its variety - full length and width - and is firm and crisp when squeezed, with a tight glossy or waxy skin rather than a matte, soft one. A mature pod detaches easily; if you have to tug hard, it is not there yet. Note that 'mature green' is a shade specific to the variety - some types mature at a deep leaf green, frutescens types (Tabasco, Piri Piri) mature at a pale yellowish-green
window.gives: the firmest flesh, the longest keeping after picking, the sharpest and most vegetal flavour with a faint bitterness, and the lowest heat the pod will ever carry. Picking green also keeps a loaded plant setting new pods

window.look: chlorophyll breaking down and carotenoids building, usually starting at the tip or as streaks with the shoulder holding green last; gloss stays high, flesh becomes more tender
window.gives: sweeter and more complex than green as the grassy edge drops away and fruity aromatic compounds appear, with heat climbing but not yet at peak - the balance pick, and generally the best stage for raw uses where sweetness and heat have to sit together. Too moist and too pale to dry

window.look: the pod coloured uniformly to whatever colour that variety finishes at - which is not always red; flesh distinctly softer than at green and gloss slightly duller
window.gives: peak sweetness as starches convert to sugars, the roundest and most complex flavour, and the highest capsaicin - capsaicin accumulates right through ripening, so a green pick always forfeits heat. This is also the only stage worth drying or grinding: dried pods and powder take their colour and concentrated flavour from a fully ripe pod, and the traditional method is to let pods dry on the plant or pick them fully ripe and hang them by their stems in strings. Softer walls make this the worst stage for stuffing and the shortest-keeping stage fresh

pepper-frutescens-variant.ripe_vs_unripe: Peppers are the crop where ripe and unripe look most alike, because green is a legitimate harvest rather than a mistake. The discriminator is never colour alone - it is size, sheen, firmness and release: fully developed dimensions for the variety, tight glossy skin, firm and crisp under a squeeze, and a pod that detaches easily. An undersized, matte, pliable pod that clings is immature and will taste thin whatever colour it is. And know your variety's mature-green shade before you judge - a pale yellowish-green pod is ready on a Tabasco and unripe on a jalapeno.
pepper-frutescens-variant.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-240 - Growing Chile Peppers in New Mexico Gardens (maturity test, ristra/hang drying); colour-stage progression from KnowThePepper - Pepper Colors Meaning: Ripeness, Heat, and Flavor
pepper-frutescens-variant.caveat: The colour-agnostic maturity test and the drying practice are extension-sourced (NMSU H-240). The stage-by-stage sweetness, texture and capsaicin trend comes from a general pepper colour guide rather than extension, so treat the direction of the trend as reliable and any specific magnitude as approximate. Final ripe colour is deliberately unnamed here - it is variety-specific and not always red.

window.look: fully developed to the variety's size, firm and crisp when squeezed, glossy skin, and it comes off the plant easily - NMSU's test is that most pods can be taken from the plant easily once mature
window.gives: the firmest wall and the sharpest, most vegetal flavour of the whole window; the stage for pickling, green sauce, stuffing and any use where structure matters. Also the highest vitamin C - in habanero it more than halves during ripening (820 down to 349 mg/100g DW)

window.look: colour coming in unevenly, usually starting at the blossom end or on the sun-facing side, before it carries over the shoulders and up under the calyx
window.gives: a real pick point, not a compromise - most of the heat is already there while the wall is still firm. Useful when you need to take fruit off to keep a plant setting

window.look: the variety's own final colour carried evenly over the entire pod including under the calyx, skin taut and not shrivelled, wall just yielding under a thumb. Final colour depends entirely on the variety - red, orange, yellow, brown, or peach are all finished states, so learn the endpoint of what you planted rather than waiting for red
window.gives: the sweetest and generally the hottest stage - measured on habanero, capsaicin rose about a third from green to ripe (3636 to 4820 ug/g), with phenolics up ~39% and flavonoids more than doubled. Best for sauce, drying and roasting; the cost is a softer wall, poorer stuffing texture and lost vitamin C

pepper-superhot-variant.ripe_vs_unripe: The window opens at mature green, so first rule out an immature pod: undersized for the variety, soft or hollow-feeling when squeezed, and clinging to the plant so it resists and risks tearing the branch. For any pepper whose final colour is not red - orange, yellow, peach, brown - the discriminator is evenness, not hue. A ripe pod carries its colour right up under the calyx and over the shoulders, has taut glossy skin with no shrivel, gives very slightly to a thumb, and detaches easily. A pod that is still green in the shoulder shadow or under the calyx is not finished, whatever colour the rest of it is.
pepper-superhot-variant.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-240 - Growing Chile Peppers in New Mexico Gardens (maturity and harvest criteria); Antioxidants 2019, 8(9):364 (measured green vs ripe capsaicinoid, phenolic and vitamin C changes)

pepper-bell-variant.window_label: correct mature green → the variety's final colour

window.look: full size for the variety with shoulders squared and filled out, skin taut and glossy rather than matte, and hard — not springy — when squeezed. A mature fruit breaks easily from the plant, but cut it instead: Illinois Extension notes less damage is done if fruits are cut rather than pulled off, leaving a short stub of stem
window.gives: firmest walls and the best structure of the whole window — the stage for stuffing, frying and freezing in halves. This is a real harvest, not a compromise: Illinois Extension states bells may be harvested green and immature, and picking at green keeps the plant setting new fruit rather than winding down into ripening the load it has (Botanical Interests advises picking in both stages to boost production)

window.look: the first patches or streaks of the variety's ripe colour, typically starting at the blossom end or lingering last in the grooves between lobes and the ring around the stem; the fruit is still hard
window.gives: part of the ripe flavour with the wall still firm, and the plant freed sooner. Illinois Extension notes peppers can be picked at any stage of development, which makes this the honest stop when the season is closing or you want continued set

window.look: the variety's own finish colour carried evenly over the whole fruit, gloss deeper, wall a touch softer under the thumb. The colour is not always red — Illinois lists red, yellow, orange and brown finishes, and warns that white, light yellow, lilac and purple sorts should be harvested before they actually ripen, because those turn red if left
window.gives: the flavour end: Illinois Extension says coloured bells left on the plant develop full flavour and ripen fully, and gain various levels of sweetness depending on the variety, while paler green and yellow tapering types carry more flavour. Do not read ripeness as automatically more nutritious — Antioxidants 2019, 8(9):364 found vitamin C moving in opposite directions between cultivars on ripening (Fresno fell 945 → 366 mg/100 g dry weight while CSU 256 rose 223 → 753). Treat colour as a flavour, texture and use decision, judged per cultivar

pepper-bell-variant.ripe_vs_unripe: The crop-wide confusion is not colour, it is green versus green: a correct mature-green pepper against an undersized immature one. Judge it by size, shape and hardness rather than hue — ready means full size for the variety, blocky or filled out with squared shoulders, skin taut and glossy, hard under a squeeze, and detaching with a clean snap (Illinois: mature fruits break easily from the plant, though cutting does less damage). Immature reads undersized, thinner-walled, green paler and more yellow-toned, surface matte, shoulders giving under thumb pressure. Any pepper picked green on purpose is being picked at a chosen stage of a longer window, not early.

pepper-sweet-variant.window_label: correct mature green → the variety's own final ripe colour

window.look: the pod has stopped lengthening and filled out to the size its variety is described at, the skin is tight and glossy, and — the extension test — the fruit is fully developed, firm and crisp when squeezed. A pod that is still short, thin-walled, or dull-skinned is undersized, not green-ripe
window.gives: the firmest wall and the most structure in the whole window: this is the stage that survives stuffing, frying and grilling without collapsing, and the flavour is at its most vegetal and least sweet

window.look: the green dulls and the variety's ripe colour appears first on the shoulders or as a stripe down one side, while the pod is still firm to the squeeze
window.gives: a partial version of the ripe flavour with most of the green stage's firmness still there — and a reliable signal that the pod is close to finished, so this is the point to start checking it daily rather than weekly

window.look: colour is even over the entire pod with no green left at the shoulder or tucked under the calyx, and the skin is still glossy. Ripe pods release easily — the extension guidance is that most pods can be taken from the plant easily when mature, so a pod that needs a hard tug is not there yet
window.gives: peak sugars and the fullest flavour the variety carries, at the cost of a slightly softer wall and shorter keeping than the green stage. Which colour that is belongs to the variety, not the crop: yellow, gold, orange, brown, purple and red can each be the END of the line, so ripeness is read from evenness, gloss and release — never from reaching red

pepper-sweet-variant.ripe_vs_unripe: Across all peppers, ripeness is read from three things rather than from hue. Evenness: no green left under the calyx or in the lobe creases. Gloss and firmness: ripe skin is bright and taut over a wall that still resists a thumb — dull matte skin means either immature or past prime. Release: a mature pod comes off the plant easily. Size alone is not ripeness (a pod can be full-size and still green-immature) and colour alone is not ripeness (several types finish in a colour that is not red, so a pod holding at yellow, gold or brown may already be done).
pepper-sweet-variant.source: NMSU Extension Guide H-240 — Growing Chile Peppers in New Mexico Gardens
pepper-sweet-variant.caveat: H-240 supplies the maturity test (fruit should be fully developed, firm and crisp when squeezed) and the detachment cue (most pods can be taken from the plant easily if mature). The colour-break stage, the gloss and evenness reads, and the wall/keeping tradeoff at ripe are general pepper behaviour synthesised across the cultivar sources fetched in this run rather than direct quotes from the guide.
